These children were said to be:<ref name=\"DugdaleAOW\"/>\n*Sir John Addurflon, Knt\n*Mary; who  married Sir Richard Herthull, Knt.\n\n=== Military Career===Thomas was knighted by [[Plantagenet-70|King Edward III]] 1 January 1328/9, and given seisin of his lands, though under age, 20 February 1328/9.<ref>''Calendar of Patent Rolls 1330-1334.'' London: H.M. Stationery Office (1893), [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015023267001&seq=64 p. 30].</ref><ref>\"Close Rolls, Edward III: February 1329,\" in Calendar of Close Rolls, Edward III: Volume 1, 1327-1330, ed. H C Maxwell Lyte (London: Her Majesty's Stationery Office, 1896), p. 429 (Feb. 20. Westminster). British History Online, accessed January 19, 2024, http://www.british-history.ac.uk/cal-close-rolls/edw3/vol1/pp427-439.</ref> He also assumed the hereditary positions of Sheriff of Worcestershire and Chamberlain of the Exchequer,<ref name=\"Edmondson37\"/> and in 1333 (although not yet twenty years of age) served in Edward III's campaign in Scotland.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/> He served on a commision to treat for a truce with Scotland in 1335, <ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/> and by 1337 he was appointed commander of the army in the north.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/>\nWarwick participated in most of Edward III's campaigns in France. In 1339 he served in the 3rd division at Vironfosse (in the Aisne), and the following year was in command at Valenciennes.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/><ref name=\"Cok372\"/>  He was also with the king at the siege of Tournai in 1340 and participated in negotiations that led to the truce of Esplechin 25 September 1340.<ref name=\"Cok372\"/> <ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/> Unfortunately the king had great trouble raising enough money to pay for his military campaigns, and Warwick was one of a small group of his most trusted advisors who were imprisoned in Mechelen from September 1340-May 1341 as sureties for the king's repaying his debt to the bankers of Mechelen and Louvain.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/>\nIn 1342 he served as Chief Ambassador to treat with Brabant and Flanders, and Philip de Valois.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/> The following year he was an ambassador to the Pope.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/><ref name=\"Cok373\">Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extinct, or dormant.'' London: St. Catherine Press (1959), [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/579047/?offset=0#page=379&viewer=picture&o=info&n=0&q= vol. 12 (2), p. 373].</ref> He was also present at the siege of Vannes.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/><ref name=\"Cok373\"/>\nIn 1346 he was among the first of the king's army to land at La Hoge, where accompanied by only one esquire and six archers he attacked an enemy force of one hundred Normans, killing sixty of them and making it possible for the rest of the English forces to disembark.<ref name=\"Beltz\"/> He later played a significant role in England's victories at [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cr%C3%A9cy Crécy] and [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Poitiers Poitiers.]<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/><ref name=\"Edmondson37\"/> Warwick gained a reputation as such a fierce warrior that Edward granted him an annuity of 1000 marks a year on condition that he continue to serve the king in war whenever he was needed.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/> \nOn 23 April 1348 he became a founding member of the Most Noble Order of the Garter, coming third in predecence only after the prince of Wales and the Duke of Lancaster.<ref>Shaw, William. ''The Knights of England.'' London: Sherralt and Huges (1906), [https://archive.org/details/knightsofengland01shaw/page/1/mode/1up?view=theater vol. 1, p. 1].</ref>\nIn 1369 he gathered \"some choice troops\" and sailed to Calais to reinforce John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, whose own army was in dire straits and surrounded by an army led by the Duke of Burgundy.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/> So terrifying was his reputation as a \"spirited warrior\" that it is said Burgundy's entire army withdrew under cover of darkness before Warwick's ship landed, to avoid risking an encounter with him.<ref>''Historia Anglicana'', 1.282, cited in Tuck, Anthony. ''Beauchamp, Thomas, eleventh earl of Warwick.'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004, rv. 4 Oct 2008), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/53085 available here] by subscription.</ref><ref name=\"Edmondson38\">Edmondson, Joseph. ''An Historical and Genealogical Account of the Noble Family of Greville.'' London: author (1766), [https://archive.org/details/historicalgeneal00edmo/page/n55/mode/1up p. 38]</ref>\n\n===Other Interests===Warwick's primary interest was in military strategy, he does not appear to have participated in internal political maneuvering in Edward III's court.<ref name=\"ODNBThomas\"/> As his own wealth continued to increase as a result of military successes he proved extremely astute at finding capable and loyal men to administer all of his various estates, which were scattered throughout England.<ref name=\"Barfield\"/> These loyal retainers were in many cases given almost complete autonomy in the day-to-day management of his estates in return for compensation from Warwick, and in some cases the properties were even enfeoffed directly to them in order for Warwick to provide marriage portions for his daughters.<ref name=\"Barfield\"/> He also maintained a network of friendships with neighboring lords, keeping them on close terms and cooperating with them on judicial commissions.<ref name=\"Barfield\"/> From 1344-1369 Warwick served as the sheriff of Warwickshire and Leicestershire.<ref>''Lists of Sheriffs for England and Wales, from the earliest times to A.D. 1831'', Public Record Office Lists and Indexes IX, 1898 (Kraus Reprint Corporation, 1963), [https://archive.org/details/listofsheriffsfo00newy/page/145/mode/1up p. 145].</ref>\nAlthough willing to delegate the management of his lands, Warwick did have an interest in building. He was responsible for rebuilding the walls of Warwick Castle (which had been completely demolished), and strengthening the gates by fortifying them with towers.<ref name=\"Edmondson38\"/> He also built the choir of the collegiate church of St Mary, Warwick, constructed a booth-hall in the market place of Warwick, and made that town toll-free.<ref name=\"Edmondson38\"/>\n\n=== Death and Burial ===Thomas de Beauchamp, 11th earl of Warwick and Marshal of England, died on 13 November 1369 of the plague, at Calais, Pas-de-Calais, Normandy, France.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/><ref name=\"Cok374\"/> He  was buried next to his wife, Katherine, who had died three months earlier on 4 August 1369, in the middle of the quire of the collegiate church at St. Mary's, Warwick.<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/><ref name=\"Cok374\"/><ref name=\"Dugdale234\">Dugdale, Sir William. ''The Baronage of England.'' (1675), [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/a36794.0001.001/247?vid=52914&node=A36794.0001.001:6.53&view=text p. 234].</ref>\n\n=== Will  of Thomas de Beauchamp ===His will, dated 6 September 1369, left bequests to the following individuals:<ref name=\"Test79\">Nicholas, Harris Nicolas. ''Testamenta Vetusta.'' London: Nichols and Son (1826), [https://archive.org/details/testamentavetust01nico/page/79 pp. 79-80]</ref><ref>Dugdale, Sir William. ''The Baronage of England.'' (1675), [https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo/a36794.0001.001/246?vid=52914&node=A36794.0001.001:6.53&view=text pp. 233-234].</ref><ref> Gibbons, Alfred. ''Early Lincoln Wills, 1280��1547'' Lincoln,: James WIlliamson (1888) [https://books.google.com/books?id=uBYRAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA30 Page 30].</ref> his son and heir, Thomas; his daughter [Philippe] de Stafford; his son William; his [as yet unmarried] daughter Isabel; his daughter Margaret (identified as a nun at Shouldham); his granddaughter Katherine ( also a nun at Shouldham and identified as a daughter of his son Guy); his daughter Alice; and his daughter [Maud] de Clifford. Also receiving bequests but whose relationship to Warwick was not stated were: Sir John Beauchamp; Sir Roger Beauchamp; and Sir Guy de Brienne.<ref name=\"Test79\"/>\nExecutors responsible for overseeing the terms of this will were: the earl of Stafford (Warwick's son-in-law); Thomas and William (Warwick's sons); Sir Roger Beauchamp; Sir Sir Guy de Brienne; Sir John Beauchamp; Sir Ralph Basset (Warwick's son-in-law); Sir RIchard Piriton (governor of Northampton); Sir William Forde; Sir Alan Fen; Sir John Blake; Sir John Harwood; Sir William Morton; and John Rous.<ref name=\"Test79\"/> Dugdale identified the last six names, perhaps incorrectly, as all being priests.<ref name=\"Dugdale234\"/> John le Rous was one of his most senior men, whom Warwick had entrusted to oversee the running of a number of his manors in Worchestershire and Gloucestershire, and to whom (sometime before 1363) he granted the legal title to several of those estates.<ref name=\"Barfield\">Barfield, Sebastian.[https://web.archive.org/web/20120717033936/http://users.powernet.co.uk/barfield/chap3.htm ''The Beauchamp Earls of Warwick 1298-1369.''] Thesis, University of Birmingham Department of Medieval History, July 1997.</ref>\nAt the time of his death , Thomas de Beauchamp held a number of castles (including Barnard Castle in Northumberland, Warwick Castle in Warwickshire, and Painscastle, Sweyneseye and Oystremouth Castles in Hereford), numerous manors and advowsons, and lands scattered throughout almost every part of England.<ref name=\"IPMThomas\">M. C. B. Dawes and J. B. W. Chapman. \"Inquisitions Post Mortem, Edward III, File 207,\" in Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem: Volume 12, Edward III, (London: His Majesty's Stationery Office, 1938), 303-314. British History Online, accessed January 23, 2024, http://www.british-history.ac.uk/inquis-post-mortem/vol12/pp303-314.</ref> His heir was his son Thomas.<ref name=\"IPMThomas\"/>\n\n==Research Notes==\n===Tomb===[[Rogers-6236|Alton Rogers]] received an e-mail dated March 25, 2008 from Terry Babbage, parish administrator for St. Mary's, Warwick providing information about the tomb and effigies of Thomas de Beauchamp and his wife Katherine, whose tomb is located in the Chancel of St. Mary's. He also provided a color photo of their tomb.\n\n===Daughter Katherine===*Richardson, probably in error, identified Katherine as \"a nun at Shouldham.\"<ref name=\"MCABeauchamp6\"/> Thomas de Beauchamp's will identifies a Katherine who is a nun at Shouldham as his granddaughter, the daughter of his eldest son Guy.<ref name=\"Test79\"/> \nAt least three other sources identify a Katherine, daughter of Thomas de Beauchamp, as a nun at Wroxhall in Warwickshire.<ref name=\"Edmondson39\"/><ref name=\"Clutterbuck\"/><ref name=\"Baker\"/> A record of 5 June 1375 names a Katherine Beauchamp as prioress of Wrotell.<ref>David C Smith and Vera M London. ''The Heads of Religious Houses England and Wales'', Vol. II, 1216-1377, Cambridge University Press, 2001, p. 625, not viewable online: citing John William Ryland, ''Records of Wroxall Abbey and Manor, Warwickshire'', Spottiswoode and Company, 1903, no. 78, [https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/102670523 Hathi Trust], stated to be public domain in United States but not viewable elsewhere</ref>\nIt is possible that these were two different women, one being Thomas's daughter (at Wroxhall) and one being his granddaughter (at Shouldham).       "notes": "[[Category: Ludlow, Shropshire]] [[Category: Warwick, Warwickshire]] \n== Biography ==\n=== Early Life ==='''Katherine de Mortimer''' was born at Ludlow Castle, Shropshire, as a daughter of [[Mortimer-77|Roger de Mortimer]], 1st Earl of March, and [[Geneville-2|Joan de Geneville]], Baroness Geneville.<ref>Richardson, Douglas, ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families.'' Salt Lake City : Douglas Richardson, 2013. Volume IV, pp 170-172 (see additional notes, [[#Richardson|below]]).</ref>{{Image|file=Amy_Utting_s_Images-5.jpg|align=l|size=160px|caption=Ludlow Castle as depicted in the <br> 18th-century by Samuel Scott, <br> painted between 1765 and 1769.}}\nKatherine’s father, Roger, was a powerful Marcher lord, who served as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland before being imprisoned in the Tower of London for leading the Marcher lords in a revolt against [[Plantagenet-378|King Edward II]]. {{Image|file=Amy_Utting_s_Images-6.jpg|align=r|size=160px|caption=An engraving of <br> the seizure of Roger de Mortimer <br> by [[Plantagenet-70|King Edward III]], produced by <br> Edmund Evans.}} Later escaping to France, Roger began an affair with the King’s wife, the Capetian [[Capet-116|Queen Isabella]], and the pair led a successful invasion of England. The King was captured after he fled to Wales, and forced to abdicate the throne. Roger was the ''de facto'' ruler of England for three years before he himself was overthrown by Edward’s son [[Plantagenet-70|King Edward III]], and executed by hanging at Tyburn in 1330, when Katherine was about sixteen.\n\n=== Marriage and Family ===On 19 April, 1319 a dispensation was issued for the marriage of [[Beauchamp-74|Thomas de Beauchamp]] to one of the daughters of Roger de Mortimer ''\"in order to extinguish the dissension caused by Thomas’s occupation of land in the borders of Wales called 'Ebuel.'\"''<ref name=\"Bliss\">Bliss, William Henry, ''[https://archive.org/details/calendarentries01offigoog/page/n201 Calendar of Entries in the Papal Registers Relating to Great Britain and Ireland].'' London : Eyre and Spottiswoode, 1895. pp 186, 242.</ref> For the term of his minority, Thomas’ custody was granted to Katherine’s father.<ref>Costain, Thomas B., ''[https://archive.org/details/threeedwards00cost/page/236 The Three Edwards].'' New York : Popular Library, 1962. pp 237-238.</ref>\nTogether, Katherine and Thomas had fifteen confirmed children.<ref>Richardson, Douglas, ''Magna Carta Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families, 2nd Edition.'' Salt Lake City : Douglas Richardson, 2011. Volume I, p 142 (see additional notes, [[#Richardson|below]]).</ref> Two other children, [[Beauchamp-230|John]] and [[Beauchamp-232|Hierome]] are part of the Beauchamp family but are unconfirmed as being born to this couple.<ref>Dugdale, William, ''[https://archive.org/details/antiquitiesofwar00dugd/page/320 The Antiquities of Warwickshire Illustrated: From Records, Leiger-Books, Manuscripts, Charters, Evidences, Tombes, and Armes : Beautified with Maps, Prospects, and Portraictures].'' London : Thomas Warren, 1656. p 321.</ref>\n# [[Beauchamp-238|Margaret]]; married [[Montfort-36|Guy de Montfort]], and later became a nun following his death. He was the eldest son, but as he predeceased his father, the title and estates were passed on to their second son.<ref>Warwick, Frances Evelyn Greville, Countess of, ''[https://archive.org/details/warwickcastlean00unkngoog/page/n126 Warwick Castle and its Earls].'' She died childless.\n\n=== Court of King Edward III ===At some point prior to 1355, Katherine became an important figure at the court of King Edward III. As a sign of royal favour she was chosen to stand as one of the godmothers to [[Hainaut-42|Queen Philippa of Hainault]]’s granddaughter [[Plantagenet-90|Philippa]], Countess of Ulster. This honour bestowed upon Katherine is described in the Friar's Genealogy as: \"Her (Philippa, Countess of Ulster) godmother also was of Warwick Countess, a lady likewise of great worthiness.\"<ref>Strickland, Agnes, ''[https://archive.org/details/livesqueensengl54strigoog/page/n414 Lives of the Queens of England from the Norman Conquest: With Anecdotes of the Courts, First Published From Official Records and Other Authentic Documents, Private as Well as Public.]'' Boston : Taggard & Thompson, 1864. Volume I, p 200.</ref>\n\n== Research Notes ==\n=== Katherine’s Date of Marriage ===As mentioned above, a marriage dispensation for Katherine and Thomas in 1319, however they did not marry until after 22 February 1325. We know this because the ''Papal Letters'' describes a dispensation issued on 22 February 1325 for the marriage of Thomas to a daughter of [[FitzAlan-586|Edmund]], Earl of Arundel,<ref name=\"Bliss\"/> and so Thomas and Katherine can't have been married before this date. Ian Mortimer, in his book ''The Greatest Traitor'' (written about Katherine’s father), details a further theory on their marriage:: ''\"Murimuth (p.57) states that at this time where was a double wedding at Hereford in which two of Roger's daughters married two heirs, namely Laurence de Hastings and Edward of Norfolk. This is almost certainly a mistake. It is unlikely that Roger's daughters, Agnes and Beatrice, could have been so advantageously matched before Roger himself was an earl, which did not occur until October 1328. Also it is unlikely that the Earl of Norfolk would have allowed his son and heir to marry Roger's daughter when he was considering rebellion against him, as he was in the summer of 1328.''\n: ''The jousting mentioned by Murimuth in the context of the double wedding is probably the same as the jousting mentioned by Knighton and the longer version of the Brut as a Round Table tournament. The earliest of these sources, the Brut, places this in 1329; Knighton (p.449) seems to have copied Murimuth in having one Hereford event, a Round Table tournament, in 1328 (his copyists in turn have mistaken \"Hereford\" for \"Bedford\" in one manuscript and \"Hertford\" in another).''\n: ''It is likely therefore that there were in fact two Mortimer double weddings, one at Hereford at the end of May 1328, and one in autumn 1329, possibly also at Hereford. If this is correct, the pair of daughters married on the first occasion were Catherine and Joan, not Agnes and Beatrice, whose husbands were granted their lands in February and June 1329 respectively.\"''\nIn a further passage in his book, one which gives a brief summary of the lives of Roger’s children, Mortimer wrote this in the passage for Catherine:: ''\"She was married after October 1326 to Thomas de Beauchamp [...] If there were two Mortimer double weddings at Hereford, one in 1328 and another in 1329, Catherine would have been in the first pair. [...] However, Roger granted these two wards their lands at different times in the first half of 1329, and this might more closely reflect their wedding dates. Thus there is reason to suppose that Catherine was married before February 1329, possibly as part of a double wedding on 31 May 1328.\"''\nHowever, despite this theory, the only definitive date that can be given is that Katherine and Thomas married at some point after 22 February 1325, and so the data fields reflect this.\n\n=== Katherine’s Date of Death ===Katherine wrote her will on 4 August 1369, yet there are several theories about when she actually died. Richardson states that she died on the same day that she wrote her will in ''Royal Ancestry,'' while The Complete Peerage suggests a date between August 4 and September 6; the September date is the date that Thomas made his will, and within it he alludes to his wife being deceased.<ref>Cokayne, George Edward, ''[https://dcms.lds.org/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE6044193 Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain and the United Kingdom].'' London : St Catherine Press, 1959. Volume XII, part II, p 374.</ref>\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />",

Because of this descent, he was a possible heir to the throne of France.\n:: \n:: Inheritance\n:: :: In due course, he inherited the County of Évreux, in Normandy, from his father, and ten years later became Philip III, king consort of Navarre, on the death of his cousin Charles IV of France. Because of their lands and their many royal relatives, Philip and his wife were influential in both France and Navarre and spent much of their lives going back and forth between them.\n:: \n:: Military achievements\n:: :: He participated in the Flemish campaign of Philip VI of France and was at the Battle of Cassel on 23 August 1328, at which the king professed to owe him his victory and his life. In June 1329, he accompanied the king of France to Amiens, where Edward III of England was giving the oath of homage for his French lands.\n:: :: In 1331, he was appointed to the king's council. He went to Avignon with the king to take up the cross from Pope Benedict XII and go on crusade with the kings of Bohemia and Aragon. The crusade was never realised.\n:: :: In 1335, Philip was at war with Aragon.       "notes": "[[Category: House of  Capet]]\n[[Category: Spain, Monarchs]]\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n== Biographie ==\nJeanne de France, fille du roi Louis X et de sa femme Marguerite de Bourgogne, fut reine de Navarre de 1328 à sa mort, et comtesse d'Evreux par mariage.\nJeanne naît le 28 janvier 1311. Elle est le seul enfant de Louis de France, fils aîné de Philippe IV le Bel et futur Louis X, et de sa première femme Marguerite de Bourgogne.\nTrois ans après sa naissance éclate le scandale de la Tour de Nesle: sa mère accusée d'adultère est emprisonnée à Château-Gaillard (Les Andelys, actuel département de l'Eure) où elle meurt en 1315 dans des circonstances suspectes. Son père, devenu le roi de France Louis X, se remarie avec Clémence de Hongrie mais meurt le 5 juin 1316 laissant sa femme enceinte. Leur fils Jean Ier le Posthume, naît en novembre 1316 mais meurt cinq jours plus tard. C'est le frère cadet de Louis X, Philippe, comte de Poitiers, qui devient roi de France sous le nom de Philippe V.\nJeanne récupère finalement la couronne de Navarre en 1328, après la mort de ses deux oncles Philippe V et Charles IV, le nouveau roi Philippe VI n'étant pas descendant des rois de Navarre. En revanche les domaines de Champagne et de Brie, qui venaient comme la Navarre de sa grand-mère Jeanne I de Champagne-Navarre (première femme de Philippe le Bel) sont définitivement rattachés au domaine royal.\nJeanne est mariée, par contrat du 18 juin 1318, à Philippe d'Evreux, fils de Charles, comte d'Evreux et frère cadet du roi Philippe le Bel. Ils ont huit enfants:# Jeanne (1325 – 3 juillet 1387), promise en 1329 à l'infant Pierre d'Aragon, devient religieuse à l'abbaye de Longchamp (c'est sa soeur Marie qui épousera Pierre d'Aragon)\n# Marie (1330 – 1347), mariée en 1338 à Pierre IV d'Aragon# Charles II le Mauvais (1332 – 1387), comte d'Évreux et roi de Navarre# Blanche (1333 – 1398), mariée en 1349 à Philippe VI de Valois, roi de France ;# Agnès (1334 – 1396), mariée en 1349 à Gaston III Fébus, comte de Foix et vicomte de Béarn\n# Philippe de Navarre (1336 – 1363), comte de Longueville ;# autre Jeanne (1339 – 1403), mariée en 1377 à Jean Ier, vicomte de Rohan# Louis de Navarre (1341 – 1376 en Albanie), comte de Beaumont-le-Roger.\nElle meurt en 1648 à Conflans et est inhumée à la basilique de Saint-Denis<ref>Contributeurs de Wikipédia, \"Jeanne II de Navarre,\" Wikipédia, l'encyclopédie libre, http://fr.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeanne_II_de_Navarre&oldid=139503820 (Page consultée le 22 août 2017).</ref>.\n\n\n== Biography ==: Reine de Navarre (1328-1349), Fue Reina de Navarra entre 1328 y 1349.\n::\n:: \n:: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\n:: :: Joan II of Navarre (January 28, 1312 ? October 6, 1349) was Queen of Navarre 1328?1349. She was the only daughter of King Louis X of France (Louis I of Navarre) and his first wife, Margaret of Burgundy. She was a member of the House of Capet.\n:: :: On the deaths of her father (1316) and her half-brother, John I (also 1316), both of whom had been kings of France and Navarre, she was excluded from the succession in favor of her uncle Philip V of France(Philip II of Navarre), abrother of Louis X and son of Philip IV of France. Philip V prevailed for a number of reasons, including her youth, doubts raised about her paternity, and the Estates-General's determination that women should not be allowed to rule France. The last reason, however, was not applicable to Navarre because there was already precedent there for succession by a female. After Philip V's brother and successor Charles IV of France (Charles I of Navarre) died in 1328, there was no male heir to either crown in the direct line from Philip IV. Instead, a more distant Philip, a descendant of Philip IV's younger brother Charles of Valois, successfully claimed the throne as Philip VI of France inpreference to Joan and a number of other females closer to the line of succession.\n:: :: Joan did become Queen of Navarre through a treaty with Philip VI, who was not a descendant of the later Kings of Navarre through Garcia Ramírez of Navarre and who could not invoke a rule against female succession in Navarre. In the treaty, she had to renounce her claims not only to the crown of France but also to her grandmother's estates in Brie and Champagne (which were merged in the French royal domain). In compensation, she received the counties of Angoulême and Mortain as well as a portion of Cotentin (Longueville). Later on she exchanged Angouleme for three estates in Vexin:- Pontoise, Beaumont-sur-Oise, and Asnière-sur-Oise.\n:: :: She reigned as Queen of Navarre until her death in 1349, together with her husband, Philip III of Navarre as king consort, 1329?1343. Philip was also Count of Évreux, the heir of Count Louis of Évreux (youngest son of Philip III of France), and thus of Capetian male blood. Because of his patrimonial lands, together with Joan's gains in Normandy and her rights in Champagne, the couple had extensive possessions in Northern France.\n:: :: Altogether, Joan and Philip had eight children. She was succeeded by their son Charles II of Navarre. Their daughter Blanche d'Evreux became the second wife of Philip VI of France.\n:: :: Although Joan never ascended the French throne, her descendants and heirs, the Kings of Navarre, were to eventually reach the throne of France when Henry IV of France inherited the crown two centuries later, in 1589. From then onwards, all Kings of France carried Joan's blood and were her heirs. The Kings of France had already been descended from her since the ascension of Henry II (who was Joan's issue in 8th generation, through for example his maternal great-grandmother Margaret of Foix-Navarre, duchess consort of Brittany, and through Margaret's husband's great-grandmother Joan of Navarre, queen of England and also duchess consort of Brittany, who herself was Joan's granddaughter); these were not, however, senior descendants of Joan.\n:: \n: Children\n:: :: Maria of Navarre (c. 1329?1347), first wife of King Pedro IV of Aragon (1319?1387).\n:: :: Blanche d?Évreux (1331?1398), second wife of the much older King Philip VI of France (1293?1350).\n:: :: Charles II of Navarre (1332?1387), King of Navarre, known as Charles le Mauvais, i.e. Charles the Bad.\n:: \n:: Agnès (1334?1396), married Gaston III, Count of Foix (1331?1391).\n:: :: Philip, Count of Longueville (1336?1363), married Yolande de Dampierre (1331?1395.\n:: :: Joanna of Navarre (1339?1403), married John I, Viscount of Rohan (d. 1395).\n:: :: Louis, Count of Beaumont-le-Roger (1341?1372), married 1358 Maria de Lizarazu, married 1366 Joanna of Durazzo (1344?1387)\n\n==Sources==\n<references />\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. III p. 35'''\n18 Jun 1318\n\n====Acknowledgements====* This person was created through the import of Acrossthepond.ged on 21 February 2011.  * WikiTree profile De France-129 created through the import of export-BloodTree.ged on Aug 19, 2011 by [[Heinzelmann-4 | Luiz Sergio Heinzelmann]]. \n* created through the import of Bwiki.ged on 03 April 2011.\n<!-- Please edit, add, or delete anything in this text, including this note.       "notes": "=== Eleanor of Anjou, Queen of Sicily ===\n'''Eleanor of Naples''' (August 1289 – 9 August 1341) was the Queen consort of Frederick III of Sicily. She was a member of the Capetian House of Anjou by birth.\nShe was the third daughter of Charles II of Naples and Mary of Hungary.\nEleanor was firstly married in 1299 to Philip de Toucy, son of Narjot de Toucy and Lucia of Tripoli. Their marriage was dissolved on 17 January 1300 because they were related and had not sought permission from the pope to marry.[1]\nOn 17 May 1302, Eleanor married secondly to Frederick III of Sicily. Her father and her new husband had been engaged in a war for ascendancy in the Mediterranean Sea and especially Sicily and the Mezzogiorno. The marriage was part of a diplomatic effort to establish peaceful relations which would lead to the Peace of Caltabellotta (19 August 1302).\nThe peace divided the old Kingdom of Sicily into an island portion and a peninsular portion. The island, called the Kingdom of Trinacria, went to Frederick, who had been ruling it, and the Mezzogiorno, called the Kingdom of Sicily contemporaneously, but called the Kingdom of Naples by modern scholarship, went to Charles II, who had been ruling it. Thus, the peace was formal recognition of an uneasy status quo.\n\nEleanor and Frederick had nine children:\n\n* Peter II of Sicily (1304–1342), successor\n* Roger (born 1305), died young* Manfred, Duke of Athens and Neopatria (1306–1317), Duke of Athens and Neopatria\n* Constance, married on December 29, 1331 to Leo IV of Armenia* Elisabeth (1310–1349), married (1328) Stephen II of Bavaria (also known as Isabella)* William, Prince of Taranto (1312–1338), Prince of Taranto, Duke of Athens and Neopatria* Giovanni di Randazzo (1317–1348), Duke of Randazzo, Duke of Athens and Neopatria, Regent of Sicily (from 1338)\n* Catherine (1320–1342)\n* Margaret (1331–1360), married (1348) Rudolf II of the Palatinate\nEleanor died on the 9 August 1341 at the Monastery of San Nicolo di Arena, she had been a widow since 1337.       "notes": "[[Category:EuroAristo_-_Profiles_that_need_work]]\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n== Biography ==\nMatteo was born on 15 Aug 1250 in Milan, Italy. In August, 1269, Matteo married Bonacossa Borri, daughter of Captain Squarcina Borri. They had ten children together. Their sixth child was Stefano, our ancestor.\nMatteo was a soldier and faithful servant of his great-uncle Ottone in his battles and conquest of power over Milan. It was Ottone who wrested control of Milan from the rival Della Torre family and established the Visconti as Lords of Milan in 1277. \n In December 1287, when Matteo was 37 years old, his great-uncle Ottone appointed him capitano del popolo (\"Captain of the People\") of Milan.  The King of Germany appointed  Matteo as Imperial Vicar over the whole of Lombardy, an office he held until his death. His sphere of influence extended to the Piedmont, Emilia, Bologna, and Genoa.\nFor many years, Matteo and Torriani struggled for the lordship of Milan which went back and forth between them. In November 1310, Matteo met the German King Henry VII at Asti and from this, received a mandate to reach a peace agreement in Lombardy. On December 4 of that year, Matteo and the archbishop Cassono della Torre signed an agreement, under which the Visconti and Torriani families shared official positions and expenses.\nIn 1313, the clashes began anew. Alternating defeats and victories continued.\n In January1321, Matteo's wife, Bonacosa Borri died. In December, the Pope asked the Archbishop of Milan, to open another case of heresy against Matteo and his son, Galeazzo.\nAt the end of May 1322 , Matteo ceded power to his son Galeazzo and retired to Crescenzago.  Matteo died on 24 Jun 1322 in Milan, Italy at the age of 71.\n\n== Sources ==\n\n\n\n== Occupation ==\n Occupation:  Signore di Milano\n\n\n== Note == Ancestor of Bartholomew Hoskins (Nancy Haile), of Haute Wyatt (Margaret Ellen Parker) and of Sarah Covell, Mrs William Nickerson (Frederick Augustus Otte).\n George L Williams, Papal Dynasties, p 216, says this man had a nephew Vercellino, who was a cousin of the Pope.       "notes": "{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n== Amédée VI de Savoie ==\nAmédée VI de Savoie, dit le Comte Vert, né le 4 janvier 1334 à Chambéry, mort de la peste à Campobasso le 1er mars 1383, est comte de Savoie, d'Aoste et de Maurienne de 1343 à 1383. Il est ainsi surnomm�� en raison d'une armure et d'une livrée de couleur verte qu'il porta lors d'un tournoi à Chambéry.\n\n=== Autres langues ===\n*[http://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadeus_VI._(Savoyen)[Deutsch]]\n*[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadeus_VI,_Count_of_Savoy[English]]\n*[http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadeo_VI_de_Saboya[Español]]\n*[http://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadeu_VI,_Conde_de_Saboia[Português]]\n\n=== Biographie ===\nIl était fils d'Aymon le Pacifique, comte de Savoie, d'Aoste et de Maurienne, et de Yolande de Montferrat.\nIl acquiert en 1355, par le traité de Paris, la province du Faucigny et signe la même année un traité avec la France qui fixe la fronti��re entre la Savoie et le Dauphiné. Il fonde en 1362 l'Ordre du Collier de Savoie qui deviendra l'Ordre de chevalerie de l'Annonciade.\nEn 1365, Amédée VI réussit à obtenir le titre de « vicaire perpétuel et héréditaire de l’Empire dans l’ancien royaume d’Arles » des mains de Charles IV du Saint-Empire de passage à Chambéry, lui permettant d'exiger l'hommage des évêques de Tarentaise, Maurienne, Belley, Sion et Genève, même si ce dernier se déroba vite.\nIl combattit son cousin Jacques, prince de Piémont avant de parvenir à un accord en 1357, qu'il impose par ailleurs au fils et successeur de ce dernier.\nAmédée VI combattit également les marquis de Salucces et de Montferrat. Guerrier, il passa les mers en 1366 pour secourir son cousin Jean V Paléologue, empereur de Constantinople, triomphant des Bulgares et arrêta pour un temps à Gallipoli, sur les Dardanelles, la marche des Turcs. Amédée VI s'engagea dans une campagne napolitaine où il mourut en 1382-1383.\nIl avait donc fondé l'Ordre de l'Annonciade, avec 12 chevaliers. Il institua à la forteresse de Pierre Chatel, dans l'Ain actuel, face à Aix, une Chartreuse avec douze pères chargés de la prière perpétuelle dans le temps où les chevaliers partaient guerroyer contre les Turcs en méditerranée.\nOn dit que le comte Amédée VI de Savoie avait adopté la couleur verte en signe d'errance tant que la compagnie des chevaliers n'aurait été complète. Le vert est bien la couleur traditionnelle des chevaliers errants. Par ailleurs avant cette institution de l'Annonciade, le comte était dit « ferré », c'est-à-dire qu'il portait un anneau de fer entourant sa cuisse, toujours selon la tradition de la chevalerie errante.\nAmédée VI et ses chevaliers incarnaient très certainement le plus bel idéal de chevalerie en un temps où celle-ci se mourait.\n\n=== Union et postérité ===\nIl épouse en 1355 Bonne de Bourbon, fille de Pierre Ier, duc de Bourbon et d'Isabelle de Valois. Par sa mère, Bonne de Bourbon est nièce du roi Philippe VI de Valois. Elle a une sœur mariée au roi Charles V. De cette union sont connus trois enfants :\n*une fille mort-née en 1358\n*Amédée VII de Savoie, dit le Comte Rouge, marié à Bonne de Berry\n*Louis (1362 † 1365)\n\n=== Homage ===\nLa Place du Comte Vert à Monthey en Suisse témoigne de l'importance qu'a eu la maison de Savoie sur le Chablais.\n\n=== Références ===\n→ : ouvrage ou article utilisé comme source pour la rédaction de cet article*Louis Charles Dezobry et Théodore Bachelet, Dictionnaire de Biographie et d’Histoire, Paris, 1863 [http://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9f%C3%A9rence:Dictionnaire_de_Biographie_et_d%27Histoire_(Dezobry_et_Bachelet)[détail de l’édition]].\n\n=== Bibliographie ===\n* [Demotz 2000] Bernard Demotz, Le comté de Savoie du XIe au xve siècle : Pouvoir, château et État au Moyen Âge, Genève, Slatkine, 2000, 496 p. Fino alla maggiore età le redini della contea furono rette dai cugini Luigi II di Vaud e Amedeo III di Ginevra. Giovane scaltro ed intraprendente, Amedeo VI partecipò in gioventù a numerosi tornei, nei quali era solito sfoggiare armi e vessilli di colore verde, tanto che venne appunto soprannominato Il Conte Verde. Era semplice per i sudditi riconoscere il loro conte: anche quando salì al trono, continuò a vestirsi con quel colore.\n\n...\nAmedeo sposò nel 1355 Bona di Borbone (1341 – 1403), figlia di Pietro I di Borbone e di Isabella di Valois,[2] donna energica e capace, che resse lo stato nei lunghi periodi in cui il marito si assentava per le guerre, che videro i Savoia improntarsi specialmente in Italia: Umberto II di Borgogna aveva infatti ceduto il Delfinato di Vienne, che i Savoia cercavano da tempo di conquistare, alla Francia, avversario davvero troppo potente.\n\n...\n\nDalla moglie Bona Amedeo ebbe:\n\n*    una figlia deceduta appena nata nel 1358;\n*    Amedeo, suo successore;\n*    Luigi (1362 † 1365).\n\nEgli ebbe inoltre un figlio naturale, Antonio, morto nel 1374.\n''in: Wikipedia, l'enciclopedia libera(http://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amedeo_VI_di_Savoia : accessed 20 Feb 2013)''",

Elle épousa Raoul (1320 ? 1346), duc de Lorraine, et eut :\n:: \n:: 1) deux filles jumelles, nées et mortes en 1343.\n:: \n:: 2) Jean Ier (1346 ? 1390), duc de Lorraine\n:: :: A la mort de son mari, elle fut régente du duché jusqu'en 1353. A partir de la fin de l'année 1347, elle entame un conflit avec Adhémar de Monteil, évêque de Metz, qui durera dix ans, entrecoupés de trêves. Elle a des relations debon voisinage avec Yolande de Flandre, comtesse régente de Bar, signe avec elle deux traités de paix, en 1347 et le 8 novembre 1348. Mais la paix est rompue en 1350 et Marie de Châtillon, Jean, comte de Salm et Waléran, comte de Deux-Ponts, pénètrent dans le Barrois et le ravagent. Yolande et l'évêque de Metz, en représailles, ravagent les environs de Nancy. Il a fallu la médiation du pape Clément VI et l'intervention du roi Jean II le Bon pour ramener lapaix en 1352.\n:: :: Marie se remaria vers la fin de 1352 avec un noble lorrain, Ferry, comte de Linange. Conformément au testament de son mari, elle dut alors partager la régence avec le comte Eberhard II de Wurtemberg.\n\nShe is buried at Clairlieu Abbey.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />* Jacqueline Carolus-Curien, Poor Duchesses: Behind the Scenes at the Court of Lorraine, Serpenoise, 2007* F.       "notes": "== Biography ==Anseau de Joinville was born in 1265 at the family's chateau near Joinville, Champagne, France.  He was the 4th son of [[Joinville-1 | Jean de Joinville]] (1224 - 24 December 1317).  Jean de Joinville, of the French aristocracy, was a companion and biographer of French King Louis IX (1214 - 1270) and instrumental in seeing the deceased monarch canonized by the Roman Catholic Church in 1297, only 27 years after his death in Moslem-ruled Tunis during the 2nd part of the 7th Crusade.  Anseau's mother was Alix de Reynel, from Champagne.  \nAnseau de Joinville was named Seigneur de Rimaucourt in Champagne, when he married his 1st wife,  Laure de Sarrebruck, daughter of Simon IV de Sarrebruck-Commercy, seigneur de Commercy, and of Mathilde de Sexefontaine, in 1302.  He inherited Reynal on the death of his older brother in 1304.  His father lived until 1317 so it was not until that late date that he became \"Sire de Joinville,\" the family's seat in the royal province of Champagne.  \nAnseau, like his father before him, was a close and loyal counselor (courtier) of the Capetian Kings of France.  In 1316 on the death of King Louis X who had no male heir, Anseau de Joinville supported the cause of Philip of Poitiers, who became King Philip V \"the Long\" that year and then reigned for six years.  Anseau joined his \"Privy Council\".   Out of favor under Philip V's successor, Charles IV \"the Handsome,\" (1322-1328), he returned to the Privy Council when Phillipe de Valois, 1st of the Valois line, took the French throne in 1328.  \nNamed \"Sénéchal [Royal Governor] de Champagne,\" by King Philip VI, Anseau de Joinville played a large role in reinforcing the kingdom's defenses, especially in the East in the face of the Germanic Holy Roman Empire, during the preparation period before the start in 1337 of the Hundred Years' War against England, then master of nearly the western third of today's France and especially Normandy and Aquitaine.  He also worked to strengthen the monarchy's finances.  In 1338 he was named one of the Presidents of the \"Cour des Comptes\" by the king.  He acquitted himself with loyalty and thrift, avoiding personal indebtedness or significant personal gain while serving the kingdom.  Finally, in 1339, King Philippe V, in recognition of his exemplary, longstanding service, appointed Anseau, Sire de Joinville, as a \"maréchal de France\" [military Marshal of France].   He passed away a few years later, on 3 January  1343, at his home in Joinville, Champagne.  He was just short of 80 years old.<ref> [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/chamdampjo.htm#HenriJoinvilledied1365 Anseau de Joinville on Medieval Lands] </ref> \n\n== Sources ==\n<references />* Medieval Lands. http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/chamdampjo.htm#AnseauJoinvilledied1342\n* {{wikidata|Q179085}}\n* http://genealogy.euweb.cz/luxemburg/luxemburg5.html",

      "notes": "==Biography==\n=== Charles II d'Alençon ===\n\n'''Autres langues'''\n*[http://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_II._(Alen%C3%A7on)[Deutsch]]*[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II,_Count_of_Alen%C3%A7on[English]]\n*[http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_II_de_Alen%C3%A7on[Español]]\nCharles II d'Alençon<sup>1</sup>  dit Charles II le Magnanime, né en 1297, mort le 26 août 1346, est le deuxième fils de Charles, comte de Valois, et de Marguerite d'Anjou, et donc frère du roi de France Philippe VI de Valois. Il est comte de Chartres, du Perche et d'Alençon.\n\n'''Biographie'''\nIl fait ses premières armes en Guyenne sous les ordres de son père et montre à son premier siège un grand courage qu'il poussa jusqu'à une aveugle témérité (1324).\nÀ la mort de son père, le 16 décembre 1325, il reçoit le comté de Chartres, les terres de Champrond, Châteauneuf-en-Thymerais et Senonches, ainsi que la forêt de Perche, conformément à un accord de partage fait par son père le 20 mai 1314. Puis son frère aîné Philippe lui remet en avril 1326 le comté d'Alençon.\nIl prit part à la bataille de Cassel (1328), la prise de Saintes (1330). Son frère Philippe devient roi de France en 1328, mais le roi d'Angleterre Édouard III revendique la couronne et refuse l'hommage. Philippe VI le nomme lieutenant général du royaume et l'envoie mater une rébellion à Saintes, suscité par les Anglais, et s'empare de plusieurs places fortes, dont Saintes.\nIl intervint ensuite en 1339 à Cambrai et en 1340 à Tournai. Le duc Jean III de Bretagne meurt en 1341 et la guerre de succession de Bretagne éclate entre sa nièce Jeanne de Penthièvre, soutenu par les Français, et Jean de Monfort, soutenu par les Anglais. Philippe VI lui donne l'Aigle qu'il a confisqué à Jean de Montfort.\nIl prend part à la bataille de Crécy (26 août 1346), où il commande l'avant-garde et y est tué.\n\n'''Mariages et enfants'''\nEn avril 1314, il épouse Jeanne, comtesse de Joigny, qui meurt le 24 septembre 1336, sans postérité.\nEn décembre 1336, il épouse en secondes noces Marie de La Cerda (v. 1319-19/11/1379) dite Marie d’Espagne, dame de Lunel, fille de Ferdinand de Castille (1275-1322), seigneur de La Cerda, et de Juana Núñez dite « la Palomilla » (1286-1351), dame de Lara. Marie de La Cerda était veuve en premières noces de Charles d'Évreux (1305-1336), comte d'Étampes. On connaît au moins six enfants issus de l'union de Charles d'Alençon et de Marie de La Cerda :\n*    Charles III d'Alençon (1337 † 1375), comte d'Alençon, puis archevêque de Lyon*    Philippe d'Alençon (1339 † 1397), élu évêque de Beauvais mais il ne fut pas consacré, archevêque de Rouen, puis cardinal.*    Pierre II le Noble († 1404), comte d'Alençon, du Perche et de Porhoët*    Isabelle († Poissy, 3 septembre 1379), nonne au prieuré de Saint-Louis à Poissy ;*    Robert († 1377), comte de Perche qui épouse Jeanne de Rohan en 1374, d'où un fils : Charles (+ jeune, avant son père) ;\n*    Isabelle (née posthume, ap. 26 août 1346).\n\n'''Bibliographie'''\n*    Patrick Van Kerrebrouck, Nouvelle histoire généalogique de l'auguste maison de France, vol. 3 : Les Valois, Patrick van Kerrebrouck, 1990 [détail de l’édition], p. 412-5*    Georges d'Heylli, Les tombres royales de Saint-Denis - Histoire et nomenclatures des tombeaux, extraction des cercueils royaux en 1793 - Ce qu'ils contenaient - Les Prussiens dans la basilique en 1871, édition de 1872.\n\n\n==Sources==\n<references />\n'''Notes et références'''#    ↑ Généalogie de Charles II d'Alençon sur le site Medieval Lands [http://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/?url=http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/CAPET.htm#CharlesValoisAlencondied1346B&title=G%C3%A9n%C3%A9alogie%20de%20Charles%20II%20d%27Alen%C3%A7on%20sur%20le%20site%20Medieval%20Lands[archive]]\n*''Wikipédia: Charles II d'Alençon (http://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_d%27Alen%C3%A7on : accessed 04 jul 2013)''",

      "notes": "[[Category: France, Needs Biography]]\n== Biography == \n:: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\n:: :: Charles of Blois (Blois, 1319 ? September 29, 1364), claimed the title duke of Brittany, from 1341 to his death.\n:: :: Charles is the son of Guy I of Blois-Châtillon, count of Blois, by Margaret of Valois, a sister of king Philip VI of France. He was a devout man, who took piety to the extreme of mortifying his own flesh. It is said that he placedpebbles in his shoes, wore ropes tight with knots near his flesh and confessed every night in fear of sleeping in a state of sin. He was nevertheless an accomplished military leader, who inspired loyalty by his religious fervour.\n:: :: On June 4, 1337 in Paris, he married Joanna the Lame, heiress and niece of duke John III. Together, Charles and Joanna fought the House of Montfort in the Breton War of Succession (1341-1364), with the support of the crown of France. Despite his piety, Charles did not hesitate in ordering the massacre of 2000 civilians after the siege of Quimper. After initial successes, Charles was taken prisoner by the English in 1347. He was released nine years afterwards against a ransom of about half a million ecús, and resumed the war against the Montforts.\n:: :: Charles died in the Battle of Auray which determined the end of the war and the victory of the Montforts. He was canonized as saint for his devotion to religion, but the process was made null by Pope Gregory XI by request of Duke John V of Brittany. Subsequently, in 1904, he was beatified.\n:: \n:: By his marriage to Joanna, he had five children:\n:: \n:: John I of Blois-Châtillon (1340?1404)\n:: \n:: Guy\n:: \n:: Henry (d. 1400)\n:: \n:: Marie (1345-1404), Lady of Guise, married in 1360 Louis I of Naples\n:: \n:: Marguerite, married in 1351 Charles de la Cerda (d. 1354)\n1373: King Edward III's praecipe directed [[Legge-318|John Legge]] and [[Weston-792|William de Weston]], to receive from [[Beauchamp-203|Roger de Beauchamp]], Constable of the castle of Devizes, the two sons of [[Blois-71|Charles de Blois]], and to deliver them to [[Morton-175|Robert de Morton]], Lieutenant of Collard de Aubrichecourt, Constable of Nottingham Castle, there to remain as hostages , till the pretensions to the duchy of Britany should be cleared<ref name=Woodfall>[https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=uWZUAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA300 Woodfall's Peerage of England]</ref>.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n== Acknowledgements ==This page has been edited according to [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Acknowledgements Style Standards] adopted January 2014.       "notes": "[[Category: House of Valois]]\n== Biography ==\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n Robert I, duc de Bar, Count of Bar, 1352-1354, Duke of Bar, 1354 - Apr. 12, 1411.  Count of Bar 1352 - 1354, Marquis of Pont-à-Mousson, Marquis of Pont-a-Mousson and Count and then Duke of the Duchy of Bar. \nRobert I de Bar, born on August 27, 1342, died April 12, 1411, was the Count of Bar (1352 to 1354), Marquis de Pont-a-Mousson (after 1354) and Duke of Bar 1354 to 1411.\nA question of precedence led to the county of Bar being raised to a Duchy.   When Pont-à Mousson was promoted to a margravate the acts mentioned its ruler, Robert de Bar, as marquis of Pont-à Mousson and count of Bar.  For the nobles Bar, this was illogical, since to the Comté de Bar was territorially much larger and more important than that of the newly-named Margravate of Pont-à-Mousson. To resolve this anomaly, Holy Roman Emperor, Charles IV de Luxembourg promoted the Comté de Bar into the Duché de Bar.\nRobert was the youngest son of Henri IV, Count of Bar, and Yolande de Flandres.\n He was less than one year old when his father died and his older brother Edward II, became Count of Bar under the regency of their mother.  As the two brothers were of weak constitution, Yolande asked and obtained from Pope ClementVI for both,  permission to eat meat during periods of abstinence.\n When his brother died, Robert was only seven years old, and the problem of regency arose differently than seven years before as his mother was about to remarry with Philippe de Navarre, Count de Longueville, the family of Navarre challenging the claim to monarchy of King Jean le Bon. On the other hand, Jeanne de Bar (1295 to 1361), Countess of Warren, daughter of Count Henri III, told the king that she was ready to assume the regency. The parliament of Paris, by judgementof June 5, 1352 decided that the Barrois was in the hand of the king, who entrusted the regency to Jeanne Bar on July 27, 1352. Yolande Flandres, who had originally renounced the regency, changed her mind and raised troops to combat Jeanne de Bar's claim.  French King Jean le Bon had to intervene and forced Yolande to renounce on July 2, 1353.\n  The French defeat by the English at Poitiers (1356) deprived Jeanne de Bar of the support of the king, who had been taken prisoner. Yolande resumed the regency and Robert was made an armed knight in December 1356 at just 12 years old.\n He was declared an adult at 15 on November 8, 1359.  He later attended the coronation of French King Charles V in Reims on May 19, 1364.  He also attended the coronation of King Charles VI on November 4, 1380.  During the reign of Charles V, he had participated in 1374 in several military expeditions that were intended to drive the English from Normandy.\n In 1401, Robert duc de Bar gave the Duchy to his son Edward, while keeping its usufruct, dismissing his grand-son Robert, son of Count Henri de Marle. The last attempt to oppose a trial by the Parliament of Paris, which lasted from 1406 to 1409, but without success.\n  The folly of Charles VI is taken to the Duke of Orleans Louis with the Duke of Burgundy Jean without Fear. Robert supports the Duke of Orleans, but after the assassination of the latter, is increasingly in the duchy of crises because of gout which prevented him from walking.\n:: He married in 1364 Marie de France (1344 to 1404), daughter of Jean le Bon, King of France, and Bonne of Luxembourg, and had 11 children:#Yolande, (1365 to 1431), married in 1380 to John I of Aragon (1350 to 1396)\n#Henri (1362 to 1397), Lord of Marle\n#Philippe (1372  to 1396), also killed at Nicopolis\n#Charles (1373 to 1392), Lord of Nogent-le-Rotrou#Marie (1374 - ?), married in 1384 Wilhelm II, Margrave of Namur (1355 ? 1418)\n#Edward III (? to 1415), Duke Bar, killed at the Battle of Agincourt\n#Louis (? to 1431), bishop of Verdun, cardinal.#Yolande la Jeune, (? to 1421), married to Adolphe Duke of Juliers and Berg (? 1437)# Jean de Bar, Lord of Puisaye (1380 to 1415), Lord of Puisaye, killed at the Battle of Azincourt, Artois, France: 25 Oct. 1415. #Bonne (d: 1400), married in 1393 to Waleran III de Luxembourg-Ligny (1357 to Feb. 1415), Count of Ligny-en-Barrois and Saint-Pol#Jeanne (? 1402); married in 1393 to Theodore II Paleologus, Marquis de Montferrat (1361 ? 1418)\nRobert I, duc de Bar, died at his capital of Bar-le-Duc, now in the French department \"Meuse,\" and was buried at the Collegial Church of Saint Maxe.  \n \nPVD's third cousin 17 times removed.\n \n== Sources ==\n\n<references />* [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_I_of_Bar Robert I of Bar article on Wikipedia] \n* [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BAR.htm#RobertIdied1411A Robert de Bar on Medieval Lands] * [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLISH%20NOBILITY%20MEDIEVAL1.htm#JohnFitzGeoffreydied1258 John fitz Geoffrey], entry in the database <span id='MedLands'>[http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/CONTENTS.htm Medieval Lands]: A prosopography of medieval European noble and royal families by Charles Cawley © Foundation for Medieval Genealogy, 2000-2017.",

Other candidates for this were Otto van Arkel and Dirk van Hoorne, lord of Perwijs. Otto lost this one as Albrecht rules in favor of Adolf.<ref>AGH 427, fol. 378; Nijhoff, Geschiedenis Gelderland II, p. CV en Kastner, Territorialpolitik, p. 197.</ref><ref>Gelders Archief [https://permalink.geldersarchief.nl/68A3E5293DA8457B9AA34734355D2010 Charter 1412] ''Adolf van Wylaick, ambtman in de Netter, zweert het verbond tussen hertog Reinoud IV, Adolf, graaf van Kleef en Mark en (Willem van Arkel) gesloten, te onderhouden.</ref>  To compensate, Otto received a few lease properties in Kleef that belonged to Utrecht and Koln.<ref>S.Muller Fz., 'De Registers en Rekeningen van het bisdom Utrecht II', Werken Historisch Genootschap, Nieuwe Serie 54 ('s-Gravenhage 1891), p. 708 en Lacomblet, Urkundenbuch, p. 785, nr. 892.</ref>\n\n{{Image\n|file=Van_Arkel-24-1.jpg\n|align=c\n|size=300\n|caption=Seal Otto van Arkel, 1379\n}}  Otto van Arkel wrote in charters in 1382 about his cities Gorinchem, Leerdam, Gasperden, Hagestein and Dalem.<ref>Bruch, Rechtsbronnen, p. 25-38 en A.C.N. van Koenheim, 'Stadsrechtverlening van Hagestein in 1382', In het Land van Brederode 7 (1982), p. 10-28.</ref><ref>Utrechts Archief [https://hetutrechtsarchief.nl/collectie/609C5C98098D4642E0534701000A17FD Charter 1382] ''Akte door Otto, heer van Arkel, houdende handvest voor de stad Gorinchem, 1382. Afschrift. </ref> As Otto expanded his territory, the lord of Vianen started to feel threatened, as his property boarders the Arkel area. This resulted in conflicts that ended in battles/cease-fires in the period 1387-1392. In 1392 the Count of Holland and Duke of Gelre intervened and a peace agreement was made that lasted until 1401. From the 1392 peace agreement in shows Otto and his son Jan were supported by theor family: Jan van Rijnenstein, Jan van Heukelom, Hendrik van Heukelom, Otto van Heukelom, Arent van Leyenburch and Roelof van Dalem.<ref>Waale, De Arkelse oorlog, p. 46.</ref><ref>Utrechts Archief [https://hetutrechtsarchief.nl/collectie/81C59872CFB320A5E053CA00A8C012A0 Charter 1392] ''Bisschop Florens staat toe, dat de stad Utrecht, ter voldoening der kosten, door haar gemaakt in den oorlog van Montfoerde, eene som van 7000 guldens ter waarde van die, welke hij onlangs te Rhenen had doen slaan, zal innen uit de morgengelden, huisgelden, maaggelden, [van den corteneede], [van den dijcrechte in Lopikerweerde te verwandelen] en uit de breuken, verschenen in den oorlog tusschen die van Arkel en van Vyanen; de stad zal die gelden met den bisschop innen, de bisschop zal daarvan ontvangen 5 en de stad 7 van elke 12 penningen. </ref><ref>Utrechts Archief [https://hetutrechtsarchief.nl/collectie/982ADFF8C8E7127BE0534701000A655F Charter 1389] ''De bisschop van Utrecht en de graaf van Holland doen uitspraak in de geschillen tusschen den heer van Arkel c.s. en de heeren van Vyanen en Ameijde c.s.</ref>\n\n{{Image\n|file=Van_Arkel-24-2.jpg\n|align=c\n|size=300\n|caption=Seal Otto van Arkel, 1391\n}}  Around 1390 Otto started to withdraw from the politcs and started to support his son Jan van Arkel. Otto probably passed away on March 26, 1396.<ref>Zie voor de discussie hierover: Waale, De Arkelse oorlog, p. 45.</ref><ref>Pauli, Chronica, fol. 88 geeft aan dat Otto stierf op \"Paasavond, Lieve Vrouwe Annunciatie\" wat voor 1396 niet klopt. De genoemde feestdag is op 25 maart terwijl Paasavond dat jaar op 1 april viel. In zijn Chronicon Hollandiae, fol. 813 schrijft Pauli echter dat Otto is gestorven \"altera die scilicet annunciationis virginisMarie que fuit p r o f e s t um p a s c h a l e \" , datwil zeggen dat het feest vóór Pasen was. Ik meen daarom dat Otto op 26 maart 1396 is gestorven.</ref><ref>Volgens een charter aanwezig in Museum Meermanno Westreenianum in Den Haag is de datum van de oorkonde 26 maart 1396. In AGH 228, fol. 205vo. wordt dezelfde oorkonde vermeld maar daarin is de datum niet te lezen. De oorkonde isechter geplaatst tussen één van 11 april en één van 13 april wat zou kunnen wijzen op een datum van 12 april 1396. Als dit correct is, kan het natuurlijk ook zijn dat Otto wel genoemd</ref> His son Jan was given his fathers properties on April 11 or May 2 fo 1396.<ref>AGH 228, fol. 210 voor 2 mei 1396 en Drossaers, Nassause Domeiraad II, p. I, nr. 827 voor 11 april 1396.</ref>\nElisabeth van Bar received on March 12, 1371 from Albrecht Count of Holland and Zeeland, the \"tol vrijheid\" of the city Leerdam. This was confirmed by Albrecht in 1389.<ref>Van Mieris IV, p. 246 voor 1371 en AGH 226, fol. 142 en 296 en Van Mieris III, p. 528 voor 1389.</ref> After Otto's death she withdraws to her property in Pierrepont. She probably lived from 1396-1409 with a grievance against her son Jan and in 1409 they reconciled.<ref>Volgens Pauli, Chronica, fol. 89 kreeg zij al snel na Otto's dood ruzie met haar zoon.</ref> In 1410 her son Jan took over her properties and she received for this annually 300 French Crone.<ref>Kemp, Heeren van Arkel, p. 168 citeert een oorkonde gegeven te Longyon van 30 januari 1410.</ref> She probably passed away shortly after this event in 1410.<ref>Waale, De Arkelse oorlog, p. 134.</ref>\nOtto and Elisabeth had one child Jan (V), but had several illegimate children:\n# Jan (V) van Arkel\n# Hendrik van Ijenstein\n# Jan van Arkel van Zoelen\n# Jan van Ravenstein\nAkte van verbintenis door Otto, heer van Arkel, om bisschop Floris van Wevelinkhoven bij te staan en zich zonder diens toestemming niet te verbinden met de heer van Vianen of zijn zoon en broers, noch met Steven van Nijevelt, 1379 sept. 5<ref>Utrechts Archief [https://hetutrechtsarchief.nl/collectie/609C5C9A703A4642E0534701000A17FD Oorkonde 1379]''Akte van verbintenis door Otto, heer van Arkel, om bisschop Floris van Wevelinkhoven bij te staan en zich zonder diens toestemming niet te verbinden met de heer van Vianen of zijn zoon en broers, noch met Steven van Nijevelt, 1379 sept. 5 ''</ref>\n----\n{|border\n|-\n|{{Image|file=Hans_Free_Space_Profile-15.jpg|size= 100}}||Lived during the:<br/> [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_and_Cod_wars '''Hook and Cod Wars''']<br/>[https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoekse_en_Kabeljauwse_twisten ''Hoekse en Kabeljauwse Twisten'']<br/>1350-1490|| He sided with the<br/>'''KABELJAUWEN'''<br/>{{Image|file=Hans_Free_Space_Profile-17.jpg|size= 75}}\n|}\n== Sources ==\n<references />* Biographisch woordenboek der Nederlanden.       "notes": "[[Category:Medieval Project, France, needs biography]]\n[[Category: House of Valois]]\n[[Category:Fontainebleau, Seine-et-Marne]]\n{{Medieval Project}}\n== Biographie  =='''Philippe VI de France''', dit « '''Philippe de Valois''' » (né en 1293, mort le 22 août 1350)<sup>1</sup>: à Nogent le Roi, fut le premier roi de France de la branche collatérale des Valois.\nArticle détaillé : [http://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbre_g%C3%A9n%C3%A9alogique_des_Valois[Arbre généalogique des Valois]].\nSurnommé le « roi trouvé », ce sobriquet lui fut donné peu après son couronnement lors de la bataille de Cassel du 23 août 1328 par les Flamands lesquels, avant la bataille, s'étaient moqués du roi de France en peignant un coq sur leur étendard avec cette inscription : ''Quand ce cocq icy chantera, le Roy trouvé cy entrera''<sup>2</sup>\nSon accession sur le trône de France en 1328 découle d'un choix politique, fait en deux temps, à la mort de Louis X le Hutin en 1316 puis à celle de Charles IV en 1328, afin d'éviter que la couronne ne passe dans les mains d'un « étranger ». Édouard III d'Angleterre, pourtant petit-fils de Philippe le Bel, est ainsi évincé au profit du neveu de ce dernier.\nLors de son avènement, il doit aussi négocier avec Jeanne II de Navarre (1311-1349), fille de Louis X le Hutin qui a été évincée de la couronne de France en 1316 pour motif qu'elle est une femme (avancement de la \"loi salique\") mais également qu'elle est soupçonnée de batardise ou illégitimité, sa mère ayant été compromise dans le scandale de la tour de Nesle quand elle était mariée au futur Louis X. Mais celle-ci revendique de manière parfaitement légitime la couronne de Navarre et les comtés de Champagne et de Brie que Philippe le Bel tenait de son épouse Jeanne Ire de Navarre. N'étant pas lui-même descendant et héritier des rois de Navarre, comme l'étaient ses prédécesseurs, Philippe VI restitue donc le royaume de Navarre à son h��ritière légitime Jeanne de Navarre, mais refuse de lui céder la Champagne et la Brie redoutant d'être confronté à un parti trop puissant.\nS'il accède à la tête de l'État le plus puissant d'Occident, il gouverne dans une période de crise qui conduit à la guerre de Cent Ans. Il manque de moyens financiers pour administrer son royaume, ce qui ne peut être obtenu que par la manipulation de la monnaie et des imp��ts supplémentaires, lesquels ne sont tolérés qu'en période de guerre. Il doit asseoir au plus vite sa légitimité. Il le fait en restaurant l'autorité royale en Flandre en écrasant les rebelles Flamands lors de la bataille de Cassel le 23 août 1328.\nPar une habile politique diplomatique et matrimoniale, il contribue à augmenter l'influence du royaume à l'Est du royaume de France. Il rachète le Dauphiné pour le compte de son petit-fils, remarie son fils à une héritière potentielle de la Bourgogne et prend une option sur le comté de Provence.\nEn conflit larvé avec le roi Édouard III d'Angleterre, il finit par obtenir de celui-ci l'hommage pour la Guyenne, mais leurs intrigues pour le contrôle des Flandres, l'alliance franco-écossaise et la nécessité de justifier l'impôt nécessaire au fonctionnement d'un État moderne, conduisent inexorablement à la guerre de Cent Ans. Celle-ci commence de manière larvée, aucun des deux rois ne pouvant obtenir suffisamment de ressources fiscales pour mener à bien leur ambition. La guerre se mène par alliés interposés, hormis en Guyenne où les forces françaises assiègent Bordeaux mais doivent renoncer faute de vivres. De la même manière si la flotte française est en grande partie détruite à la bataille de l'Écluse en 1340, Édouard III ne peut concrétiser cette victoire sur terre et l'alliance germano-anglaise qu'il a organisée se disloque faute de pouvoir tenir ses promesses p��cuniaires.\nAprès la mort du duc Jean III de Bretagne, en avril 1341, un conflit successoral oppose Jean de Montfort à Charles de Blois pour la succession de Bretagne. Philippe VI arbitre en faveur de son neveu, Charles de Blois. Jean de Montfort s'allie aux Anglais, qui débarquent à Brest en 1342 et occupent l'ouest de la Bretagne, ce jusqu'en 1397.\nLe véritable tournant du conflit a lieu en juin 1344, quand Édouard III obtient du Parlement anglais des ressources fiscales importantes pour deux ans. Philippe ne peut répondre qu'en recourant à des mutations monétaires qui entraînent des dévaluations très impopulaires car elles déstabilisent l'économie. Fort de ses ressources financières, Édouard III est capable d'attaquer en force sur au moins deux fronts. Il regagne du terrain en Aquitaine et surtout inflige une défaite écrasante à Philippe à la bataille de Crécy le 26 août 1346. Ce dernier n'a plus les moyens d'empêcher le roi d'Angleterre de prendre Calais après onze mois de siège (1347).\nC'est complètement discrédité et en pleine épidémie de peste qu'il meurt en 1350.\n\n===Jeunesse===\nPhilippe de Valois est le fils aîné de Charles de Valois, frère cadet du roi Philippe le Bel, et de Marguerite d'Anjou (1273-1299). Il est donc cousin des trois fils de Philippe le Bel, (Louis X, Philippe V et Charles IV), lesquels se succèdent sur le trône de France entre 1314 et 1328.Philippe de Valois se marie en juillet 1313 avec Jeanne de Bourgogne (v. 1293-1349).\n\n===Union et Descendance===En juillet 1313, Philippe VI de Valois épouse en premières noces Jeanne de Bourgogne (v. 1293-1349), fille de Robert II (1248-1306), duc de Bourgogne (1272-1306) et roi titulaire de Thessalonique, et d'Agnès de France (1260-1325). De cette union sont issus au moins huit enfants:# Jean (1319-1364), qui deviendra roi de France sous le nom de Jean II, dit « Jean le Bon » (1350-1364), et postérité ;# Marie de France (1326-1333), épouse Jean, duc de Limbourg (1300-1355), sans postérité ;\n# Louis (17 janvier 1328-id.), sans postérité ;\n# Louis (8 juin 1330 - 23 juin 1330), sans postérité ;\n# Jean (1333-id.), sans postérité ;# Philippe (1336-1375), comte de Valois et premier duc d'Orléans (1344-1375), sans postérité légitime ;\n# Jeanne (1337-id.), sans postérité ;\n# N., fils, (1343-id.), sans postérité.Devenu veuf de Jeanne de Bourgogne, décédée le 12 décembre 1349, le roi épouse en secondes noces à Brie-Comte-Robert, le 11 ou 29 janvier 1350 (selon les sources), Blanche de Navarre (v. 1333-1398), dite Blanche d'Évreux, fille de Philippe III (1301-1343), comte d'Évreux (1319-1343) et roi de Navarre à titre « consort », et de Jeanne II (1311-1349), reine de Navarre (1328-1349) et comtesse de Champagne. De cette union est issue une fille posthume :# Jeanne, dite Blanche (1351-1371), qui meurt peu de temps après ses fiançailles avec Jean Ier (1350-1396), duc de Gérone, roi d'Aragon (1387-1396) et de Valence, sans postérité.\nPhilippe VI de Valois aurait eu deux fils naturels :\n# Jean d'Armagnac (+ après 1350), sans alliance ;# Thomas de la Marche (1318-1361), capitaine, né de Béatrice La Berruère. Certains auteurs le donnent fils naturel de Charles de la Marche, alors qu'il était comte de la Marche. Jeanne was known as 'la Boiteuse (the Lame)' and was Queen (Reine) consort de France, as the wife of [[Valois-119|Philippe VI de Valois, Roi de France]], from 1328 until her death.\n==== Birth date ====There appears to be no reliable sources that state that Jeanne was born on 24 June 1293 as stated in her biography on the English version of Wikipedia, nor that that she was born at Besancon.  There are some current resources that have her birthdate as about 1293 to 1294<ref>Cawley, 2012; Kerrebrouck, 2000; Kerrebrouck, 1990.</ref> but again there doesn't seem to be any medieval sources that confirm this time period.  However she was named in her father's will dated 25 March 1298<ref>Cawley, 2013.</ref> and obviously must have been born before that date.\n==== Inheritance ====Jeanne inherited the domains of Courtenay and Chantecoq, and Biervliet and Blaton and was confirmed in these before King Philippe IV at Fontainebleu in July 1313.<ref>Kerrebrouck, 2000, p. 585.</ref>\n\n=== Family ===\n==== Marriage and children ====The end of July 1313 was also when she married at Fontainebleau, Philippe de Valois, the future Philippe VI, Roi de France, the eldest son of Charles (Capet), Duc de Valois, and his first wife Marguerite d'Anjou. He was the eldest son of Bolesław III the Generous, Duke of Legnica-Brieg by his first wife, Margaret of Bohemia.\n Wenceslaus married Anna (b. ca. 1325 – d. 1367), daughter of Duke Casimir I of Cieszyn, by 1338. They had five children:\n\n*    Rupert I (b. 27 March 1347 – d. bef. 12 January 1409).\n*    Wenceslaus II (b. 1348 – d. 30 December 1419).\n*    Bolesław IV (b. ca. 1349 – d. 3/4 March 1394).*    Hedwig (b. ca. 1351 – d. 1 August 1409), married on 10 February 1372 to Henry VI, Duke of Głogów-Żagań.\n*    Henry VIII (b. ca. 1355 – d. 12 December 1398).\n\n=== Birth ===\n: Birth:   ABT 1308 TO ABT 1310\n:: Place:  Schlesien, Deutschland(HRR)\n\n=== Death ===\n: Death:    2 JUN 1364\n:: Place:  Liegnitz, Schlesien, Deutschland(HRR)\n\n=== Burial ===\n: Burial:  Church of God\n::: City:  Liegnitz\n::: State:  Schlesien\n::: Country:  Deutschland(HRR)\n::: Note:  {geni:place_name} Church of God\n\n=== Note ===\n: Note:  {geni:about_me} Wenceslaus I of Legnica\n:: \n:: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\n:: :: Wenceslaus I of Legnica (Polish: Wac?aw I legnicki; b. ca. 1318 - d. 2 June 1364), was a Duke of Namys?ów since 1338 and of Legnica-Brieg since 1342 until his death, but with further divisions with his brother Louis I.\n:: :: He was the eldest son of Boles?aw III the Generous, Duke of Legnica-Brieg by his first wife, Margaret of Bohemia. He was named after his maternal grandfather, King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia.\n:: \n:: [edit]Life\n:: :: The circumstances about Wenceslaus's childhood and adolescence were unknown. The first attested presence of the young heir of Legnica-Brieg was only in 1329, when he, alongside with his father, paid homage to King John of Luxemburg -his uncle, husband of his maternal aunt Elisabeth-.\n:: :: Boles?aw III's prodigality infuriated Wenceslaus, who, worried about the fate of the family's patrimony, rebelled against his father. Boles?aw III didn't want to fight with his son, and give to him the Duchy of Namys?ów as an independent fief, in 1338. Four years later (1342), Boles?aw III decided to abdicated all his lands to his two surviving sons -Wenceslaus and his younger brother Louis I- in exchange of Namys?ów, who was almost immediately sold by Boles?aw III to King Casimir III the Great. Alongside with his second wife, Katharina ?ubi?, Boles?aw III retired to the small towns Brieg and O?awa, who he retained as their residence.\n:: :: The two brothers initially decided co-rule without any land divisions, in order to pay the huge debts of the Duchy. The resources of Legnica were little, because their excentric father had sold several parts of land, and even the extraction of gold from the mines of Miko?ajowice revealed insufficient.\n:: :: In 1345 finally the brothers decided the formal division of their authority and rule. Louis convince his older brother to ceded him the overlordship over Legnica in exchange of the towns of Z?otoryja, Chojn��w, Chocianów and Lubin (Lüben).\n:: :: However, Wenceslaus changed his mind about this unequal division of the Duchy of Legnica only one year later. Two strong reason motivated him: he was seriously ill, and after eight years of childless marriage, his wife expecting their first child. Wenceslaus claimed all the inheritance of Legnica; in exchange, he promised to name Louis as his sole heir, even if his unborn child was a son. At the end, Louis resigned his lands to Wenceslaus; in exchange, he received a monetary compensation of 400 pieces of silver per year and the possession of the palace of Buczyna.\n:: :: The unexpectedly renunciation of Louis without fight maybe was dictated by the fact that his brother was dying, and he soon became again in the ruler of Legnica. However, it soon became apparent that Wenceslaus, despite his illness, doesn't any intentions to die. In addition, the situation was more complicated after the birth of the first of Wenceslaus's four sons, Rupert.\n:: :: Louis want the annulment of his resignation over Legnica on basis of the suspension of the compensatory payment, but without success. The situation remained in an unstable peace until the death of Boles?aw III (21 April 1352), whobroke in the civil war between the brothers.\n:: :: The war going on with varying fortune between both sides during six years (during were failed the mediation attempts of Duke Konrad I of Ole?nica, Przec?aw von Pogarell, Bishop of Wroclaw, and Emperor Charles IV). The war ended only in July 1359 when was settled an arrangement between the brothers, under which Wenceslaus -who actually lost the final battle- was compelled to give to Louis the Duchy of Brieg (who returned to him after the death of their stepmother, Katharina ?ubi?) and half of Chojnów as an independent Duchy (the other half of Chojnów, with Byczyna, was already sold by Wenceslaus to Duke Bolko II of Schweidnitz). Another additional concession of Wenceslaus to his younger brother was to pay of 4,500 pieces of silver for damages.\n:: :: In addition to the conflict with his brother, Wenceslaus was also involved in promoting the rule of the House of Luxemburg in Silesia and so in 1348 he represented the Emperor as a mediator in the dispute between the Bishop of Wroclaw Przec?aw von Pogarell and the local nobility. Eleven years later, in 1360, he was again a mediator in the tried to turn rozs?dzi? dispute between Duke Konrad I of Ole?nica and Duke Przemyslaus I of Cieszyn (Teschen) over the control of the Duchy of Bytom-Ko?le.\n:: :: By February 1348 Wenceslaus was also part of the suite of Emperor Charles IV, who travel to Bautzen in order to arrange a meeting with Frederick II, Margrave of Meissen and Langrave of Thuringia with the purprose of settled their frontiers disputes.\n:: :: During the entire period of his reign, the main problem of Wenceslaus was the financial difficulties of his Duchy. From his father Boles?aw III, the Duke also inherited his enormous debts. It is therefore not surprising that most of the Duchy was soon rented to a neighboring Princes and Bishops, and even ordinary Knights and townspeople.\n:: :: Despite the disastrous financial situation of Legnica, Wenceslaus decided to founded a Benedictine monastery and Kolegiate in Legnica called \"Church of God\" (pl: Bo?ego Grobu). In order to raise the prestige of his own for severalyears he ordened the creation of a gold coin called \"wac?awki\", who was used in his Duchy since them.\n:: :: Wenceslaus died on 2 June 1364 and was buried in the Church of God in Legnica, who was then under construction. His excommunication as a punishment for unpaid debts, led major complications. It was only in 1365 when his sons finally obtain the pardon for him. Wenceslaus's beautiful tombstone survived until our days and was currently in the Legnica Cathedral.\n:: \n:: [edit]Marriage and Issue\n:: :: By 1338, Wenceslaus married with Anna (b. ca. 1325 - d. 1367), daughter of Duke Casimir I of Cieszyn. They had five children:\n:: \n:: Rupert I (b. 27 March 1347 - d. bef. 12 January 1409).\n:: :: Wenceslaus II (b. 1348 - d. 30 December 1419), Bishop of Lubin (1375-82) and Wroclaw (1382-1417).\n:: \n:: Boles?aw IV (b. ca. 1349 - d. 3/4 March 1394).\n:: :: Hedwig (b. ca. 1351 - d. 1 August 1409), married on 10 February 1372 to Henry VI, Duke of G?ogów-?aga?.\n:: :: Henry VIII (b. ca. 1355 - d. 12 December 1398), Canon at Breslau (1378), Administrator of the Bishopric of Wroclaw (1379) and Bishop of Leslau (1389).\n:: \n:: [edit]References\n:: \n:: Complete Genealogy of the House of Piast-Silesia\n:: \n:: SILESIA\n:: \n:: This article was translated by his Polish Wikipedia version.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n* [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenceslaus_I_of_Legnica Wikipedia: Wenceslaus I of Legnica]* WikiTree profile Von Schlesien-Liegnitz-1 created through the import of export-BloodTree.ged on Aug 19, 2011 by [[Heinzelmann-4 | Luiz Sergio Heinzelmann]].       "notes": "[[Category:Lüneburg, Niedersachsen]]\n[[Category:Braunschweig, Niedersachsen]]\n== Biography == {{Nonmigrating Ancestor |addinfo= Magnus II. (Torquatus) von Braunschweig-Lüneburg was Sovereign of the [[Space:Fürstentum_Lüneburg|Principality of Lüneburg]] |flag=Furstentum_Luneburg.png |tooltip=Fürstentum Lüneburg/Principality of Lüneburg}}\t\n\n'''Magnus II Torquatus''', also known as Magnus with the Silver Chain, was born in 1328. He was a Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg from 1369 until he died in 1373 and belonged to the House of Welf.\nMagnus was the eldest son of [[Welf-27|Magnus I]] and [[Aschersleben-32|Sophia von Brandenburg]] (1300–1356). Initially, he served as an administrator in Sangerhausen and then as a bailiff from 1368. \nIn 1369, after the death of his father, he inherited the Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. A few months later, the father of his sister-in-law, Mechtild of Brunswick-Lüneburg, Duke Wilhelm II of Lüneburg, also died. \nMagnus had been designated as his heir and would have been entitled to inherit according to the Welf house laws, as his father Magnus I was a second cousin of the deceased. However, Emperor Charles IV considered the imperial fief to have reverted to the empire and enfeoffed the Ascanian dukes Albert of Saxony-Wittenberg and his uncle Wenzel with the principality, triggering the Lüneburg War of Succession.\nMagnus II married Catherine of Anhalt-Bernburg (d. 1390), a daughter of Prince Bernhard III of Anhalt-Bernburg (d. 1348). They had eleven children:\n\n# Elisabeth ⚭ Duke Gerhard VI of Schleswig-Holstein (d. 1404)\n# Friedrich (1357–1400) ⚭ Anna of Saxony (d. 1426)# [[Braunschweig-14|Bernhard]] (d. 1434) ⚭ Margaret of Saxony (before 1370–1418)\n#[[Braunschweig-15|Heinrich der Milde]] (d. 1416)# Agnes I (d. 1410) ⚭ Duke Albert I of Brunswick-Grubenhagen (1339��1383)\n# Helene ⚭ Count Eric I of Hoya\n# Elisabeth (d. 1420) ⚭ Count Maurice IV of Oldenburg (1380–1420)# Agnes II (before 1356–before 1434) ⚭ Duke Albert III of Mecklenburg, King of Sweden from 1363# [[Braunschweig-13|Sophie]] (1358–1416) ⚭ Duke Eric IV of Saxony-Lauenburg (1354–1411)\n# Mechthild (1370–??) ⚭ Count Otto III of Hoya (d. 1428)\n# Otto II (ca. 1364–1406)\nThe following years were marked by military conflicts with the Wittenbergers. After Lüneburg sided with the Wittenberg dukes due to repeated financial demands from Magnus, he attempted to take Lüneburg but failed. Magnus died on July 25, 1373, from fatal injuries sustained in a duel with his brother-in-law, Count Otto I of Schaumburg, during the Battle of Leveste at the Deister.\n\nMagnus II was buried in the Church of St. Michaelis in Lüneburg.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\nSee also:\n*{{wikidata|Q657947|de}}",
