      "notes": "[[Category: Battle of Marchfeld, 1278]]\n== Biography == \n[http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BOHEMIA.htm#OtakarPremyslIIdied1278 Přemysl Otakar II] at Medieval Lands Project\n'''Ottokar II''' (Czech: Přemysl Otakar II.) (c. 1233 – 26 August 1278), called '''The Iron and Golden King''' (Czech: král železný a zlatý), was the King of Bohemia  from 1253 until 1278. He also held the titles Duke of Austria (1251–1276), Duke of Styria (1260–1276), Duke of Carinthia (1269–1276), Duke of Carniola (1269–1276), and lord of Pordenone.\nOttokar was the second son of King Wenceslaus I of the Přemyslid dynasty, and through his mother, Kunigunde of Hohenstaufen, was related to the Hohenstaufen family, being a grandson of Philip of Swabia.\n\n<font size=4>Biography</font>\nOttokar was originally educated for the role of an ecclesiastical administrator. However, after the death in 1247 of Vladislaus, Margrave of Moravia, Ottokar's older brother and the heir of Bohemia, Ottokar became the heir. According to popular oral tradition, Ottokar was profoundly shocked by his brother's death and did not involve himself in politics, becoming focused on hunting and drinking. In 1248 he was enticed by discontented nobles to lead a rebellion against his father, King Wenceslaus. During this rebellion he received the nickname \"the younger King\" (mladší král).\nWenceslaus managed to defeat the rebels and imprisoned his son.[1] Ottokar II held the title of King of Bohemia from 31 July 1248 to November 1249.[2]\nFather and son were eventually reconciled to assist the King's aim of acquiring the neighbouring Duchy of Austria. The Duchy had been without a ruler since the death of Duke Frederick II in 1246. Wenceslaus initially attempted to acquire the duchy by marrying his heir, Vladislav, to the last Duke's niece Gertrude. That match had been cut short by Vladislav's death and Gertrude's re-marriage to Herman VI, Margrave of Baden. The latter was rejected by the Austrian estates and could not establish his rule in Austria. Wenceslaus used this as pretext to invade Austria in 1250 – according to some sources, the estates called upon him in to restore order.\nWenceslaus released Ottokar very soon and in 1251 made him Margrave of Moravia and installed him, with the approval of the Austrian nobles, as governor of Austria. Ottokar entered Austria, where the estates acclaimed him as Duke. To legitimize his position, Ottokar married the late Duke Frederick II's sister Margaret, who was his senior by thirty years and the widow of Henry of Hohenstaufen (who, ironically, had been engaged to Ottokar's aunt Saint Agnes of Bohemia prior to marrying Margaret). Their marriage took place on 11 February 1252.[2][3]\nIn 1253, King Wenceslaus died and Ottokar succeeded his father as King of Bohemia. After the death of the German King Konrad IV in 1254, Ottokar also hoped to obtain the Imperial dignity for himself, but his election bid was unsuccessful and Richard of Cornwall was elected instead.\n\n<font size=4>Building up of the empire</font>\nFeeling threatened by Ottokar's growing regional power, his cousin Béla IV, King of Hungary, challenged the young King. Béla formed a loose alliance with the Duke of Bavaria and claimed the Duchy of Styria, which had been a component of Austria since 1192. The conflict was quelled through the Pope's mediation. It was agreed that Ottokar was to yield large parts of Styria to Béla in exchange for recognition of his right to the remainder of Austria. However, after a few years the conflict resumed and Ottokar defeated the Hungarians in July 1260 at the Battle of Kressenbrunn and ended years of disputes over Styria with Béla IV.\nBéla now ceded Styria back to Ottokar, and his claim to those territories was formally recognized by Richard of Cornwall, King of the Romans, the nominal liege lord of all German lands. This peace agreement was also sealed by a royal marriage. Ottokar ended his marriage to Margaret and married Béla's young granddaughter Kunigunda of Slavonia. Kunigunde became the mother of his children. The youngest of them became his only legitimate son, Wenceslaus.\nOttokar II also led two crusade expeditions against the pagan Old Prussians and founded Königsberg in 1255, which was named in his honour and later became the capital of Prussia.\nIn 1266 he inherited Egerland, in 1269 Carinthia, part of Carniola and in 1272 he acquired Friuli. His claim was once again contested by the Hungarians on the field of battle. After another victory he became the most powerful king within the Empire.\n\n<font size=4>The way to the final battle</font>\nA new election for the Imperial German throne took place in 1273. But Ottokar was again not the successful candidate. He refused to recognize his victorious rival, Rudolph of Habsburg, and urged the Pope to adopt a similar policy. At a convention of the Imperial Diet at Nuremberg in 1274, Rudolph decreed that all imperial lands that had changed hands since the death of Emperor Frederick II must be returned to the crown. This would have deprived Ottokar of Styria, Austria, and Carinthia.\nIn 1276 Rudolph placed Ottokar under the ban of the empire and besieged Vienna. This compelled Ottokar in November 1276 to sign a new treaty by which he gave up all claims to Austria and the neighbouring duchies, retaining for himself only Bohemia and Moravia. Ottokar's son Wenceslaus was also betrothed to Rudolph's daughter Judith. It was an uneasy peace. Two years later, the Bohemian king tried to recover his lost lands by force. Ottokar found allies and collected a large army, but he was defeated with Hungarian assistance and killed at the Battle of Dürnkrut and Jedenspeigen on the March on 26 August 1278.\n\nHis son Wenceslaus II of Bohemia succeeded him as King of Bohemia.\n\n<font size=4>Marriage and children</font>\nOn 11 February 1252, Ottokar married Margaret, Duchess of Austria. Margaret was sick and left the marriage childless when she was repudiated in 1261.[3] On 25 October 1261, Ottokar married his second wife Kunigunda of Slavonia. They probably had four children.[4]\nOttokar also had two natural sons and some daughters. The most important of this issue was Nicholas I, Duke of Troppau (Czech: Mikuláš I. Opavský, Polish: Mikołaj I Opawski). His first-born child was never accepted as the crown prince to the Bohemian crown by the sitting pope, and was therefore in 1269 given the Duchy of Opava instead.\n\nThe most significant of Ottokar's natural children are as follows:\n*    Nicholas I, Duke of Troppau (1255–1318) (Mikuláš I. Opavský), the king's first-born son and also an ancestor of the Přemyslid dynasty in Opava.\n*    John, provost of Vyšehrad\n\nFrom the marriage with Kunigunda there were four children:\n*    Henry of Bohemia (1262–1263)?.*    Kunigunde of Bohemia (January 1265 – 27 November 1321), married Boleslaus II of Masovia.*    Agnes of Bohemia (5 September 1269 – 17 May 1296), married Rudolf II, Duke of Austria.\n*    Wenceslaus II of Bohemia (17 September 1271 – 21 June 1305).\n\n<font size=4>Legacy</font>\nOttokar is considered the greatest King of Bohemia, together with Charles IV. He was a founder of many new towns (about 30—not only in Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia, but also in Austria and Styria) and incorporated many existing settlements through civic charters, giving them new privileges. He was a strong proponent of trade, law and order. Furthermore, he instituted open immigration policies through which skilled German-speaking immigrants settled in major cities throughout his domains. Thus he can be called the founder of the third state de facto, within his domains. The great eastern German city of Königsberg was named in his honour as a tribute for his support of the Teutonic Knights in their war with the pagan Sambians.\nAs Czech traditional law was different from that reigning in his other domains, many principles introduced during his reign formed core of the Czech law for the following centuries. From his time stems the oldest preserved source of Czech law, Zemské desky, and also the oldest written Czech communal law, recorded in the founding deeds of the respective towns. By supporting the city of Jihlava with its mines he laid foundation to the silver wealth of the Bohemian kings. Privilegies of civic chartres usually excluded the towns from obedience towards the traditional comital district courts held by members of nobility. This can be seen as a second rupture of the traditional Czech legal system (after the Church gained its general freedoms half a century before), but also as a step towards equality and a first form of today's civil law.\nIn the country, Ottokar's introduction of the Law of Emphyteusis into the Czech law is sometimes interpreted as \"Germanization\". In fact it was a progress (for the subjects under this law were liberated from any bodily obediances, except for paying rent - and tax, if such was declared). Free selling and leaving of such subject estates could also be bought and soon became common. As early medieval slavery did not exist already, and serfdom was not known yet - it was gradually introduced only after the Hussite wars by the victorious nobility - Ottokar can be safely called that one of Czech rulers, who did the most for real equality of people before empress Maria-Theresa (1740–1780) and emperor Josef II (1780–1790). This change of legal environment in the Bohemian lands was not introduced by some single law or decree, but by the way of example, by systematic founding of villages chartered according to this law.\nHe issued also a general privilege to the Jews (1254), which established principles of incorporation of the Jews into the Czech society, until 1848. The Jews got some positions (such as servants of crown), thereby being little less subject to religious hatred. Instead of being able to claim only the support of individual lords, the Jews could from then on claim support of any royal officer, when their privileges were threatened.\nOttokar followed with a systematic policy of strengthening his domains by building fortifications. Besides supporting towns, he built many fortresses himself - Zvíkov Castle, Křivoklát Castle or Bezděz Castle in Bohemia, Hofburg Palace in Austria etc. - and also induced his vassals to build castles. A sign of rising strength of Bohemia and other lands, it was also a reaction on Mongol raids in the previous period (see Béla IV of Hungary). Conflict for the title of ownership to these fortified places built by members of nobility was probably the source of uprising (1276), which cost Ottokar the Austrian lands, and two years later (in an attempt for reconquest) his life.\nSome of the fortresses built by Ottokar were for centuries the strongest in Bohemia. Interestingly enough, Bezděz Castle served as a prison for his son Wenceslaus II of Bohemia for short time after Ottokar's death. The castle was safe deposit for the Bohemian legal records Zemské desky and many spiritual and temporal treasures during the destructive civil strife of Hussite wars (1419–1434) in Bohemia. It was first and last conquered in 1620, but only after it was long deserted, and in that state defended by rebelling subjects against regular army. Still the Swedes held it important enough to station a detachment there before 1648.\nBefore conflict with Rudolf of Habsburg, besides his own domains, he exacted influence over number of relatives, allies and vassals in Germany: Margraviate of Brandenburg etc. - and spiritual princedoms: Archbishopric of Salzburg, Patriarchate of Aquileia and others. Since the death of Konradin in 1268 he was an heir of the House of Hohenstaufen's claim to the imperial crown. He however did not raise this claim, staying content with informal influence in Germany. In 1267 he was appointed protector of the royal domains (of the Holy Roman Empire) east of the Rhine by the Roman king Richard of Cornwall. He held this office till 1273.\nHe is a famous figure both in history and in folkloric legend. In the Divine Comedy by Dante, Ottokar is seen outside the gates of Purgatory, in amiable companionship with his imperial rival Rudolph. He is also the protagonist of a tragedy by the 19th-century Austrian playwright Franz Grillparzer.\nIn the painting, \"Přemysl Otakar II: The Union of Slavic Dynasties,\" part of Alfons Mucha's 20-canvas work, The Slav Epic, Ottokar is depicted at his niece's wedding celebration, forging alliances with other Slavonic rulers in attendance.\n\n<font size=4>Ancestry</font>\n\nAncestors of Ottokar II of Bohemia\n<table style=\"font-size: 90%;       "notes": "[[Category:Medieval Project needs work]]\n{{Medieval Project}}\n== Biography ==\n\n==Research Notes==\n: Note:  {geni:about_me} Kunigunda of Slavonia\n:: \n:: From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia:: Kunigunda Rostislavna (1245 ? September 9, 1285) [Czech: Kunhuta] was Queen consort of Bohemia and its regent from 1278 until her death. She was a member of the House of Chernigov, and a daughter of the ruler of Slavonia.\n:: :: She was presumably born in Russia, in the domains of her paternal grandfather Michael of Chernigov, Grand Prince of Kiev, to Rostislav Mihailovich, future ruler of Belgrade and Slavonia, and his wife Anna of Hungary. After the death of her father's father, Kunigunda's family relocated to Hungary, where her mother's father, Bela IV of Hungary, made her father governor of certain Serbian-speaking regions in the Danube Valley. Her father proclaimed himself King of Bulgaria in 1256 but did not stay there to defend his kingship.\n:: :: Kunigunda was married to King Premysl Otakar II of Bohemia (ca. 1233 ? 1278) in Bratislava on October 25, 1261, following his divorce from Margaret, Duchess of Austria (ca. 1204 ? 1266) who was elderly and barren, and unable to provide heirs for the King. Kunigunda, 41 years Margaret's junior, bore Otakar several children, the youngest being his only legitimate son Wenceslaus (Vaclav, 1271-1305).\n:: :: Genuine heirs of the Babenberg asserted their rights against King Otakar in Austria. The young Kunigunda's grandfather Bela IV had been Otakar's rival.\n:: :: The Czech king Otakar tried in 1278 to recover his lands lost to Rudolph I of Germany. He made allies and collected a large army, but he was defeated by Rudolph and killed at the Battle of Dürnkrut and Jedenspeigen on the March onAugust 26, 1278.\n:: :: Moravia was subdued and its government entrusted to Rudolph's representatives, leaving Kunigunda, now Queen Regent of Bohemia in control of only the province surrounding Prague, while the young Wenceslaus was betrothed and marriedto one of Rudolph's daughters, Judith.\n:: :: Kunigunda married secondly a Bohemian magnate, Zavish, Lord of Falkenstejn and Rozmberk in Prague June 2, 1284. Zavish survived her, married again, and was executed on August 24, 1290.\n:: :: Kunigunda's son Wenceslaus II kept the kingdom of Bohemia, and also succeeded in obtaining Poland and Hungary although not very sustainably. Ultimately she is one of the pivotal ancestresses of the Luxembourg and the Habsburg.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />* [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/RUSSIA,%20Rurik.htm#KunigundaRostislavnadied1285 Kunigunda Rostislavna] at Medieval Lands Project",

There was no issue from this marriage.\nHe married secondly, between about 1283-1287 (a dispensation was issued by Pope Nicholas IV 24 February 1290, because they were related in 4th degree), Margareta von Rügen (born about 1265-1270), the daughter of Wizlaw II, Fürst von Rügen, and his wife, Agnes von Braunschweig.\n\nThey had five children:#Eufemia, born about 1286-1288, married about 1300-1304, Christoffer II Eriksen, King of Denmark;#Margareta, born about 1286-1288, married (1) 1299, before November, Nikolaus I von Mecklenburg, Herr zu Rostock (died 25 November 1314); (2) about 1316-1324, dispensation issued 12 September 1324, Johann I, Duke of Steinau;#Wartislaw, born 1291, succeeded his father as Duke of Pomeranai in Wolgast;\n#Jutta, Abbess of Krummin, died after 12 March 1336;#Elisabeth, married 1316, before 16 June, (dispensation issued 1 July 1346), Erich I, Duke of Sachsen in Ratzeburg und Lauenburg, and died after 16 October 1349.\nBogislaw died 19 February 1309, and was buried in Marienkirche, Stettin.<ref>Cawley, Charles, 'Pomerania' version 3.1, 15 July 2015, in ''Medieval Lands: A prosopography of medieval European noble and royal families'', (http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/POMERANIA.htm#BogislawIVdied1309A : viewed 19 July 2015).</ref>\n\n== Research Notes ==\nDoB is given on \"Genealogics\" as about 1255-1258.\nProbably Bogislaw IV Herzog von Pommern of the Greifen family (House of Griffin), b. bef. 1278, d. 24 Feb 1309. Il était fils de Roger d'Armagnac, vicomte de Fezensaguet, et Puelle d’Albret.\nEn 1249 il contesta la possession de l'Armagnac et du Fézensac à la guerre avec Arnaud Odon (1205 † 1256), vicomte de Lomagne et d'Auvillars, époux de Mascarose Ire d'Armagnac († 1249), héritière des comtés d'Armagnac et de Fezensac, et père de Mascarose II de Lomagne (†1256). Dans cette guerre Géraud était soutenu par son suzerain, Raymond VII, comte de Toulouse. Capturé, il fut libéré contre une rançon et continua la lutte avec succès. Durant sa captivité, sa mère, Pucelle d’Albret, fit, en son nom, hommage du Fezensaguet à Alphonse de Poitiers, successeur de Raymond VII, pour continuer à bénéficier de son soutien. Ce n'est qu'en 1255, que Gaston, vicomte de Béarn réussit à réconcilier les adversaires.\nEn 1256, après la mort sans enfants de Mascarose II de Lomagne, Géraud, étant son plus proche parent, hérité des comtés d'Armagnac et de Fezensac. À la suite des multiples querelles avec le sénéchal du Languedoc, il fut capturé et emprisonné deux ans château de Péronne. He was son of King Louis IX of France and Margaret of Provence.  In 1272, Robert married Beatrice of Burgundy, heiress of Bourbon and had the following issue:\n\n* Louis I, le Boiteux (1279–1342), first Duke of Bourbon* Blanche (1281–1304), married in 1303 in Paris Robert VII, Count of Auvergne and Boulogne, grandmother of Joan I, Countess of Auvergne* John (1283–1316), Baron of Charolais, married c. 1309 Jeanne d'Argies and had issue\n* Mary (1285–1372, Paris), Prioress of Poissy\n* Peter (1287 – aft. 1330), Archdeacon of Paris* Margaret (1289–1309, Paris), married firstly in 1305 Raymond Berengar of Andria and secondly in 1308 John I, Marquis of Namur\n During his first joust, in 1279, Robert suffered head injuries which rendered him an invalid for the remainder of his life.\n Robert is considered the founder of the House of Bourbon, a family which, with the passing of centuries came to govern as Kings of Navarre (1572-1830), Kings of France (1589–1848), Kings of the Two Sicilies (1735–1860), dukes of Parma (1748–1796 and 1847–1859), grand dukes of Luxembourg (1964–present) and Kings of Spain (1700–present).\n : Name:  Robert Capet De Clermont /Ct De Clermont/<ref>Ancestry Family Tree https://www.ancestry.com/family-tree/person/tree/6436419/person/-1281598764/facts</ref>\n: Name:  Robert /de France/<ref>Ancestry Family Tree: https://www.ancestry.com/family-tree/person/tree/6436419/person/-1281598476/facts</ref>\n\n: Name:  Robert II Capet de France Comte de Clermont\n:: MAR de France\n:: Nickname:  Robert of Clermont\n\n=== Birth ===: 1256 Paris, Isle De France, France<ref name=\"hofun\">hofundssonAnces.ged</ref>\n: Date:  ABT 1256 Paris, Isle de France, France\n\n=== Death ===\n: 7 FEB 1315/16\n: BET 07 FEB 1316 AND 1317<ref name=\"hofun\"/>\n: 7 FEB 1317 TO ABT FEB 1317 Paris, Isle de France, France\n: 1317-02-07 Paris, Seine, France\n\n=== Baptism ===\n:  ABT 1256\n\n=== Christening ===\n: 1256\n: ABT 1256  France -       "notes": "[[Category:Medieval Project, France, needs biography]]\n[[Category:Eighth Crusade]]\n[[Category:House of Capet]]\n[[Category:Tournament of Compiègne (1278)]]\n{{Medieval Project}}\n\n== Biography ==Philippe III le Hardi, roi de France / Phillip III, The Bold, King of France.  \nHe was called \"the Bold\" on the basis of his abilities in combat and on horseback and not his character.\n\n=== Jeunesse ===: Cadet de famille, le prince Philippe n'était pas destiné à régner sur un royaume. C'est à la mort de son frère aîné Louis en 1260 qu'il devient le prince héritier. Il a alors quinze ans et présente beaucoup moins d'aptitudes que son frère, étant de caractère doux, soumis, timide et versatile, presque écrasé par les fortes personnalités de ses parents.\n: Sa mère Marguerite lui fait promettre de rester sous sa tutelle jusqu'à l'âge de trente ans, mais son père le roi Saint Louis fait casser le serment par le pape, préférant bonifier son fils par une éducation sans faille. C'est ainsi que le pape Urbain IV relève Philippe de son serment le 6 juin 1263. À cet effet, il lui adjoint à partir de 1268 pour mentor Pierre de La Brosse. Saint Louis se charge en outre de lui prodiguer ses propres conseils, rédigeant en particulier ses Enseignements, qui inculquent avant tout la notion de justice comme premier devoir de roi. Il reçut également une éducation très tournée vers la foi. Guillaume d'Ercuis était en outre son aumônier, avant d'être le précepteur de son fils, le futur roi Philippe IV.\n: Dans la mouvance du traité de Corbeil, conclu le 11 mars 1258 entre Jacques Ier d'Aragon et son père, Philippe fut marié en 1262 à Isabelle d'Aragon à Clermont par l'archevêque de Rouen Eudes Rigaud. Il en eut quatre garçons : Louis (1264-1276), Philippe, Robert (1269-av. 1276) et Charles (ainsi qu'un fils mort-né fin janvier 1271). En 1270, il accompagne son père à la huitième croisade, à Tunis. Peu avant son départ, Saint Louis avait remis la régence du royaume entre les mains de Mathieu de Vendôme et Simon II de Clermont-Nesle, comte de Clermont, auxquels il avait en outre confié le sceau royal. Après la prise de Carthage, l'armée est frappée par une épidémie de dysenterie, qui n'épargne ni Philippe, ni sa famille. Son frère Jean Tristan meurt le premier le 3 août, puis, le 25, vers 15 heures, le roi Louis succombe à son tour. Pour empêcher la putréfaction de la dépouille du souverain, on a recours au mos Teutonicus<.\n: Philippe est donc proclamé roi sous le nom de « Philippe III » à Tunis. Sans grande personnalité ni volonté, très pieux, mais bon cavalier, il doit davantage son surnom de « Hardi » à sa vaillance au combat qu'à sa force de caractère. Il se révèle incapable de commander aux troupes, affecté qu'il est de la mort de son père. Il laisse son oncle Charles Ier d'Anjou négocier avec Abû `Abd Allah Muhammad al-Mustansir, sultan hafside de Tunis, et conclure une trêve de dix ans qui lui permet de revenir en France. Ce dernier obtient le versement d'un tribut du calife de Tunis en échange du départ des crois��s. Un traité fut conclu le 28 octobre 1270 entre les rois de France, de Sicile, de Navarre et leurs barons d'une part ; le calife de Tunis de l'autre.\n: D'autres morts endeuillent encore cette débâcle. En décembre, à Trapani, le beau-frère de Philippe, le roi de Navarre Thibaut de Champagne trouve la mort. À Trapani, en Sicile, son épouse, la sœur du souverain, Isabelle de France, rejoint inopinément son mari dans la mort. Enfin, un mois plus tard, en Calabre, l'épouse du souverain, Isabelle d'Aragon, alors enceinte de son cinquième enfant, fait une malheureuse chute de cheval. Elle se brise la colonne vertébrale, fait une fausse-couche et meurt dans d'affreuses douleurs à Cosenza.\n: Philippe III arrive à Paris le 21 mai 1271, et rend avant tout hommage aux victimes, qui furent bien sûr nombreuses aussi parmi les soldats. Dès le lendemain ont lieu les funérailles de son père. Le nouveau souverain est sacré roi de France à Reims le 15 août 1271.\n: L'avènement de Philippe III s'accompagne rapidement d'un bouleversement dans le paysage politique : la mort du roi d'Angleterre Henri III et la fin d'une vacance du trône impérial longue de 19 ans. En outre, la préoccupation de l'Europe n'est plus aux croisades. Ainsi, alors que celles-ci avaient été des composantes majeures du règne de son père, le sien sera surtout marqué par des conflits territoriaux, des contestations d'héritages et des guerres de vassalité, phénomène qui va encore s'accentuer pendant le règne de son fils.\n: Conservant la plupart des conseillers de son père, ainsi que Eustache de Beaumarchès, sénéchal de Poitou, de Toulouse et d'Auvergne, Philippe III a pour grand chambellan Pierre de La Brosse qu'il fait pendre en 1278.\n: Par des héritages, annexions, achats, unions, et guerres, Philippe III s'attache sans cesse à agrandir le domaine royal et y affermir son autorité.\n: En 1271-1272, il opère sa première transaction territoriale en incorporant au domaine royal l'héritage de son oncle Alphonse de Poitiers : le comté de Toulouse, le Poitou et une partie de l'Auvergne. Par le traité d'Amiens de 1279, il est cependant contraint de céder l'Agenais, la Saintonge et le Ponthieu au roi d'Angleterre Edouard Ier. Il hérite également du comté du Perche et du comté d'Alençon de son frère Pierre décédé en 1283.\n: Il a l'occasion de faire ses premiers faits d'armes personnels en 1272, quand il convoque l’ost royal contre les comtes de Foix et d'Armagnac qui lui contestent son pouvoir. Armagnac se rend, et Foix, battu, est emprisonné. Il lui restitue cependant ses terres en 1277. Il achète également les comtés de Nemours et de Chartres en 1274 et 1284. Il acquiert aussi diverses villes, telles Harfleur ou Montmorillon. Il retire également au roi de Majorque l'autorité sur Montpellier. En revanche, il cède au pape Grégoire X le comtat Venaissin en 1274.\n: Il mène une politique matrimoniale efficace, étant l'instigateur du mariage de sa cousine Mahaut d'Artois avec le comte Othon IV de Bourgogne, préparant ainsi le rapprochement de cette région, terre impériale (l'actuelle Franche-Comté), avec le royaume. Il intervient aussi en Navarre après la mort d'Henri Ier de Navarre qui laisse une fille Jeanne sous la tutelle de sa mère Blanche d'Artois et de Ferdinand de la Cerda. Blanche d'Artois fiance Jeanne au fils de Philippe, le futur Philippe le Bel. La Champagne et la Navarre sont administrées par les Français de par le traité d'Orléans de 1275, et la Champagne est définitivement rattachée au domaine en 1314. Le mariage a finalement lieu en 1284.\n: Du point de vue des institutions, Philippe III introduit plusieurs nouveautés. Il fixe la majorité des rois de France à quatorze ans. Il affermit la justice royale au détriment des justices seigneuriales, instituant un tribunal royal dans chaque bailliage ou sénéchaussée. Il frappe d’amendes les nobles ne répondant pas à la convocation à l'ost royal. Il crée un impôt sur les transmissions de fiefs. Enfin, il institutionnalise la ségrégation envers les juifs.\n: En Castille, après la mort de son beau-frère Ferdinand de la Cerda en 1275, Philippe III prend sans succès le parti des enfants de celui-ci contre Don Sanche, désigné successeur par le roi Alphonse X.\n: En Italie, il soutient le pape Martin IV contre les gibelins, faisant une expédition punitive en Romagne. Il soutient également la politique sicilienne de son oncle Charles d'Anjou, après les massacres des Vêpres siciliennes en 1282. Pierre III d'Aragon, considéré comme l'instigateur du massacre, est excommunié par le pape qui lui enlève son royaume et le donne à Charles de Valois, lequel ne peut le conserver.\n: En 1285, après l'affaire de Sicile, Philippe III, sans son oncle Charles d'Anjou mort en début d'année, engage la croisade d'Aragon et attaque sans succès la Catalogne (siège de Gérone du 26 juin au 7 septembre 1285). Son armée touchée par une épidémie de dysenterie, il est défait en septembre à Las Formiguas, et est obligé de faire retraite. Celle-ci est désastreuse, l'armée française est à nouveau défaite le 1<sup>er</sup> octobre à la bataille du col de Panissars, et lui-même meurt à Perpignan le 5 octobre 1285.\n: Mort loin de la capitale, se pose la question du traitement de son corps, la technique de l'embaumement antique ayant été perdue. La putréfaction du cadavre est alors limitée par l'éviscération et la technique funéraire du mos Teutonicus. Il est le premier roi de France à disposer de la tripartition du corps (delaceratio corporis, « division du corps » en cœur, entrailles et ossements), ses entrailles étant conservées à Narbonne, ses os rejoignant la nécropole royale de Saint-Denis, son cœur étant confié à son confesseur dominicain qui l'offre aux Jacobins de Paris. Cette pratique de sépultures multiples, pourtant interdite par une décrétale du pape Boniface VIII en 1299, est reprise ensuite par les rois puis les reines et les proches de la dynastie capétienne car elle permet la multiplication des cérémonies (funérailles du corps, la plus importante, puis funérailles du cœur et funérailles des entrailles) et des lieux où honorer le roi défunt.\n: Pierre d'Aragon mourant un mois plus tard, Gérone se livre à son successeur, et le nouveau roi de France, Philippe IV le Bel décide le retour en France.\n: Le 28 mai 1262 à Clermont-Ferrand, il épouse en premières noces Isabelle d'Aragon (1247-1271), fille du roi Jacques Ier d'Aragon. Ayant accompagné le roi à la Huitième croisade, elle meurt tragiquement d'une chute de cheval, en Calabre, sur le chemin du retour, alors enceinte de son 5e enfant.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n* Richardson, Douglas. Fue hermana de Pedro III de Aragón y de Jaime II de Mallorca. De su matrimonio nacieron:\n*Luis de Francia (1264-1276)\n*Felipe IV de Francia (1268-1314), Rey Felipe IV\n*Roberto de Francia (1269-1271)\n*Carlos de Francia, Conde de Valois (1270-1325)\n\n=== Ancestros ===Sus ancestros llegan a los reyes de Croacia y Hungría por la vía materna, los Príncipes de Kiev así como Emperadores Bizantinos y los Condes de Barcelona por la vía paterna.\n\n=== Traduccion al Idioma Castellano ===\n:Isabel de Aragón, reina consorte de Francia.\n:Consorte de 1270 - 28 de enero 1271\n:Consorte de Felipe III\nIsabel de Aragón (1247 - 28 enero 1271), infanta de Aragón, fue, por el matrimonio, la reina consorte de Francia en la Edad Media entre 1270 y 1271. \nElla era la hija de Jaime I el Conquistador, Rey de Aragón y Conde de Barcelona, ??y de su segunda esposa, Violante de Hungria,  hija de Andrés II de Hungría. Fué hermana de Pedro III de Aragón y de Jaime II de Mallorca. \nEn Clermont, el 28 de mayo 1262, se casó con el futuro Felipe III de Francia, hijo del rey Luis IX y Margarita de Provenza. Tuvieron cuatro hijos:\n#Louis (1265-1276).\n#Felipe IV \"el Hermoso\" (1268-1314), rey de Francia.\n#Robert (1269-1271).\n#Carlos de Valois (1270-1325).\nElla acompañó a su marido en la Octava Cruzada contra Túnez. Sus hijos más jóvenes se unieron a ella en el viaje.\nDe camino a casa, se detuvieron en Cosenza, Calabria. Su hijo menor, Robert, cayó enfermo y murió poco después. Embarazada de seis meses de su quinto hijo, de 11 de enero 1271 sufrió una caída de su caballo después de haber reanudado el viaje de regreso a Francia. Isabel dio a luz un hijo prematuro, muerto. Nunca se recuperó de las lesiones y el parto, y murió diecisiete días más tarde, el 28 de enero. Su marido tomó su cuerpo y sus dos hijos muertos y, cuando finalmente regreso en Francia, la enterró en la Basílica de San Denis. Su tumba, al igual que muchas otras, fue profanada durante la Revolución Francesa en 1793.\n\n=== Descendencia ===A través de sus hijos  Felipe y Carlos tiene muchos nietos y sus nietas se casaron con reyes, duques y emperadores. Su nieta Isabel se cas�� con Eduardo II de Inglaterra y fue la madre de Eduardo III de Inglaterra; otra nieta, Blanca, se casó con Carlos IV, emperador del Sacro Imperio y era la madre de Catalina de Bohemia. Otra nieta de Isabel se casó con Pedro I, duque de Borbón y fue la madre de Luis II, duque de Borbón y Juana, reina de Francia. Isabel tenía una nieta llamada Catalina II de Valois, la princesa de Acaya que se convirtió en emperatriz de América después de la muerte de su madre. Cuatro de sus nietos, se convirtieron en reyes de Francia: Luis X de Francia, Felipe V de Francia, Carlos IV de Francia y Felipe IV de Francia, los tres primeros eran hijos de Felipe e Isabel, Cuando su hijo mayor no produce herederos sobrevivientes, el trono pasó a Charles, el hijo de Felipe, quien comenzó la Cámara de los Valois. A través de su nieto Felipe IV de Francia, Isabel es un antepasado de los reyes franceses y de los líderes de muchos países a través de sus nietas, bisnietas, hasta el final de la monarquía francesa. Su bisnieta, grande fue Catalina de Valois, nieto de Catalina fue Enrique VII de Inglaterra,  cuyo hijo fue Enrique VIII de Inglaterra y sus tres hijos fueron Eduardo VI, Mar��a I e Isabel I.\n\n=== Muerte ===Acompañó a su marido en la que sería la Octava Cruzada y murió por una caída de caballo que sucedió en Cosenza, Calabria, Italia, cuando volvía de ésta, el 11 de enero de 1271 estando embarazada del que podría haber sido su quinto hijo. Dio a luz a un prematuro que falleció al nacer. Ella murió 17 días después a consecuencia de la caída y una probable septicemia postparto. Fue enterrada en la Basílica de Saint-Denis y su tumba fue profanada al igual que muchas otras durante la Revolución francesa en 1793.\n''Wikipedia: Isabel de Aragón (reina de Francia) (http://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isabel_de_Arag%C3%B3n_(reina_de_Francia) : accessed 14 Mar 2013)''\n----\n\n\n== Biography ==\n'''Isabella of Aragon''' (1247 – 28 January 1271), infanta of Aragon, was, by marriage, queen consort of France from 1270 to 1271.\nIsabel de Aragón was born in 1243.<ref name=\"lines of succession\">Jirí Louda and Michael MacLagan, Lines of Succession: Heraldry of the Royal Families of Europe, 2nd edition (London, U.K.: Little, Brown and Company, 1999), table 46. Hereinafter cited as Lines of Succession.</ref> She was the daughter of Jaime I, Rey de Aragón and Yolante Arpád.<ref name=\"lines of succession\"/> She married Philippe III, Roi de France, son of Louis IX, Roi de France and Marguerite de Provence, on 28 May 1262 at Clement-en-Auvergne.<ref name=\"pedigrees\">Marcellus Donald R. von Redlich, Pedigrees of Some of the Emperor Charlemagne's Descendants, volume I (1941; reprint, Baltimore, Maryland, U.S.A.: Genealogical Publishing Company, 2002), page 64. Hereinafter cited as Pedigrees of Emperor Charlemagne, I.</ref> She died on 28 January 1271 at Cosenza, Calabria, Italy, from a fall from a horse.<ref name=\"pedigrees\"/>\n\n=== Life ===She was the daughter of King James I of Aragon and his second wife, Violant of Hungary, daughter of Andrew II of Hungary.  She was a granddaughter of Yolanda de Courtenay.\nIn Clermont on 28 May 1262, she married the future Philip III of France, son of king Louis IX and Margaret of Provence. They had four sons:\n# Louis (1265–1276).\n# Philip IV \"the Fair\" (1268–1314), King of France.\n# Robert (1269–1271).\n# Charles of Valois (1270–1325).\nShe accompanied her husband on the Eighth Crusade against Tunis. On their way home, they stopped in Cosenza, Calabria.   It was then under Angevin rule as part of the Kingdom of Sicily.  Six months pregnant with her fifth child, on 11 January 1271 she suffered a fall from her horse after they had resumed the trip back to France. Isabella gave birth to a premature stillborn son.<ref>[[Wikipedia:Isabella_of_Aragon,_Queen_of_France]].</ref> She never recovered from her injuries and the childbirth, and died seventeen days later, on 28 January. Her husband took her body and their stillborn son and, when he finally returned to France, buried her in Saint Denis Basilica. Her tomb, like many others, was desecrated during the French Revolution in 1793.\n\n=== Descendents ===Through her sons Philip and Charles she has many grandchildren, and her granddaughters were married off to Kings, Dukes and Emperors. Her granddaughter Isabelle married Edward II of England and was the mother of Edward III of England, another granddaughter, Blanche married Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor and was the mother of Katharine of Bohemia. Another granddaughter Isabella married Peter I, Duke of Bourbon and was the mother of Louis II, Duke of Bourbon and Joanna, Queen of France. Isabella had a granddaughter called Catherine II of Valois, Princess of Achaea who became Latin Emperess after her mother's death. Four of her grandsons became King of France they were Louis X of France, Philip V of France, Charles IV of France and Philip IV of France, the first three were sons of Isabella's eldest son Philip and because non produced surviving heirs the throne passed to Charles's son Philip, who began the House of Valois. Through her grandson Philip IV of France Isabella is an ancestor of French Kings and she would be an ancestor of leaders of many countries through granddaughters, great granddaughters, right up to the end of the French monarchy. Her great, great granddaughter was Catherine of Valois, Catherine's great grandson was Henry VII of England, Henry's son was Henry VIII of England and his three children were Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\nSee also:\n* Richardson, Douglas.       "notes": "[[Category:Magna Carta Project Needs Re-review]][[Category:Bigod-2 Descendants]][[Category:Bigod-1 Descendants]][[Category:Battle of Sluys]][[Category:Battle of Cressy]][[Category:Siege of Calais (1346)]]\n{{Magna Carta}}\n== Biography ==Hugh de Hastings, Knt., born about 1310 (aged 24 in 1334), was the younger son of [[Hastings-1246|John de Hastings]], Knt., 1st Lord Hastings, by his father's second marriage to [[Despenser-13|Isabel le Despenser]].<ref name=MCA2>Douglas Richardson. ''Magna Carta Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families'', 4 vols., ed. Kimball G. Everingham. 2nd edition. Salt Lake City, UT: the author, 2011, vol. II, pages 111-113, ELSING 6.</ref>\n\n===Inheritance===Hugh was heir in 1333 to his full brother, [[Hastings-2900|Thomas de Hastings]].<ref name=MCA2/> Hugh was not his father's heir. However after his full brother died he was his mother's heir, and he was also a successful military leader in the time of Edward III, and an example of the way in which Edward and his clique emphasized bonds of kinship and knightly comradery.\nNote that he and his brother were only half siblings to his father's main heirs, children of his first wife. This became important in later debates about Hastings inheritances. Of course they had no claim on the first wife's Pembroke heritage.\nFrom his brother he inherited Sutton Scotney, from his mother's family, but the lands his family was to be more well-known for came from his wife's Foliot inheritance.\n\n===Titles and Military Service===Sir Hugh de Hastings was Steward to Queen Philippe of Hainault in 1344 and Captain and Lieutenant of the King in Flanders in 1346.<ref name=MCA2/> He fought at the Battle of Sluys on 24 June 1340 in the retinue of the Earl of Derby<ref name=CP6/> and accompanied the Earl of Derby to Gascony in 1345.<ref name=MCA2/> In 1346, he was called upon to raise an army in Flanders for the war in France and, by August of that year, he delivered an army of about 60,000 Flemings to fight with the king at the Battle of Crecy on 26 August 1346.<ref name=MCA2/><ref name=CP6/> \n\n===Marriage and Children===Hugh married before 18 May 1330 to [[Foliot-27|Margery Foliot]], elder daughter of Richard Foliot, Knt., and Joan de Brewes (or Breuse).<ref name=MCA2/> They had two sons and three daughters:*[[Hastings-2907|John]], son and heir, born about 1330, died unmarried before 1360<ref name=MCA2/>*[[Hastings-275|Hugh]], Knt., born about 1335, died September 1369, married Margaret (or Margery) de Everingham<ref name=MCA2/>\n*Isabel, married Saier de Rochford<ref name=MCA2/>*Margery, married first to Sir Nicholas Castell and second to John de Boyland<ref name=MCA2/>\n*[[Hastings-1623|Maud]], married Robert de la Mare<ref name=MCA2/>\n\n===Death and Will===Sir Hugh de Hastings died in July 1347 and was buried at Elsing, Norfolk (Richardson says he died on 21 July, CP says he died 29 or 30 July),<ref name=MCA2/><ref name=CP6/> his Inquisition Post Mortem states he died on 29 or 30 July.<ref name=IPM>''Inquisitions Post Mortem, Edward III, File 85, #47\" online at [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/inquis-post-mortem/vol9/pp29-43 British History Online].</ref> He made a will on 22 July 1347 at Old Ford, Middlesex (le Aldford 'juxta London��) and proved 9 August 1347 (Richardson says 5 August), naming  ''Margeriam consortem meam carissimam'' (my dear consort Margery) as an executor.<ref name=CP6/> By writ dated 30 July 1347, IPMs were held at Nottingham, York, Southampton and Norfolk, all named his son, John de Hastynges, aged 16-19 years or older, as his heir.<ref name=IPM/>\nThe manors that he and his wife had jointly held were released to her on 7 September 1347 and 5 October 1347.<ref name=CP6/> His widow, Margery, died 8 August 1349 and was buried at Friars Minor, Doncaster,<ref name=MCA2/> at the Furnivalle Chapel, on 30 August 1349.<ref name=CP6/>\n\n===Burial===There was a window in Elsing, now destroyed, commemorating Hugh and his wife Margery, which showed arms of Hastings quartering Valence, and Hastings impaling Foliot. The parish church for Elsing is St. Mary's, a medieval, still active village church with lots of medieval details. Its nave roof is the biggest in East Anglia at just over 12 meters, and one of the biggest in England. The chancel has a magnificent brass image of Sir Hugh de Hastings, Lord of the Manor, with angels as if entering paradise, above that St. George and Edward III surmounted by the Queen of Heaven.\nA copy of the brass is still on public view in the church. It shows 8 relatives and comrades at arms weeping for him. Their relationships were explained in full by John Ravilious.<ref>[https://www.mbs-brasses.co.uk/index-of-brasses/sir-hugh-hasting Monumental Brass Society], Sir Hugh Hastyngs</ref>\n\nFor Sir Hugh de Hastings tomb and brasses: *[http://www.norfolkchurches.co.uk/elsing/elsing.htm Churches of Norfolk], St. Mary, Elsing*[https://www.mbs-brasses.co.uk/index-of-brasses/sir-hugh-hasting Monumental Brass Society], Sir Hugh Hastyngs*[https://archive.org/stream/churchheraldryn03farrgoog#page/n100/mode/2up ''The Church Heraldry of Norfolk''], page 67.\n\n==Research Notes==\n===Other Data from ''Complete Peerage''===\nFrom ''Complete Peerage'', vol. II, page 495, ELSING.</ref>\n\n===Other Data from ''Dictionary of National Biography''===\nFrom ''Dictionary of National Biography'', vol. 25::He married Margery, elder daughter and eventual heiress of Sir Jordan Foliot, in whose right he acquired estates at Elsing and Gressenhall, Norfolk; he served in Flanders in 1340, and on 25 Feb. 1342 was summoned to parliament, but received no later summons. In 1343 he held a command in Flanders, when three hundred prisoners were captured (Knighton ap. Scriptt. Decem, 2586), and in the same year was in Brittany. He accompanied Henry, earl of Derby (afterwards Duke of Lancaster), to Gascony in 1345, was with him at Bergerac in July, and in the fight at Auberoche in October. In 1346 he formed one of the garrison at the siege of Aguillon (Froissart, iii. 48, 67, 124–5). He died in 1347 and was buried in Elsing Church, which he had built; in the east window there are portraits of Hastings and his wife, with the arms ‘or, a maunche gules,’ and in the chancel there is a very fine brass to his memory (Gough, Ancient Sepulchral Monuments, vol. i. pt. ii. 98–101; Carter, Specimens of Ancient Sculpture, pp. 13, 14, 38, with plates). On a marble slab in the chancel there is the inscription, ‘Yis churche hathe been wrowt by Howe de Hastyng and Margaret hys wyf.’ Margery Hastings died in 1349.\"<ref>Charles Lethbridge Kingsford. \"Hastings, Hugh\" in ''Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900'', vol. 25. Margaret de Clare.</ref><ref>Lipscomb, George. ''The History and Antiquities of the County of Buckingham.'' London: J. & W. Robins (1847), [https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=taAgAQAAMAAJ&pg=GBS.PA200&hl=en vol. 1, pp. 200-201].</ref> She was reported in various sources as being 18, 20, 21, and 22 years of age at the time her brother Gilbert died at Bannockburn in 1314; Richardson estimates her birthdate to have been about 1292/3 and that is the guesstimate used in this profile.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"RAStratAud10\">Richardson, Douglas. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families''.  5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham. Salt Lake City: by the author (2013), vol. 5, pp. 79-81 STRATTON AUDLEY 10. Hugh de Audley.</ref><ref>Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extince, or dormant.'' London: St Catherine Press (1910), [https://archive.org/details/completepeerageo01coka/page/346/mode/1up vol. 1, pp. 346-347]</ref><ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\">Hamilton, J.S. ''Clare, Margaret de, Countess of Gloucester (c.1291/2?-1342).'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004, rev. 3 Jan 2008), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/39593 available here] by subscription.</ref> Her parents held vast estates in England, Wales, and Ireland and it is not known for certain on which of these properties Margaret was born.\nMargaret's father was a soldier, statesman, and shrewd politician who held enormous influence throughout the kingdom.<ref name=\"ODNBGilbert\">Knowles, Clive H. ''Clare, Gilbert de [called Gilbert the Red], seventh earl of Gloucester and sixth earl of Hertford (1243-1295).'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/5438 available here] by subscription.</ref>  He died 7 December 1295,<ref name=\"RAClare8\">Richardson, Douglas. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families.'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham. Salt Lake City: by the author (2013), vol. 2, pp. 195-206 CLARE 8. Gilbert de Clare.</ref> when she was only about two years old. She had three siblings: an older brother, [[Clare-537|Gilbert]], and two sisters; [[Clare-89|Eleanor]] and [[Clare-101|Elizabeth]]. <ref name=\"RAClare8\"/> After de Clare's death, her mother secretly married (second) [[Monthermer-2|Ralph Monthermer]], a squire in earl Gilbert's household whom she had earlier persuaded her father to knight.<ref name=\"ODNBJoan\">Ward, Jennifer C. ''Joan [Joan of Acre], countess of Hertford and Gloucester (1272-1307).'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004, rv 7 Jan 2016), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/14821 available here] by subscription.</ref> The king was so infuriated by this that he had Monthermer thrown into prison in Bristol Castle, but relented and released him after several weeks.<ref name=\"RAClare8\"/><ref name=\"ODNBJoan\"/> Monthermer eventually became a favorite of the king, received the title of earl of Hertford and Gloucester during Joan's lifetime, and the Clare estates were restored to both he and his wife.<ref name=\"RAClare8\"/><ref name=\"ODNBJoan\"/> Joan had two sons and a daughter with Monthermer, <ref name=\"RAClare8\"/><ref name=\"ODNBJoan\"/> and Margaret likely grew up in her mother's household as part of this extended family.\n\n===Marriage to Piers Gaveston===Margaret was married (first) to [[Gaveston-1|Piers Gaveston]], Knt., Earl of Cornwall, Lord of the Isle of Wight, Chamberlain of the Household, Guardian and Lieutenant of England, Lieutenant of Ireland, Keeper of the Castles and Honours of Knaresborough and Wallingford, Justice of the Forest North of Trent, and Constable of Berkhampstead, Carlisle, Nottingham, and Scarborough Castles, on 1 November 1307  at Berkhamsted.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/><ref>Doyle, James E. ''Official Baronage of England.'' London: Longmans, Green, and Co. (1886), [https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=MjAwAAAAYAAJ&pg=GBS.PA438&hl=en vol. 1, p. 438]. Doyle erroneously gives the date of their marriage as 1309.</ref> Gaveston, who was a younger son of [[Gaveston-4|Arnaud de Gabaston]] (a Gascon knight) and [[Marsau-1|Caramonde de Marsan]], was a favorite and close advisor to Edward II, Margaret's uncle, but his influence over the king led to rising hostility from the other magnates at court and eventually to Gaveston's exile.<ref name=\"ODNBPiers\">Hamilton, J.S. ''Gaveston Piers, earl of Cornwall (d. 1312).'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004, rv 3 Jan 2008), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/10463 available here] by subscription.</ref>  One of Edward II's first acts after his father's death was to recall Gaveston and to confer upon him the earldom of Cornwall and the Isle of Man, subsequently arranging a marriage between his niece, Margaret, and Gaveston which he hoped would earn his favorite at least the support of Margaret's brother, the influential earl of Gloucester.<ref name=\"ODNBPiers\"/><ref name=\"Maxwell186\">Maxwell, Sir Herbert (translator). ''The Chronicles of Lanercost 1272-1346.'' Glasgow: J. Maclehose (1913), [https://archive.org/details/chronicleoflaner00maxwuoft/page/186/mode/1up?q=Piers+Gaveston pp. 186].</ref>\nUnfortunately the title conferred on Gaveston and his marriage into one of the kingdom's most prominent families only further infuriated the king's most senior advisors.<ref name=\"ODNBPiers\"/> Eventually even Margaret's own brother, Gilbert, earl of Gloucester, joined the other magnates in demanding that Piers once again be sent into exile.<ref name=\"Maxwell186\"/> Parliament decreed that if Gaveston left the kingdom completely he would be given an annuity for life of £200 for himself and £100 for Margaret (if she were willing to leave the kingdom with him), but the king secretly arranged for Gaveston and Margaret to go to Ireland instead, giving him letters of introduction stating that \"wheresoever he should go within the lands of the King of England, he should be received with the glory and honour due to the person of the king himself.\"<ref name=\"Maxwell187\">Maxwell, Sir Herbert (translator). ''The Chronicles of Lanercost 1272-1346.'' Glasgow: J. Maclehose (1913), [https://archive.org/details/chronicleoflaner00maxwuoft/page/187/mode/1up?q=Piers+Gaveston pp. 187].</ref> Gaveston was also provided with many \"precious and valuable articles\" from the king's treasury and charters sealed with the Great Seal but which were blank...\"whereon [Piers] might write whatever he chose.\"<ref name=\"Maxwell187\"/> The magnates alarm at the influence Gaveston held over their king does not seem to have been unwarranted.\nMargaret had one daughter from her marriage with Piers Gaveston: ''(see [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Clare-613#Research_Notes Research Note])*[[Gaveston-7|Joan de Gavaston]]; born 12 January 1312;<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/> contracted as an infant to marry John Multon, son of Thomas Multon, lord of Egremont<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/> but died 13 January 1325<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/> before any marriage occurred.\nThe king was eventually able to arrange for Gaveston's return from exile but at a great cost politically. On 19 June 1312 Gavaston was assassinated by his political enemies, on the orders of the Earl of Lancaster and the Earl of Warwick.<ref name=\"ODNBPiers\"/><ref>Maxwell, Sir Herbert (translator). ''The Chronicles of Lanercost 1272-1346.'' Glasgow: J. Maclehose (1913), [https://archive.org/details/chronicleoflaner00maxwuoft/page/198/mode/1up?q=Piers+Gaveston pp. 198].</ref> In September 1312 the king granted to Margaret lands valued at 2000 marks per annum (an amount equal to the value of the earldom) for her support (this arrangement was changed on December 1316 but the new settlement gave her an identical annual revenue).<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/>\nIn 1314, Margaret was co-heiress to her brother, Gilbert de Clare, Knight, Earl of Gloucester and Hertford, by which she inherited the Castle, borough, and lordship of Newport; manors of Wentlloog and Machen, Monmouthshire; the Castle and manor of Tonbridge, Kent; and various other manors including in Chipping Ongar, Essex, Campden and Thornbury, Gloucestershire, Naseby, Rothwell, and Whiston, Northamptonshire, Rotherhithe, Surrey.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"RAStratAud10\"/>\n\n===Marriage to Hugh Audley===On 28 April 1317, in King's Chapel at Windsor, Berkshire, England, Margaret married (second) [[Audley-6|Hugh de Audley]], Knt., second son of [[Audley-9|Hugh de Audley]], Lord Audley, Justice of North Wales, Steward of the King's Household, Constable of Montgomery Castle, and Sheriff of Staffordshire, by his wife [[Rous-154|Iseult Rous]].<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"RAStratAud10\"/><ref>''Archaeologia.'' London: Society of Antiquaries of London (1836), [https://archive.org/details/s2id13276850/page/337/mode/1up vol. 26, pp. 337-337]</ref> Margaret's inherited wealth (as her brother's co-heir) had once again made her a valuable matrimonial prospect, and Edward II arranged the marriage to Audley, one of his most trusted remaining advisors, as a reward for services Audley had previously rendered the king.<ref name=\"ODNBAudley\">Maddicott, J.R. ''Audley, Hugh, Earl of Gloucester (c.1291-1347).'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004), [https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/37134 available here] by subscription.</ref> There was one child from this marriage, a daughter:*[[Audley-130|Margaret de Audley]]; born before 1324;.<ref name=\"MCAStafford6\"> Richardson, Douglas. ''Magna Carta Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families'', 4 vols., ed. Kimball G. Everingham, 2nd edition. Salt Lake City: the author (2011), volume 4, pp. 72-74 STAFFORD 6. Margaret de Audley.[https://www.google.co.uk/books/edition/_/8JcbV309c5UC?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PA84&bsq=Margaret+Audley Google books]</ref> married before 6 July 1336 [[Stafford-78|Ralph de Stafford]];<ref name=\"MCAStafford6\"/><ref>Beltz, George Frederick. ''Memorials of the Most Noble Order of the Garter.'' London: W. Pickering (1841), [https://archive.org/details/memorialsofmostn00beltuoft/page/33/mode/1up p. 33].</ref> died 7 September 1349<ref name=\"RAStafford7\">Richardson, Douglas. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families'', 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham. Salt Lake City: the author (2013), vol. 5, pp. 9-11 STAFFORD. 7. Ralph de Stafford.</ref>\nAudley's status as a trusted senior advisor of the king ended when, along with his father, he supported the earl of Lancaster in the insurrection of 1321-2 and in March of that year he was taken prisoner at the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Boroughbridge Battle of Boroughbridge], his lands were seized, and his life spared only due to Margaret's direct appeal to her uncle, the king.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"ODNBAudley\"/><ref name=\"Cooke\">Cooke, William Henry. ''Collections Towards the History and Antiquities of Hereford.'' London: John Murray (1882), [https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=t4gcAQAAMAAJ&pg=GBS.PA8&hl=en pp.8-9].</ref> Margaret herself was held at Sempringham Priory during this time and not allowed to leave the priory's grounds.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/> It is likely that their daughter was born during the early months of Margaret's captivity. \nWhen Edward III took the throne, Audley pledged his allegiance to the new king and his lands were restored to him.<ref name=\"Cooke\"/> He served in nine parliaments under Edward III; was one of the marshals of the royal army and later an ambassador to France; and on 16 March 1336/7 was created earl of Gloucester.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"Cooke\"/><ref>Banks, Thomas Christopher. ''Baronies in Fee.'' Ripon: William Harrison (1844), [https://archive.org/details/baroniaanglicaco01bankuoft/baroniaanglicaco01bankuoft/page/n126/mode/1up p. 103]</ref>\n\n===Death===Margaret predeceased her (second) husband, dying 9 (or 13) April 1342.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref>Weever, John. ''Ancient Funerall Monuments...'' London: Thomas Harper (1631), [https://archive.org/details/ancientfunerallm00weev/page/323/mode/1up p. 323].</ref> She was buried at Queenhithe, London ([https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Michael_Queenhithe St. Michael Queenhithe], a church in the City of London in what is now Upper Thomas Street, first mentioned in the 12th century but destroyed during the Great London Fire of 1666, rebuilt by famed 17th century architect Sir Christopher Wren, and demolished in 1876).<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"RAStratAud10\"/> At her death, the Countess of Gloucester held several manors in Devon and Newport in Essex as part of the dower lands she had received from her marriage to Gaveston.<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/> Her heir was her daughter Margaret, Countess Stafford.<ref name=\"ODNBMargaret\"/> \nHugh de Audley, earl of Gloucester, died 10 November 1347.<ref name=\"MCAStafford5\"/><ref name=\"ODNBAudley\"/>\n\n==Research Notes==\n===2nd Daughter with Piers Gaveston?===John B. Hunt theorized in 1959 that Gaveston and Margaret's daughter Joan was actually born in 1309 and that they had a second daughter, named [[Gaveston-3|Amie]], who was born in 1312.<ref>Hunt, John. G. ''Piers de Gavaston.'' The American Genealogist, vol. 35 (1959), pp. 100-106, [https://www.americanancestors.org/databases/american-genealogist-the/image?volumeId=11866&pageName=100&previousPage=DatabaseSearch&databaseId=283&refreshed=true available here] by subscription.</ref>  Hunt further expanded on this idea in a second article, published in the ''American Genealogist'' in 1961.<ref>Hunt, John G. ''Piers de Gavaston: Second Paper.'' The American Genealogis, vol. 37 (1961), pp. 47-47, [https://www.americanancestors.org/databases/american-genealogist-the/image?pageName=45&volumeId=11878&rId=134743839 available here] by subscription. </ref> Although he presents fairly convincing (circumstantial) evidence that Gaveston may have had a natural daughter named Amie, there is no documentary evidence supporting Margaret de Clare as her mother. More recently, J.S. Hamilton has debunked Hunt's arguments by pointing out, among oher things, the huge fuss and expenditures that Edward II made both when his niece married and when Joan was born: the king not only threw a lavish celebration on the occasion of Joan's birth, but after Gaveston's death arranged to have his daughter educated at the convent at Amesbury with another royal niece, Eleanor of Hereford. The two girls received a joint annual allowance of 100 marks.<ref>PRO E 101/325/13 m.5, cited in Hamilton, J. S. “Another Daughter for Piers Gaveston? Amie de Gaveston, Damsel of the Queen’s Chamber.” Medieval Prosopography 19 (1998): 177–86. http://www.jstor.org/stable/44946288. </ref> It is almost inconceivable that Margaret could have given birth to another child with no record surviving of this, either in the royal wardrobe books, other exchequer accounts, or in any contemporary chronicles, and that the king would have made no effort to provide for a second legitimate daughter belonging to his own niece..<ref> Hamilton, J. S. “Another Daughter for Piers Gaveston? Amie de Gaveston, Damsel of the Queen’s Chamber.” Medieval Prosopography 19 (1998): 177–86. http://www.jstor.org/stable/44946288. </ref>  \n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\nSee also:*Hardy, Thomas Duffus. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families.'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham. Salt Lake City: by the author (2013), vol. 1, pp. 287-291 BEAUCHAMP 10. Guy de Beauchamp.</ref><ref name=\"ODNBGuy\">Hamilton, J.S. ''Beauchamp, Guy de, tenth earl of Warwick.'' Oxford Dictionary of National Biography online edition (23 Sep 2004, rv 3 Jan 208). (1886), [https://play.google.com/books/reader?id=DO8IAAAAIAAJ&pg=GBS.PA577 pp. 578-579].</ref> Guy's exact date of birth is unknown, but was likely to have been about 1271 (aged 27 and more in 1298 when his father died;<ref>\"Inquisitions Post Mortem, Edward I, File 86,\" in Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem: Volume 3, Edward I, ed. J.E.E.S. Sharp and A.E. Stamp (London: His Majesty's Stationery Office, 1912), 375-387. British History Online, accessed January 10, 2024, http://www.british-history.ac.uk/inquis-post-mortem/vol3/pp375-387, #477.</ref> and 30 years and more when his mother died in 1301<ref> \"Inquisitions Post Mortem, Edward I, File 100,\" in Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem: Volume 4, Edward I, ed.J E E S Sharp and A E Stamp (London: His Majesty's Stationery Office, 1913), 9-16. British History Online, accessed January 10, 2024, http://www.british-history.ac.uk/inquis-post-mortem/vol4/pp9-16, #24.</ref>).\nOn his father's death in 1298, Guy succeeded as earl of Warwick.<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/><ref>Cawley, Charles. Foundation for Medieval Genealogy online database (2001). [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLISH%20NOBILITY%20MEDIEVAL.htm#_Toc56410532 Earls of Warwick - Beauchamp].\n</ref>\n\n===Military Career and Positions Held===Guy de Beauchamp held the hereditary titles of '''Sheriff of Worcester''' and '''Chamberlain of the Exchequer.'''<ref name=\"Cok370\">Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extinct, or dormant.'' London: St. Catherine Press (1959), [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/579047/?offset=0#page=379&viewer=picture&o=info&n=0&q= vol. 12 (2), p. 370].</ref> On 25 March 1296 he was knighted by Edward I,<ref>Moor, Rev. C. ''The Knights of Edward I.'' Great Britain: John Whitehead and Son, Ltd. (H.S.P. 80) (1929), [https://www.forgottenbooks.com/en/books/KnightsofEdwardI_11360019 pp. 70-71].</ref> and on 22 July 1298 he fought in the king's division at the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Falkirk Battle of Falkirk].<ref name=\"Cok370\"/><ref name=\"DNB\">Round, John Horace. [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography,_1885-1900/Beauchamp,_Guy_de ''Beauchamp, Guy de.''] Dictionary of National Biography archive edition online.</ref> For his bravery on the field, he was granted 1000 marks of the lands previously held by Geoffry de Mowbray and John de Strivelyn, and the land of Drungrey and castle of Amesfeld once held by Andrew de Chartres.<ref>Bain, Joseph (ed.). ''Calendar of Documents Relating to Scotland.'' Edinburgh: H.M. General Register Office (1881), [https://archive.org/details/calendarofdocume02edin/page/258/mode/1up vol. 2, p. 258, no. 1009].</ref>\nHe was called to serve in the campaign against Scotland (from 1299-1314)  and in 1301 was one of seven earls whose seal was appended to a letter to the pope, rejecting the pope's authority on the question of Scottish independence.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/>\nWarwick further distinguished himself at the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caerlaverock_Castle#Siege_of_Caerlaverock Siege of Caerlaverock] and later at the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sieges_of_Stirling_Castle#Siege_of_1304 Siege of Stirling Castle].<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/> For these services he was granted Barnard Castle and the town of the same name which had been held by John Balliol, as well as the manor of Gaynefford and all lands in that bishopric held in dower by Agnes, late wife of Hugh de Balliol, and lands in Querington which had been held in dower by Eleanor, late wife of Alexander de Balliol.<ref>Lyte, Sir Henry C.M. ''Calendar of Charter Rolls 1226-1516.'' London: H.M. Stationery Office (1903), [https://archive.org/details/calendarofcharte03grea/page/79/mode/1up vol. 3, p. 79].</ref><ref>''Calendar of Patent Rolls, Edward I 1301-1307.'' London: H.M. Stationery Office (1898), [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015009161343&seq=540 p. 492].</ref>\nHe was present on 7 July 1307 at Edward I's death bed, and was one of the magnates charged by the king to safeguard Prince Edward and to never let the prince's favorite, [[Gaveston-1|Piers Gaveston]], return to the kingdom.<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/><ref name=\"Dugdale\">Dugdale, Sir William. ''The Baronage of England.'' (1675),[https://quod.lib.umich.edu/cgi/t/text/pageviewer-idx?cc=eebo;c=eebo;idno=a36794.0001.001;node=A36794.0001.001:6.53;seq=242;vid=52914;page=root;view=text pp. 229-231], Guy de Beauchamp.</ref>  When Edward II immediately recalled Gaveston from exile and granted him the earldom of Cornwall, Warwick was the only earl to refuse to put his seal on Gaveston's charter.<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/> Gaveston nicknamed Warwick \"the black hound of Arden\" due to his dark complexion, and the hostility between the two men was noted by contemporary historians.<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/><ref name=\"DNB\"/> In 1307 Warwick, renowned for his skills as a warrior, was unhorsed by Gaveston at a tournament at Wallingford, after which Warwick was said to have sworn that \"the hound would live to bite [Gaveston].\"<ref>Walden, Howard de. ''Some Feudal Lords and Their Seals.'' London: de Walden Library (1904), [https://archive.org/details/somefeudallordst00howauoft/somefeudallordst00howauoft/page/n77/mode/1up pp. 16-17] </ref> \nWarwick advocated strongly for the appointment of \"ordainers\" to reform the king's household and realm, and was himself chosen to serve in this group.<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/><ref name=\"DNB\"/> The Ordainers forced the king to  exile Gaveston for a third time, and when Gaveston once again returned  to England a small group of magnates, which included Warwick and the earls of Lancaster, Hereford and Pembroke, captured and ultimately beheaded him without a trial. According to the ''Annales Londonienses'' it was Warwick who ordered that Gaveston's body be left at the side of the road, unburied.<ref>Stubbs, William (ed.). ''Annales Londonienses.'' London: Longman and Co. (1882), [https://books.google.com/books?id=P5o4AQAAMAAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false p. 207].</ref> Gaveston's murder came close to setting off a civil war between the king and the rebel earls, although a long year of negotiations finally resulted in their being pardoned.<ref name=\"DNB\"/> Warwick held so much power that the king \"...was obliged to grant [a pardon] to him, but never loved him afterward.\"<ref name=\"Edmondson\"/> Despite receiving a pardon, Warwick refused to serve in the king's army at the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bannockburn Battle of Bannockburn].<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"DNB\"/><ref name=\"Dugdale\"/>\n\n===Marriage to Isabel de Clare===He married (first) sometime after 4 March 1291 (date of letter)<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/> and before 11 May 1297 (date of papal dispensation allowing them to remain in the marriage despite being related in the fourth degree of kindred, and declaring any future children to be legitimate)<ref>\"Regesta 48: 1296-1297,\" in Calendar of Papal Registers Relating To Great Britain and Ireland: Volume 1, 1198-1304, ed. W H Bliss (London: Her Majesty's Stationery Office, 1893), 563-574. British History Online, accessed January 11, 2024, http://www.british-history.ac.uk/cal-papal-registers/brit-ie/vol1/pp563-574, 5Id. May. St. Peter's (f.245d.).</ref>[[Clare-63|Isabel de Clare]], a daughter of [[Clare-98|Gilbert de Clare]], 6th Earl of Gloucester and Hertford, and [[Lusignan-82|Alice de Lusignan]] of Angoulême.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"Cok371\">Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extinct, or dormant.'' London: St. Catherine Press (1959), [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/579047/?offset=0#page=379&viewer=picture&o=info&n=0&q= vol. 12 (2), p. 371].</ref>  Isabel is said to have been born 10 March 1262/3,<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"Cok371fn.j\">Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extinct, or dormant.'' London: St. Catherine Press (1959), [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/579047/?offset=0#page=379&viewer=picture&o=info&n=0&q= vol. 12 (2), p. 371, fn.J].</ref> which would have made her anywhere from 28-34 years of age at the time of this marriage. Guy and Isabel were separated in or before 1302 (when she was 39 years of age), and there were no children from the marriage.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/> It is possible that Isabel's age and the lack of an heir is what precipitated their separation.  Isabel remarried about 1316 (at the age of 53 years), as his second wife, [[Berkeley-42|Maurice de Berkeley]], 2nd lord Berkeley.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"Cok371fn.j\"/>\n===Marriage to Alice de Toeni===Guy de Beauchamp married (second) before 28 February 1309/10 [[Toeni-8|Alice de Toeni]], daughter of [[Toeni-7|Ralph de Toeni]], Knt. of Flamstead, and the widow of [[Leybourne-13|Thomas de Leybourne]], Knt. Leybourne, Kent.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp10\"/><ref name=\"Cok371\"/><ref>Munford, Rev. George. ''An Analysis of the Domesday Book of Norfolk.'' ''The History and Antiquities of the County of Northampton.'' London: J.B. ''The History and Antiquities of Hertford.'' London: Nichols, Son, and Bentley (1815),[https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog/188626?availability=Family%20History%20Library vol. 1, p. 358].</ref> died 13 November 1369<ref name=\"Baker\"/> <ref name=\"RABeauchamp11\"/><ref name=\"Clutter358\"/><ref name=\"Blomefield\">Blomefield, Francis. \"Hundred of Wayland: Saham-Tony,\" in An Essay Towards A Topographical History of the County of Norfolk: Volume 2, London: W Miller (1805), 319-330. [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography,_1885-1900/Beauchamp,_Guy_de ''Beauchamp, Guy de.''] Dictionary of National Biography archive edition online.</ref> He was buried at Bordesley Abbey, Warwickshire, a Cistercian house to which he had earlier given his private library (which consisted of 42 volumes, a substantial collection of books during that time<ref>Hicks, M.A. ''Who's Who in late medieval England.'' London: Shepheard-Walwyn (1991), [https://archive.org/details/whoswhoinlatemed0000hick/page/46/mode/2up pp. 44-46]</ref>).<ref name=\"ODNBGuy\"/><ref name=\"Cok372\">Cokayne, George Edward. ''The Complete Peerage of England, Scotland, Ireland, Great Britain, and the United Kingdom: extant, extinct, or dormant.'' London: St. Catherine Press (1959), [https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/579047/?offset=0#page=379&viewer=picture&o=info&n=0&q= vol. 12 (2), p. 372].</ref>\n\n===Will===Guy’s Will was dated 25 July 1315. In it he requested burial at Bordsley Abbey, Warwickshire; named his second wife Alice; two of his daughters, Maud and Elizabeth; and his sons John and Thomas.<ref>Nicholas Harris Nicolas. ''Testamenta Vetusta'', Vol. I, Nichols and Son, 1826, pp. 53-54, [https://archive.org/details/testamentavetust01nico/page/52/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref><ref>Tegg, William. ''Wills of Their Own.'' London: William Tegg & Co. (1876), [https://books.google.com/books?id=lY80AAAAIAAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false pp. 6-7.]</ref>  Three of his daughters were not named in his will: it is likely that as all of his children were six years of age or younger provision had not yet been made for the youngest of them. His heir was his eldest son Thomas, who was about two years of age,  and who, after his father's death, became a ward of the king.<ref name=\"RABeauchamp11\"/><ref name=\"Blomefield\"/><ref name=\"Cok372\"/><ref> ''Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem and Other Analogous Documents preserved in the Public Record Office.'' The castle and manor of Leybourne, Kent were briefly taken into the control of the Crown: Alice was given full possession of them on 17 September 1307, paying a fine of 100 shillings.<ref name=\"Thomas de Leyburne IPM\"/>\nTwo years later, in 1309, following the death of her childless brother Robert, Alice became a wealthy woman, inheriting property scattered across a number of counties in East Anglia and southern England, along with two castles in Radnorshire, Wales.<ref name=\"Robert de Toeni IPMs\"/> Very soon after she became the wife of [[Beauchamp-75|Guy de Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick]]: they married between 12 January and 28 February 1309/10. His possible previous marriage, to [[Clare-63|Isabel de Clare]] (daughter of Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester), had been either annulled or may never have been completed or consummated.<ref name=\"MCA 1.136\"/><ref name=\"RA 1.287\"/><ref name=\"Cokayne Warwick\">G E Cokayne. Like her second husband,  William had been involved in the death of Piers Gaveston. Orders were given for Alice's rights to be respected.<ref>The National Archives, ref. SC 8/153/7633, [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C9209822 Discovery Centre catalogue entry]</ref><ref>The National Archives, ref. SC 8/153/7634, [https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C9209823 Discovery Centre catalogue entry]</ref> \nAlice died before 8 January 1325, when writs were issued for her Inquisitions Post Mortem.       "notes": "[[Category: Earls of March]][[Category:Ireland, Governors]] [[Category:Ireland, Bruce Invasion of Ireland]] [[Category: 14th Century]] [[Category:EuroAristo_-_Profiles_that_need_work]][[Category:Lordship of Radnor]][[Category:Early Barony of Wigmore]]\n{{Easily Confused\n|profile1=[[Mortimer-77|Roger Mortimer]] 1st Earl of March\n|profile2=[[Mortimer-51|Roger Mortimer]] 2nd Earl of March\n|profile3=[[Mortimer-81|Roger Mortimer]] son of 1st Earl of March\n}}\n==Biography==Roger was a Marcher Lord. He led the baronial opposition to Edward II's favorites (1320-22) and was imprisoned before fleeing to France. There he became the lover of Edward's Queen, Isabella, with whose support, he secured Edward's deposition and murder in 1327. He then ruled England in the  name of Edward's son, Edward III, until the latter caused him to be executed.\n\"Roger was the first of several members of his family to attempt to seize the throne of England. ...  A descendant of Norman knights who had accompanied William the Conqueror. In 1304 he became 8th Baron of Wigmore on the death of his father, the 7th Baron. He led the baronial opposition to Edward II's favorites (1320-22) and was imprisoned before fleeing to France.  There he became the lover of Edward's Queen Isabella with whom he secured Edward's deposition and murder in 1327.  He then ruled England in the name of Edward's son Edward III, until the latter caused him to be hanged as a traitor.\"<ref>www.rootsweb.com/~gumby/cgi-bin/igmget.cgi/n=Winch?I05845]  (broken link not on archive.org 29 March 2024)</ref>\n\" He fought the Scots and made attempts to remove the King's favorites, at first with some success. In 1323 he was imprisoned in the Tower of London, but escaped to France, an event he later commemorated by building St Peter's chapel in the outer bailey of Ludlow Castle. \n \"In France, Mortimer allied with [[Capet-116|Queen Isabella]], who deserted her effeminate husband, [[Plantagenet-378|King Edward II of England]]. They raised an army, invaded England and forced Edward to abdicate in favor of his youngest son,  [[Plantagenet-70|Edward III]]. \nMortimer entertained Isabella at his castles on the Welsh borders where they became infamous lovers. Meanwhile, [[Plantagenet-378|Edward II]] was cruelly murdered at Berkeley Castle in 1327.<ref> by Thomas de Gournai and [[Maltravers-5|John Mautravers]] for [[Mortimer-77|Roger Mortimer]].  Jones, Joseph, [http://bit.ly/1fKUn3O Brief outlines of English history]. retrieved 2014-05-05, [[Bairfield-1|amb]]</ref> \n \"Following Edward's death, Mortimer, acting as regent, was the virtual ruler of England, but he over-reached himself and aroused the anger of other barons. In October 1330 he was arrested at Nottingham and sentenced to death. He was executed at Tyburn in London. \n \"Later, the ambitions of the Mortimers became part of the great dynastic struggles of the mid-15th century which became known as the \"War of the Roses.\" \n \"In 1330, Sir William Eland conducted King Edward through a passage in Nottingham Castle when he seized Lord Mortimer, and brought him out of the castle. This was afterwards called Mortimer's Hole, in memory of that unfortunate nobleman, a name which is erroneously given to the principal vault.\"<ref>Our Folk & Our Folk Revisited:  https://web.archive.org/web/20070403231551/http://www.aritek.com/hartgen/htm/corbet_2.htm#name2249</ref>\nIt is alleged that William Ogle and Sir Thomas Gurney murdered King Edward II in 1327, allies of Roger Mortimer.<ref>\"THE PLANTAGENETS\" by Dan Jones  2013 pp. 357-358</ref>\n===Vitals===\n::   Alt. Church Of Grey F, Shrewsbury, ShropshireNote:  Although Douglas Richardson states that Mortimer was buried at the Grey Friars Church in Shrewsbury Shropshire, per the 14th century Wigmore Chronicles and at Wigmore Abbey per Wikipedia, the author Ian Mortimer in his book \"The Greatest Traitor\" states that Roger de Mortimer was buried at the Grey Friars Church in Coventry.\nThe reason for this belief is as follows:Upon his death at Tyburn Elms in London, Roger de Mortimer's body was appropriated by the Coventry friars eager to obtain such an eminent corpse.Some doubts remain as to whether Mortimer's body was relocated to Wigmore. A petition from his wife Joan dated 1332 suggests he might have remained buried at Coventry, despite Edward III's order of the previous years which may have ordered burial elsewhere such as possibly the Grey Friars Church in Shrewsbury.Since Coventry was a city within (his lover) Queen Isabella's sphere of influence, it is possible that she persuaded her son Edward III to leave Mortimer buried in the friary there.The church of the Grey Friars in Coventry and Shrewsbury were destroyed in Henry VIII's Dissolution of the Monasteries in the 16th century as well as Wigmore Abbey in Herefordshire. As with the tombs of numerous other nobles of that era, the actions of that time has caused Roger de Mortimer's burial place to be lost.\n\n===Titles===\n::  2. Cr.
