De skall ha fått åtminstone två barn; \n* '''Magnus''' Eriksson\n* '''Eufemia''' Eriksdotter\n\nMaken Erik dog i fångenskap på Nyköpingshus 1318.\n1327 gifte sig änkehertiginnan Ingeborg med '''Knut Porse''' , de fikk två barn innan han avlider 1330; \n* '''Håkan''' \n* '''Knut'''  \nBåde Håkan och Knut dog i digerdöden 1350. Efter sönernas död ärvde hon hertigdömet Halland.\n\nIngeborg själv dog den 17 juni 1361.\n\n==Biography==\n:{{EuroAristo Sticker}}Ingebjørg Håkonsdotter was Håkon V only legitimate child and was from birth used as a political piece. Norwegian Law of Succession was changed (in 1302) so that a genuine born daughter and her legitimate son was moved up into third place in the line of succession and real born  daughter in seventh place. It was the first time that Norwegian succession opened for a reigning queen, and choice of spouse was therefore given even greater political significance. \nThe Alliance between King Haakon V, and the Swedish dukes was finally confirm in 1312, when Ingebjørg Haakonsdotter was married on 29,Sept.that year with Erik Magnusson (1282 - 1318), and her cousin Ingebjørg Eriksdotter was married to Waldemar Magnusson (1280 - 1318) (duke of Finnland from 1302).Ingebjørg Haakonsdotter's son Magnus 7.Eriksson, became a King both in Norway and Sweden only 3 years old.  As a queen mother and for Norway with her own right of succession to the throne, Ingebjørg was given a prominent position in both countries, but without a formal place in the national goverment. But gradually she teied to gain independent influence on the national government in order to continue duke Erik's Nordic policy, now in the name of her son King Magnus.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references/>\n*Isl.Ann.\n*Erikskrönikan, ed. of S.-B.       "notes": "[[Category:House of Ivrea]]\n[[Category:Battle of Écija (1275)]]\n[[Category: House of Bourgogne]]\n[[Category:This Day In History November 23]]\n[[Category:This Day In History April 04]]\n[[Category:Tournament of Compiègne (1278)]]\n[[Category:Spain, Monarchs]]\n== Biography ==\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n{{Notables Sticker}}\n===Alfonso X, King of Castile and León===Alfonso X (also occasionally Alphonso X, Alphonse X, or Alfons X), 23 November 1221 – 4 April 1284, called the Wise (Spanish: el Sabio), was the King of Castile, León and Galicia from 30 May 1252 until his death. He was of the House of Ivrea, a medieval Frankish dynasty of Burgundian origin which rose to prominence in Italy in the tenth century, even briefly holding the Italian throne. They also ruled the County of Burgundy in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. A cadet branch ruled the Kingdom of Galicia from 1111 and the Kingdoms of Castile and León from 1126 until 1369.\nBorn in Toledo, Spain, Alfonso was the eldest son of Ferdinand III of Castile and Elizabeth (Beatrice) of Swabia. His mother was the paternal cousin of Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. His maternal grandparents were Philip of Swabia and Irene Angelina. For the first nine years of his life he was only heir to Castile until his father succeeded his own father Alfonso IX of Leon and united the kingdoms of Castile and Leon. Alfonso succeeded his father as King of Castile and León in 1252.\n\n\n===Family===: m.       "notes": "[[Category:House of Plantagenet]][[Category:Earls of Lancaster]]\n[[Category:Ninth Crusade]][[Category:Early Honour of Lancaster]][[Category:House of Lancaster]][[Category:Early Barony of Leicester]][[Category:Early Barony of Monmouth]][[Category:Earls of Leicester]][[Category:Feudal Barony of Tutbury]]\n\n==Biography==\n\n{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Lancaster\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-17.png}}\n\n===Names===\n:Edmund Plantagenet, 1st Earl of Lancaster and Leicester (16 Jan 1245 – 5 Jun 1296)\n: Edmund Crouchback\n\n===Titles===\n: King of Sicily \n: Earl of Leicester\n: Earl of Lancaster \n: Count of Aumale \n\n===Birth and Parentage===\nEdmund Crouchback was born 16 January 1245, and was the second surviving son of King Henry III of England of the House of Plantagenet and Queen Eleanor of Provence (Eleanore Berenger).  <ref name=\"edmund\"> Wikipedia, Edmund Crouchback, http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Crouchback </ref>\nEdmund was born in London. He was a younger brother of Edward I of England, Margaret of England, and Beatrice of England, and an older brother of Katherine of England.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===Public Life, Part 1===\nIn his childhood he had a claim on the Kingdom of Sicily, but he never ruled there. \nIn 1255 (at the age of 10) he was invested ruler of the Kingdom of Sicily and Apulia by the Bishop of Romania, on behalf of Pope Innocent IV. In return his father undertook to pay the papacy 135,541 marks and fight a war to dislodge Manfred of Sicily from the kingdom. Upon Innocent's death, Pope Alexander IV confirmed Edmund's grant of Sicily.[2] Henry's barons refused to contribute to what they called the \"Sicilian business\" and ultimately Henry was only able to pay 60,000 marks. Stephen Runciman says the grant of the kingdom was revoked by Pope Alexander IV on 18 December 1258;[3] Baines and Harland state that this occurred in 1263 under Pope Urban IV. Edmund renounced his claim to the crown of Sicily.  <ref name=\"edmund\"/>\nAt about the same time Edmund was granted Sicily, he was made Earl of Chester.[2] In 1263, the Earldom of Chester was transferred to his elder brother Edward, who required the palatinate income.  <ref name=\"edmund\"/>\nIn 1265 he was granted all the lands of Simon de Montfort and from 1267 he was titled Earl of Leicester. In that year he also began to rule Lancashire, but he did not take the title Earl of Lancaster until 1276. \nEdmund soon obtained, however, important possessions and dignities, for soon after the forfeiture of Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester on 25 October 1265, Edmund received the Earldom of Leicester[2] and later that of Lancaster. He was granted the honour of the Stewardship of England and the lands of Nicolas de Segrave. He also acquired the titles and estates of Lord Ferrers, that included the earldom of Derby, and the Honour of Hinckley Castle.In 1267 he was granted the lordship of Builth Wells in opposition to the then holder, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd (the last prince of an independent Wales). To help him conquer the land he was also granted his elder brother's lordships of the Trilateral of Skenfrith, Grosmont and White Castle together with Monmouth. After the civil war in 1267, he was appointed High Sheriff of Lancashire. Henry III created his second son Earl of Leicester in 1267, granting the honour and privileges of that city. The following year, he was made Constable of Leicester Castle, a royal possession in the king's name. By now Crouchback had a reputation for being a ruthless and ferocious warrior, but he was not in England fighting de Montfort.[4]<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===First Marriage to Aveline de Forz===\nm.1 8 April 1269 Aveline de Forz dau of William de Forz, 4th Earl of Albemarle and Isabel de Reviers, Countess of Aumale (also known as Isabella de Fortibus, Countess of Devon).  She died just 4 years after the marriage at 15, and was buried at Westminster Abbey.  The couple had no children, though some sources believe she died in childbirth or shortly after a miscarriage.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===Public Life, Part 2===\nIn 1271 he accompanied his elder brother Edward on the Ninth Crusade to Palestine. Some historians, including the authors of the Encyclopædia Britannica article on him, state that it was because of this that he received the nickname Crouchback (which means \"cross back\") indicating that he was entitled to wear a cross stitched into the back of his garments.Edmund remained loyal to his brother, Edward I, who confirmed the Charter grants of 1265, 1267, and 1268-9, in a document of Inspeximus in 1284, and by parliament in the Great Charter of Leicester.[5] He fequently acted as an ambassador abroad. In 1291, he was sent as Governor of Ponthieu, on behalf of his second wife, Blanche of Artois.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\nOn his return from the Crusade of 1271-2 he seems to have made Grosmont Castle his favoured home and undertook much rebuilding there. His son Henry, 3rd Earl of Lancaster was apparently born there in 1281.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===Second marriage to Blanche d'Artois===\nHe married (2nd) in Paris, on 3 February 1276 to Blanche of Artois, widow of Enrique (or Henri) I, King of Navarre, Count of Champagne and Brie, and daughter of Robert I of Artois and Matilda of Brabant. <ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===Children of Edmund and Blanche===\n\nWith Blanche he had three children:\n#[[Plantagenet-315|Thomas, 2nd Earl of Lancaster]], (born 1278, executed 22 March 1322)#[[Plantagenet-129|Henry, 3rd Earl of Lancaster]] (born 1281, died 22 September 1345)#[[Plantagenet-302|John of Lancaster]], seigneur of Beaufort (present day Montmorency, Aube, arrond. d’Arcis-sur-Aube, canton de Chavanges) and Nogent-l’Artaud (Aisne, arrond. de Château-Thierry, canton de Charly), France. He married before July 1312 Alix de Joinville, widow of Jean d’Arcis, seigneur of Arcis-sur-Aube and Chacenay (died in or before 1307), and daughter of Jean de Joinville, seigneur de Joinville (Haute-Marne, arrond. Vassy, ch.-I. canton), Seneschal of Champagne, by his 2nd wife, Alix, daughter and heiress of Gautier, seigneur of Reynel. They had no issue. He died in France shortly before 13 June 1317. See Foundations 1(3) (2004): 198–199.\nOther children shown as being from this marriage are not, and further research is required to determine where they belong:\n\n#[[Leycester-9|Nicholas]]\n#[[Plantagenet-309|Mary]]\n\n===Public Life, Part 3===\nBetween 1276 and 1284 he was also Count of Champagne and Brie, governing those counties in right of his second wife, Blanche of Artois, until her daughter from a previous marriage came of age. His nickname, \"Crouchback\" (meaning \"crossed -back\"), refers to his participation in the Ninth Crusade.[1]<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\nEdmund's duty to the church included the foundation of the Nuns of Clara, Minories, at St Aldate's. In 1291, his estate paid for the establishment for the Chapel of Savoy, in memory of his mother, at St Clement Danes. Filial piety was part of the chivalric code of an honourable knight. He was a generous benefactor to the monastery of Grace Dieu in Leicestershire, and the nuns at Tarrant Crawford.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\nHe also helped establish a major Grey friars monastery at Preston in the duchy of Lancaster. In 1281 he supervised the construction of Aberystwyth Castle for King Edward I to subjugate the Welsh. The next year he accompanied Roger Mortimer on campaign against Llywelyn, defeating and capturing the prince.He took an army to Bordeaux for his brother. Amongst the nobles[6] was the Earl of Lincoln and 26 banneret knights. During the siege of Bayonne the English ran out of money, so the army melted into the countryside. Broken-hearted the warrior-prince Edmund Crouchback died on 5 June. His body was carried to England and was interred on 15 July 1296 at Westminster Abbey, London.<ref name=\"edmund\"/>\n\n===Death and Burial===\nHe fell ill on 13 May 1296 and died while on campaign on 5 June 1296, <ref name=\"edmund\"/>when besieging Bordeaux for his brother on 5 June 1296 in Bayonne, and was interred on 15 July 1296 at Westminster Abbey. In 1298, his widow Blanche of Artois received a third of Edmund's estates as part of her dowry. <ref>''Calendar of inquisitions post mortem and other analogous documents preserved in the Public Record Office /prepared under the superintendence of the Deputy Keeper of the Records.'' (1904 ), Vol. 3. (p.288), no.423.  London : Printed for H.M. Stationery Office by Mackie and to be purchased from Eyre and Spottiswoode. [https://archive.org/details/calendarofinquis03lond/page/288/mode/1up?q=%22king%27s+brother%22 Internet Archive.] Accessed 28 Jun 2026.</ref>\nAdditional note. (Royal Tombs of Medieval England) Edmund was buried first in the Minories church near Aldgate, London, a Franciscan nunnery founded by the earl and his second wife, Blanche of Champagne, four years earlier. In 1300 Edmund was reburied in Westminster Abbey, his heart remaining at the Minories. As early as the 1290s the tombs of Henry III's son, Edmund, Earl of Lancaster, and his wife, Aveline de Forz, were erected outside the Confessor's Chapel to the north of the Westminster High Altar, a position of considerable sanctity, but one removed from the most sacred relics, suggesting that considerations of seniority were being applied.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. I page 144''' \n\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. III page 476''' \nBLANCHE OF ARTOIS, married (1st) ENRIQUE (or HENRI) I el Gordo, King of Navarre, Count Palatine of Champagne and Brie [see Blois 7]; (2nd) EDMUND OF ENGLAND, Knt., Earl of Lancaster, Leicester, and Derby [see Lancaster7]. \n\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. I page 395''' \n\n*Royal Tombs of Medieval England M. Wikipedia. Accessed April 28, 2026. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traidenis</ref> He belonged to the early Lithuanian ruling elite, but his ancestry is not documented in surviving medieval sources.   His wife's name is unknown, and he had at least one known child:\n\n*[[Traidenaitė-1|Gaudemunda (abt.1260-abt.1288)]]\nHis daughter Gaudemunda later married into the Piast dynasty of Masovia, forming a dynastic alliance between Lithuania and Poland.\nThere are conflicting traditions regarding Traidenis’ death. Some chronicles describe his assassination around 1283, others report a natural death, and a third account claims he was killed by mercenaries in 1282. None of these accounts are confirmed by reliable contemporary sources.\n==Research Notes==The previously assigned name “Kentauras” is not supported by medieval sources. There are no 13th–14th century records identifying Traidenis or his family with a “Kentauras” dynasty. The term appears in later speculative or legendary genealogical traditions that attribute symbolic or mythic ancestry to early Lithuanian rulers. It is not attested in modern sources as a dynastic house for this period. Traidenis is more accurately identified as a member of the early ruling elite of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and he is not known to have a documented hereditary surname or dynastic family name in surviving medieval sources.\n== Sources ==\n<references />"

      "notes": "[[Category: Spain, Monarchs]]\n{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Capet\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-3.png}}\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\nPhilippe V de France, Philippe le Long (the Tall), born circa 1292/1293, died 2-3 January 1322 at Longchamp (Paris), Regent of France (June-December 1316), then roi de France (King of France) 1316 to 1322, the second last King of the direct Capetian dynasty. Also King of Navarre as Felipe II.\n\n== Biography ==\n=== Origins ===Philippe was born about 1292 or 1293<ref>Kerrebrouck, p.163 & note 5, p. 166.</ref>, the second son of [[Capet-575|Philippe IV 'le Bel', roi de France]] and his wife [[Navarre-49|Juana (Jeanne), Queen of Navarre]].  He was recognised as Comte palatin de Bourgogne and Sire de Salins, through the rights of his wife in a treaty dated 26 June 1310 and was granted the title and lands of Comte de Poitiers for himself and his heirs in December 1311.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 163.</ref>\n\n=== Regent and King ===Philippe's elder brother Louis X died on 5 June 1316, leaving a four year old daughter Jeanne from his first marriage to Marguerite de Bourgogne, and his second wife Klemencia (Clemence) d'Anjou, Princess of Hungary was pregnant.  After some opposition, Philippe was created Regent of both France and Navarre from 16 July 1316 and continued as such after the birth of his nephew Jean on 14 November 1316.  Jean died after only five days and Philippe took the initiative and was annointed and crowned King (roi de France) on 6 January 1317 at Cathedral of Notre Dame, at Rheims by Archbishop Robert de Courtenay.<ref>Kerrebrouck.</ref> \nThere was still some doubt about the legalities of his actions, particularly in overturning the rights of his niece Jeanne, and on 2 Februrary 1317 Philippe assembled at Paris, many nobles, churchmen and some bourgeois as well as the doctors from the University to make a judgement. On 3 February this assembly proclaimed what was to become the Salic Law, that 'a woman does not succeed to the throne of France' (femme ne succede pas au royaume de France).<ref>Tuchman, p. 44-45; Franklin, p. 34.</ref>\n\n=== Family ===\n'''Marriage'''\nPhilippe married Jeanne de Bourgogne, later comtesse palatin de Bourgogne as Jeanne II, and comtesse d'Artois, as Jeanne I.  She was the elder daughter of Othon (Otto) IV de Chalon, comte palatin de Bourgogne, and his second wife, Mahaut (Mathilde) d'Artois, comtesse d'Artois.  She was born sometime between 1291-1294<ref>see her biography for further discussion</ref> and definitely before 2 March 1294/95 when a marriage contract was signed at Vincennes (Val-de-Marne).  Their marriage was then celebrated at Corbeil (Marne) in January 1306/07.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 164; Cawley; Anselme, p. 94.</ref>\nIn Spring of 1314, Jeanne was charged with adultery along with her sister Blanche, the wife of her brother-in-law Charles (IV) of France, and her sister-in-law, Marguerite de Bourgogne, wife of Louis (X), in what is known as the [http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tour_de_Nesle_Affair&oldid=577048163 Tour de Nesle Affair].  Although both Marguerite and Blanche were found guilty, Jeanne was proven innocent, largely through the efforts of her husband, and returned to him about Christmas 2014.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 169, note 45</ref>\n\n'''Children'''\nPhilippe and Jeanne were definitely the parents of the following five children;#Jeanne (III), born 1 or 2 May 1308, eventually succeeded her mother as comtesse palatin de Bourgogne & comtesse d'Artois; betrothed at Louvre, Paris 6 April 1313 to Hughes V, Duc de Bourgogne (born 1294, died May 1315) and secondly to his brother and successor, Eudes IV, Duc de Bourgogne, 29 September 1316 at Nogent-sur-Seine (Aube)who she married 18 June 1318 at Paris;#Marguerite, born 1309, succeeded to Bourgogne and Artois on the death of her great-nephew; married by contract 21 June 1320 at Paris and in person 22 July 1320, Louis I de Flandre, comte de Flanders;#Isabelle, born 1310, married (1) by treaty 18 June 1316 at Lyon (Rhone) and by contract at Dole (Jura) 17 May 1323 and celebrated the same day; Guigues VIII, Dauphin de Viennois (died 28 July 1333); (2) circa 1339, Jean III, Seigneur de Faucogney;#Blanche, born in 1311 or 1312, promised as a child as a nun at Abbaye de Longchamp, taking the habit as a Franciscan nun 1319, and died 26 April 1358;#Louis (or Philippe), born 1316 (possibly 24 June)<ref>Cawley has this date, citing ''Flores historiarum'' by Bernard Guidonis, but it is repeated by no other source and may not be reliable</ref> , died young 18 February 1317 and buried in Church of Cordeliers, Paris.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 166</ref>\n\n'''Additional children'''\nAlthough there is every reason to suppose that Philippe and Jeanne might have had additional children, particularly during the periods 1312-1315 and 1317-1322, the following are disputed;#Additional son, died young, perhaps named Philippe.  A number of sources,<ref>Franklin, p. 36, and some Wikipedia articles</ref> gives them a son named Philippe, born in 1313, but this is generally thought to be confused with a son of that name, of Charles IV and Blanche de Bourgogne;#Daughter unnamed born 1322 is mentioned in the French version of the Wikipedia article for Jeanne de Bourgogne but with no references or sources.  Apart from wikipedia articles in other languages, no other source mentions this child.\n\n=== Death and burial ===Philippe had been suffering from dysentery for a number of months and died at Longchamps the night of the 2-3 January 1322.  He was buried at Abbaye royale de St Denis.\n \n=== Further information ===\nIn English\nWikipedia: [http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Philip_V_of_France&oldid=586867090 Philip V of France]\n\nFrench\nWikipedia.fr [http://fr.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Philippe_V_de_France&oldid=100114740 Philippe V de France]\n\n== Sources ==\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. III page 35''' \n\n== Bibliography ==*Anselme, Pere, Augustin dechausse (continue par) du Fournay, (revue, corrigee & augmentee parle) Pere Ange & la Pere Simplicien, Augustins dechausses, (1726), ''Histoire genealogique et chronologique de la maison royale de France, des Pairs, Grands Officiers de la couronne et de la Maison du Roy''; Tome Premier, 3rd ed, Paris : Claude Robustel; reprinted 1967, Editions du Palais Royal, Paris.       "notes": "{{Succession\n|image=Bourgogne-349.png\n|position1=Comte de d'Artois \n|before1=[[Artois-67|Mahaut d'Artois]]<br>1302-1329\n|after1=[[Capet-697|Jeanne de Capet de France]] <br>1330-1347\n|years1=1329-1330\n}}\n{{Succession\n|image=Chalon-70.png\n|position1=Comte de Bourgogne\n|before1=[[Chalon-70|Othon de Chalon de Bourgogne]]<br>1279-1303\n|after1=[[Capet-697|Jeanne de Capet de France]] <br>1330-1347\n|years1=1303-1330\n}}\n== Biography ==\n{{EuroAristo Sticker}}Jeanne de Bourgogne (or de Chalons) was the eldest daughter of Othon (Otto) IV de Chalons, Comte Palatin de Bourgogne (Burgundy) and his second wife, Mahaut d'Artois-Capet, Comtesse d'Artois.  She was eventually to succeed her parents as Jeanne II, Comtesse palatine de Bourgogne and Jeanne I, Comtesse d'Artois and she was also Queen (Reine) consort of France from 1316-1322 as the wife of Philippe V (Capet), Roi de France.\n=== Birth date ===Deciding on a date of birth for Jeanne de Bourgogne depends somewhat on the date of her parent’s marriage and although there appears to be a general consensus on this date; the 9 June 1291<ref>Cawley, 2012 & 2013; Kerrebrouck, p. 228; Le Hete, p. 74</ref>, there are some suggestions that it may have occurred earlier.  Cawley (2013) quotes a statement from ''Gesta Philippi Tertia Francorum Regis'' of Guillaume de Nangis that dates the marriage to about 1284 or 1285.  Othon’s first wife, Philippe de Bar, is last mentioned in June 1283 and probably died by the end of that year,<ref>Le Hete, p. 80, note 72, citing Georges Poull, La Maison souveraine et ducale de Bar, p. 242.</ref> which makes a marriage with Mahaut d’Artois-Capet possible in the period 1284 - 1285.\nThe other factor in estimating a date of birth for Jeanne is the various treaties between her father and Philippe IV, King of France.  Kerrebrouck (p, 228) gives 12 June 1291 as the date of the treaty signed at Evreux, and Le Hete (p. 75) has Jeanne born before 15 January 1292, which may suggest the date of another treaty, but it is not clear whether either of these actually name Jeanne; for instance, Alix, Othon’s daughter from his first marriage, may have still been alive on 12 June 1291.<ref>Le Hete, p.  74.</ref>  However the treaty of Vincennes on 02 March 1294/95 definitely names Jeanne and Philippe as the children being contacted in marriage, and confirms their succession to the Comte palatin de Bourgogne.\nJeanne must therefore have definitely been born before 02 March 1294/95, but if her parents married on 09 June 1291, than it seems unlikely (though not impossible) that Jeanne was born 'before 15 January 1291/92' and even more unlikely that she was born 'before 12 June 1291'.  Cawley’s (2013) date, of before 2 March 1291 is only really possible if the year should  be 1291/92.  If her parents married earlier though, then, any of these dates could be accepted.  An earlier date of birth is also more appropriate for the birth of her first child in May 1308 (see below) but again a later date is not out of the question.\n\n=== Family ===\n==== Marriage ====Jeanne married Philippe de France , the second son of Philippe IV in person at Corbeil (Marne) in January 1306/07.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 164; Cawley; Anselme, p. 94.</ref> He was recognised as Comte palatin de Bourgogne and Sire de Salins, through the rights of his wife in a treaty dated 26 June 1310.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 163.</ref>\nIn Spring (March – May) of 2014, Jeanne was charged with adultery along with her sister Blanche, the wife of her brother-in-law Charles (IV) of France, and her sister-in-law, Marguerite de Bourgogne, wife of Louis (X), in what is known as the [http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tour_de_Nesle_Affair&oldid=577048163 Tour de Nesle Affair] and imprisoned in the chateau de Dourdan.  Although both Marguerite and Blanche were found guilty, Jeanne was proven innocent, largely through the efforts of her husband, and returned to him about Christmas 2014.<ref>Kerrebrouck, p. 169, note 45</ref>\n\n==== Children ====Jeanne and Philippe were definitely the parents of the following five children; <ref>see Kerrebrouck, pp. 164-166</ref>#Jeanne (III), born 1 or 2 May 1308, eventually succeeded her mother as comtesse palatin de Bourgogne & comtesse d'Artois; betrothed at Louvre, Paris 6 April 1313 to Hughes V, Duc de Bourgogne (born 1294, died May 1315) and secondly to his brother and successor, Eudes IV, Duc de Bourgogne, 29 September 1316 at Nogent-sur-Seine (Aube) who she married 18 June 1318 at Paris;#Marguerite, born 1309, succeeded to Bourgogne and Artois on the death of her great-nephew; married by contract 21 June 1320 at Paris and in person 22 July 1320, Louis I de Flandre, comte de Flanders;#Isabelle, born 1310, married (1) by treaty 18 June 1316 at Lyon (Rhone) and by contract at Dole (Jura) 17 May 1323 and celebrated the same day; Guigues VIII, Dauphin de Viennois (died 28 July 1333); (2) circa 1339, Jean III, Seigneur de Faucogney;#Blanche, born in 1311 or 1312, promised as a child as a nun at Abbaye de Longchamp, taking the habit as a Franciscan nun 1319, and died 26 April 1358;#Louis (or Philippe), born 1316 (possibly 24 June)<ref>Cawley has this date, citing ''Flores historiarum'' by Bernard Guidonis, but it is repeated by no other source and may not be reliable</ref> , died young, aged 7 months, 18 February 1317 and buried in Church of Cordeliers, Paris.\n\n==== Additional children ====Although there is every reason to suppose that Philippe and Jeanne might have had additional children, particularly during the period 1317-1322, the following are disputed;#Additional son, died young, perhaps named Philippe.  A number of sources,<ref>Franklin, p. 36, and some Wikipedia articles</ref> gives them a son named Philippe, born in 1313, but this is generally thought to be confused with a son of that name, of Charles IV and Blanche de Bourgogne;#Daughter unnamed born 1322 is mentioned in the French version of the Wikipedia article for Jeanne de Bourgogne but with no references or sources.  Apart from wikipedia articles in other languages, presumably copied from the French article, no other source mentions this child.\n\n=== Widowhood ===Philippe had been suffering from dysentery for a number of months and died at Longchamps the night of the 2-3 January 1322.  He was buried at Abbaye royale de St Denis.  Jeanne seems to have mostly retired to the estates in Bourgogne, where she ruled wisely under the guidance of her mother, and succeeded her in Artois when she died 27 October 1329.  However Jeanne didn’t survive her mother for long; she died 21 January 1329/1330 at Roye, Somme and was buried in the eglise des Cordeliers in Paris on 27 January.\n\n== Further information ==In English [http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joan_II,_Countess_of_Burgundy&oldid=577025420 Wikipedia: Joan II, Countess of Burgundy]  (this makes a number of claims about Jeanne but has only one reference)\nIn French [http://fr.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeanne_II_de_Bourgogne&oldid=99142588 Wikipedia: Jeanne II de Bourgogne]\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n*Anselme, Pere, Augustin dechausse (continue par) du Fournay, (revue, corrigee & augmentee parle) Pere Ange & la Pere Simplicien, Augustins dechausses, (1726), ''Histoire genealogique et chronologique de la maison royale de France, des Pairs, Grands Officiers de la couronne et de la Maison du Roy''; Tome Premier, 3rd ed, Paris : Claude Robustel; reprinted 1967, Editions du Palais Royal, Paris.\n*Cawley, Charles, (2012), \"Medieval Lands: France, Capetian Kings\", v. 2.2 (updated 23 September), ''Foundations of Medieval Genealogy'', (http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/CAPET.htm : viewed 12 January 2014).\n*Cawley, Charles, (2013), \"Medieval Lands: Burgundy Kingdom Nobility\", v. 2.4 (updated 02 March), ''Foundations of Medieval Genealogy'', (http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BURGUNDY%20Kingdom.htm#_Toc310954261 : viewed 01 March 2014).\n*Franklin, Alfred, (1906), ''Des noms et des dates: Les rois et les gouvernements de la France de Hugue Capet a l'annee 1906'', 2nd ed., Paris : H.       "notes": "[[Category:Catholic Saints]]\n[[Category:Universidad de Salamanca]]\n[[Category:This Day In History May 30]]\n[[Category:This Day In History August 05]]\n[[Category:Spain, Monarchs]]\n== Biography ==\nFerdinand III was the son of [[Castilla-106|Alfonso IX Leon]] and [[Bourgogne-212|Berengaria of Castile]]. He was King of Castile from 1217 and King of León from 1230 as well as King of Galicia from 1231.\nThe exact date of Ferdinand's birth is unclear. It has been proposed as early as 1199 or even 1198, although more recent researchers commonly date Ferdinand's birth in the Summer of 1201.<ref>[[Wikipedia:Ferdinand_III_of_Castile]].</ref>  Ferdinand was born at the [[Wikipedia:ES:Monasterio_de_Nuestra_Señora_de_Valparaíso|Monastery of Valparaíso (Bellofonte)]] near Peleas de Arriba, Province of Zamora, Kingdom of Castile.\nAs the son of Alfonso IX of León and his second wife Berengaria of Castile, Ferdinand is descendant of Alfonso VII of Leon and Castile on both sides of his parents, as his paternal grandfather Ferdinand II of Leon and maternal great grandfather Sancho III of Castile were the sons and successors of Alfonso VII. Ferdinand has other royal ancestors from his paternal grandmother Urraca of Portugal and his maternal grandmother Eleanor of England a daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. The marriage of Ferdinand's parents was annulled by order of Pope Innocent III in 1204, due to consanguinity.\nFerdinand III died 30 MAY 1252 and is buried at the Cathedral Santa María in Seville.<ref>Cawley, Charles. ''Medieval Lands: A prosopography of medieval European noble and royal families''. Hosted online by the Foundation for Medieval Genealogy (FMG), accessed 2025, [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/CASTILE.htm#_FERNANDO_III_1217-1252 Kings of Castile and León].</ref>\nFerdinand was buried in the Cathedral of Seville by his son, Alfonso X. His tomb is inscribed in four languages: Arabic, Hebrew, Latin, and an early version of Castilian. He was canonized as St. Ferdinand by Pope Clement X in 1671. Today Saint Fernando can still be seen in the Cathedral of Seville, for he rests enclosed in a gold and crystal casket worthy of the king. His golden crown still encircles his head as he reclines beneath the statue of the Virgin of the Kings. Several places named San Fernando were founded across the Spanish Empire in his honor.\n\n===Saint Ferdinand III===\n\n: King of Leon and Castile\n\n: Third Order of St. Francis\n: b. c.1198 near Salamanca;<ref name=Wikipedia>: [[Wikipedia:Ferdinand III of Castile|Wikipedia]] states 05 Aug 1199 – 30 May 1252, while the Catholic Encyclopedia says he was born c.1198. Whether this is due to the medieval calendar cycle -- generally set back a year -- is unknown. Wikipedia took birth dates from what appears to be a secondary source.</ref>\n: d. 30 May 1252 Seville<ref>: Catholic Encyclopedia and Wikipedia confirm this date.</ref>\n\n: burial: cathedral of Seville\n\n: 1671: Canonized by Clement X\n\n: Feast: 30 May\n\n===Occupation===\n* 1217: King of Castile\n* 1230: crown of Leon\n* 1236: conquest of Cordoba\n* 1248: conquest of Seville \n* Turned mosques into cathedrals\n* Founded University of Salamanca\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\nSee also:\n* Richardson, Douglas. ''Un Magnate Catalan En Le Corte De Alfonso Vii : Comes Poncius De Cabreira Princeps Çemore.'' Madrid: Prensa y Ediciones Iberoamericanas, 69; there is no ebook available but this page is available to view on [https://books.google.es/books?id=HDkEM31ggx0C&pg=PA60&lpg=PA60&dq#v=onepage&q&f=false Google Books] (accessed 30 Mar 2024).</ref>  The document was signed by Ponce's cousin Fernándo Fernández on behalf of Ponce's three sons, Juan, Fernando and Pedro.  This indicates that they were minors since they couldn't sign on their own behalf.  His birth year estimate is based on this information.#''Rico Hombre'' was a title for the Magnates of the kingdom.  They held \"enormous riches, political power, and social prestige and [were] closely related to the very crown.\"<ref>Mesa Enrique Soria. 2013. ''La Nobleza En la España Moderna Cambio y Continuidad''. Madrid: Marcial Pons Ediciones de Historia, 64-65; quoted in [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk%3AImmemorial_nobility Wikipedia] (accessed 30 Mar 2024).</ref>#The Spanish and Portuguese naming custom of this time was (given name) + (father's given name patronymic + location).  So Pedro was named \"Pedro / Ponce de Cabrera\" and Aldonza was \"Aldonza / Alfonso de León.\"  However, their children adopted a new naming standard:  (given name + father's given name patronymic) + (permanent surname Ponce de León). So their eldest son was named \"Fernán Pérez (patronymic of Pedro) / Ponce de Leon.\" By the next generation, the patronymic name was dropped and they just used (given name) + (Ponce de León).\n\n==Sources==\n<references />\nSee also:* Calderón Medina, Inés. 2008. \"El Impulso Nobiliario a La expansión Del Císter En El Reino De León.         {

      "notes": "[[Category:England Managed Profiles, Pre-1500 PPP]]\n[[Category: Early Barony of Berkhamsted]]\n[[Category: England, Monarchs]][[Category:Early Honour of Lancaster]]\n[[Category:House of Plantagenet]]\n[[Category: Westminster Abbey, Westminster, Middlesex]]\n[[Category:Battle of Lewes]]\n[[Category:Battle of Evesham]]\n[[Category:Second Barons' War]]\n[[Category:Second Battle of Lincoln]]\n[[Category:Time Team]]\n{{England}}\n{{Succession\n | position1 = King of England\n | years1 = 1216 - 1272\n | before1 = [[Plantagenet-143|John]]\n | after1 = [[Plantagenet-2|Edward I]]\n }}\n==Biography==\n{|\n||{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Plantagenet\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-16.png\n}}\n|}\n===Birth and Parents===Henry was the eldest son of [[Plantagenet-143|King John]] and his second wife [[Angoulême-40|Isabella of Angoulême]]. He was born at Winchester, Hampshire on 1 October 1207.<ref>John A C Vincent (ed.). ''Lancashire Lay Subsidies, Vol. 1, Henry III to Edward I'', The Record Society for the Publication of Original Documents Relating to Lancashire and Cheshire, 1893), p. 35, [https://archive.org/details/lancashirelaysu00offigoog/page/n102/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref><ref name=\"ODNB\"> ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by H W Ridgeway for 'Henry III', print and online 2004, revised online 2023</ref>\n\n===Early Years and Minority===In about 1212 King John placed Henry under the guardianship of [[Roches-15|Peter des Roches]], who was Bishop of Winchester.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nHenry succeeded to the throne on his father's death on 19 October 1216, during a period of civil war. He was crowned at Gloucester Abbey (now Gloucester Cathedral) on 28 October, having been knighted the previous day by [[Marshal-4|William Marshal]], who was formally appointed regent the next month. The rebels were decisively defeated in the Battle of Lincoln on 20 May 1217.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nFollowing William Marshal's death in May 1219, the Papal legate Pandulf became formally \"first counsellor and chief\" of England, with Peter des Roches continuing to act as Henry's tutor, and [[Burgh-19|Hubert de Burgh]] as Justiciar, but the real power lay with Hubert. In 1221 Pandulf stepped down, and Peter des Roches's tutorship was ended. From 1223 Hubert de Burgh arranged for Henry to be present at some military campaigns.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===First Years of full Power===On 8 January 1227, when he was 19, Henry's minority officially ended, but Hubert de Burgh retained much of his power. Hubert was keen to invade Poitou, and on 3 May 1230 Henry landed in France in full royal regalia. The expedition was a failure.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nThere had been plans for Henry to marry a sister of [[Dunkeld-4|Alexander II]], King of Scotland, but these were succeeded by a proposal that he should marry [[Dreux-49|Yolande]], sister of [[Bretagne-29|Jean le Roux]], Duke of Brittany. This also came to nothing.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nHubert de Burgh's power and influence were rapidly declining, with Peter des Roches coming into the ascendant. At the end of July 1232 Hubert was deprived of the Justiciarship.<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by F J West for ‘Burgh, Hubert de, earl of Kent (c.1170–1243)’, print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref> Over the following months Peter des Roches became the most powerful figure in Henry's government. This was not for long: increasing opposition from Barons and leading ecclesiastics led to Peter des Roches being deprived of his offices in May 1234.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Marriage to Eleanor of Provence; Children===In 1235 Henry sought to marry [[Dammartin-5|Jeanne de Ponthieu]], a well-connected heiress, but this was forbidden by the Pope after Louis IX of France intervened. Instead, he became betrothed to [[Provence-162|Eleanor of Provence]]. A charter recording the agreement for their marriage was dated 22 June 1235.<ref>Charles Cawley, “Medieval Lands�� database entry for [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLAND,%20Kings%201066-1603.htm#HenryIIIdied1272B Henry III]</ref> They married in January 1236.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"ODNB Eleanor of Provence\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Margaret Howell for 'Eleanor of Provence', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref> There is disagreement about the exact marriage date and the marriage place: see [[#research notes|research notes (below)]]. They had five children:* [[Plantagenet-2|Edward]], the future Edward I, born at Westminster in the night of 17-18 June 1239<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Michael Prestwich for 'Edward I', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref>* [[Plantagenet-1229|Margaret]], born at Windsor Castle, probably about October 1240 (sources differ as to her exact birth date), who married [[Dunkeld-60|Alexander III]] of Scotland<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by T F Tout (revised by Norman H Reid') for 'Margaret [Margaret of England] (1240–1275)', print an online 2004</ref>* [[Plantagenet-175|Beatrice]], born at Bordeaux on 25 June 1242, who married [[Dreux-22|Jean]], future Duke of Brittany, in 1260<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>* [[Plantagenet-562|Edmund, known as Edmund Crouchback]], born (probably at Westminster) on 16 January 1245<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Simon Lloyd for 'Edmund [called Edmund Crouchback], first earl of Lancaster and first earl of Leicester', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref>* [[Plantagenet-278|Katherine]], born on 25 November 1253,<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> who was disabled and died young, probably by October 1257<ref name=\"ODNB Eleanor of Provence\"/><ref>Charles Cawley, entry for Katherine in “Medieval Lands” database under [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLAND,%20Kings%201066-1603.htm#HenryIIIdied1272B Henry III]</ref><ref name=\"Richardson\">Douglas Richardson. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham (Salt Lake City: the author, 2013), Vol. 1, pp. 58-63, ENGLAND 6</ref>\n\n===Middle Years of Henry III's Reign===A few months after his marriage, Eleanor of Provence's uncle William of Savoy was made head of the royal Council. This marked the start of a period in which Henry relied to a great extent on his wife's relatives.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn the mid-1230s [[Montfort-35|Simon de Montfort]] began a liaison with Henry's sister [[Plantagenet-19|Eleanor]]. Henry consented to a secret marriage, which took place in his Westminster chapel on 7 January 1238. The marriage was condemned by the Archbishop of Canterbury because Eleanor had sworn a vow of perpetual chastity after the death of her first husband [[Marshal-43|William Marshal]]. It lead to a baronial rebellion led by Henry's brother [[Plantagenet-39|Richard of Cornwall]]. William of Savoy managed to smooth things over, with a payment to Richard of Cornwall of 16000 marks, a colossal sum.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> Simon de Montfort was made Earl of Leicester in February 1239, and he and Richard of Cornwall were godparents of Henry's eldest son, born in June 1239. A few weeks later, following a quarrel, Simon was sent into exile for a few months.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1242 Henry made an ill-prepared and ill-financed attempt to recover some of the French lands lost by King John. He himself narrowly escaped capture, when he fell into a trap laid by the French. He returned to England in the autumn of 1243.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn March 1245 Henry initiated the rebuilding of Westminster Abbey, a project on which he lavished considerable sums over the rest of his life.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nOn 30 April 1247, following some years of intermittent resistance to him, Henry was formally recognised as feudal overlord of Wales. But his attempts in the later 1240s to persuade Parliament to finance another attempt to wrest lands from the French failed. Henry sought to make good his lack of income by forced loans, increasing the financial demands he made on his non-baronial subjects, and other measures, making his regime increasingly unpopular.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nWith Gascon barons restive, Henry appointed Simon de Montfort Lieutenant of Gascony in 1248. Simon alienated the barons, and open rebellion broke out. Simon was recalled and made to answer charges in 1252: he briefly returned to Gascony, where further rebellion erupted, and Simon was finally dismissed in October that year. Henry's half-brother [[Lusignan-23|Geoffrey de Lusignan]] arranged a truce. In August 1253 Henry himself led an expedition to Gascony. By the next summer, Gascony seemed largely pacified. It was part of extensive domains that were granted to Henry's son Edward soon after.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn March 1250 Henry took a crusading vow, and in the following years gathered funds for this, but his crusade never took place. In 1255 the Pope consented to Henry abandoning this vow and substituting an attempt to secure the crown of Sicily for his son Edmund, in return for a promise of a payment of 135000 marks.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> \nHenry was by now increasingly in debt. Adding to his troubles, there was substantial friction between his wife's Savoyard family and his increasingly powerful Lusignan half-brothers, and a major uprising started in Wales, led by [[Ap_Gruffudd-74|Llywelyn ap Gruffudd]]. In 1258 Henry's wife's uncle [[Savoie-1251|Peter of Savoy]], Simon de Montfort and others forced Henry to agree to the Provisions of Oxford, under which a Council of 15 magnates was chosen to govern England, and the Lusignans were driven out of England.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1259 Henry concluded a peace agreement with Louis IX of France. While he was abroad, his son Edward and Simon de Montfort rebelled: the uprising largely petered out on Henry's return to England in the spring of 1260. His relations with Edward were patched up, but Edward still worked in alliance with Simon, gaining effective control of the royal Council. In 1261 Henry, with the backing of the Pope, abjured the Provisions of Oxford. While he seemed to have regained power over the following months, he did not secure a rapprochement with Simon de Montfort. Henry and Simon de Montfort went to France to seek the arbitration of Louis IX: Henry fell gravely ill while in Paris in 1262. Louis's attempts to reconcile Henry and Simon failed.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> \n\n===Simon de Montfort's Rebellion===In 1263, invited by discontented Barons, Simon de Montfort came back to England. In 1264, full-scale rebellion erupted. Henry managed to capture Simon's son Simon at Northampton, but, on 14 May, his forces were heavily defeated in the Battle of Lewes. Henry surrendered, and his son Edward was held as a hostage.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> \nSimon de Montfort now effectively held the reins of power but failed to secure general support, and he alienated some key Barons. On 28 May 1265 Henry's son Edward escaped from custody with the help of [[Clare-98|Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester]], who had earlier supported Simon but then switched sides. Going to quell an uprising of the lords of the Welsh marches, Simon was defeated by Edward and killed in the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265, along with many of his adherents. Henry himself, still in Simon's power, had been taken to the battlefield and put in Montfortian armour - he was wounded and his life was saved only when he announced who he was. The remaining rebels were subdued over the next two years. Rebels' lands were confiscated but, under the Dictum of Kenilworth, most of them were allowed to pay fines to regain them. London, which had supported Simon, faced a substantial fine of 20000 marks.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Last Years===Gilbert de Clare considered that he had been inadequately rewarded for his part in the defeat of Simon de Montfort. In April 1267 he marched on London, which gave him its support. In June Gilbert made his peace with Henry. As part of the agreement, the terms of the Dictum of Kenilworth were eased.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn September 1267 a compromise settlement was reached with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd. He was formally recognised as Prince of Wales, and his territorial gains were accepted. In return, he paid homage to Henry and undertook to pay 3000 marks a year into the royal Exchequer.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn his final years Henry faced considerable financial problems, though a parliamentary grant of tax revenues in 1270 somewhat eased these. That year, there was an elaborate ceremony to mark the transfer of the body of Edward the Confessor to Westminster Abbey, the rebuilding of which was still unfinished.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Death and Burial===In March 1271 Henry fell gravely ill and the royal Council asked his son Edward to return from crusading. A few weeks later Henry recovered, and, for the second time, took a crusading vow himself. He fell ill again that December. He rallied once more, but died at Westminster on 16 November 1272. On 20 November he was buried in what had been the coffin of Edward the Confessor. An elaborate new tomb was prepared, and his remains were quietly transferred to this in the night of 11 May 1290. Henry was the first monarch to have a burial service with his body already in a coffin, as opposed to being on top of a bier. On 30 December 1290 his heart was, in accordance with his wishes, handed over to nuns of the Abbey of Fontevrault in Anjou, where Henry II, Eleanor of Aquitaine, and Richard I had been buried.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref>Westminster Abbey website, page for [https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/royals/henry-iii#i11912 Henry III], accessed 18 July 2025</ref>\n\n==Research Notes==\n===Date of Marriage===The ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' entry for Henry III says that Henry III and Eleanor of Provence were betrothed at Canterbury, Kent on 14 January 1236 and married at Westminster on 20 January 1236.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> This accords with the 13th century chronicle of Matthew Paris.<ref>Matthew Paris (ed.       "notes": "[[Category:England Managed Profiles, Pre-1500 PPP]][[Category:Early Barony of Mitford]][[Category: Feudal Barony of Pevensey]]\n{{England}}\n\n==Biography=='''Eleanor of Provence''' (c. 1223 – 24/25 June 1291[1]) was Queen consort of England as the spouse of King Henry III of England from 1236 until his death in 1272.\n\n===Birth and Parents===Eleanor was the second daughter of [[Provence-164|Raymond Berenguer]], Count of Provence, and [[Savoie-1174|Beatrice of Savoy]]. Her birth date is unknown: her entry in the ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' gives an estimate about 1223:<ref name=\"ODNB\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Margaret Howell for 'Eleanor of Provence', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref> This would be consistent with her marriage date and the birth date of her first child. Charles Cawley's 'Medieval Lands' database says she was born in Aix-en-Provence, but gives no sourcing.<ref name=\"Medlands\">Charles Cawley. [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/PROVENCE.htm#EleonoreMHenryIIIEnglanddied1272 Eleanore de Provence], entry in “Medieval Lands” database,m accessed 19 July 2025</ref>\n\n===Marriage and Children===Eleanor married [[Plantagenet-167|Henry III of England]].<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> A charter recording the agreement for their marriage was dated 22 June 1235.<ref>Charles Cawley, “Medieval Lands” database entry for [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLAND,%20Kings%201066-1603.htm#HenryIIIdied1272B Henry III]</ref> They married in January 1236. She had not seen her husband until then.<ref>Thomas B Costain, ''The Magnificent Century'', Doubleday and Company, Garden City, New York, 1959, p. 140</ref> There is disagreement about the exact marriage date and the marriage place: see [[#research notes|research notes (below)]]. The ceremony was lavish,<ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by H W Ridgeway for 'Henry III', print and online 2004, revised online 2023</ref> and Eleanor was dressed in a shimmering golden gown which was tightly-fitted to the waist, and then flared out in wide pleats to her feet. The sleeves were long and lined with ermine.<ref>Thomas B Costain, ''The Magnificent Century'', p. 129</ref> \n\nEleanor and Henry III had five children:* [[Plantagenet-2|Edward]], the future Edward I, born at Westminster in the night of 17-18 June 1239<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Michael Prestwich for 'Edward I', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref>* [[Plantagenet-1229|Margaret]], born at Windsor Castle, probably about October 1240 (sources differ as to her exact birth date), who married [[Dunkeld-60|Alexander III]] of Scotland<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by T F Tout (revised by Norman H Reid') for 'Margaret [Margaret of England] (1240–1275)', print an online 2004</ref>* [[Plantagenet-175|Beatrice]], born at Bordeaux on 25 June 1242, who married [[Dreux-22|Jean]], future Duke of Brittany, in 1260<ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\"/>* [[Plantagenet-562|Edmund, known as Edmund Crouchback]], born (probably at Westminster) on 16 January 1245<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Simon Lloyd for 'Edmund [called Edmund Crouchback], first earl of Lancaster and first earl of Leicester', print and online 2004, revised online 2008</ref>* [[Plantagenet-278|Katherine]], born on 25 November 1253,<ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\"/> who was disabled and died young, probably by October 1257<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref>Charles Cawley, entry for Katherine in “Medieval Lands” database under [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLAND,%20Kings%201066-1603.htm#HenryIIIdied1272B Henry III]</ref><ref name=\"Richardson\">Douglas Richardson. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham (Salt Lake City: the author, 2013), Vol. 1, pp. 58-63, ENGLAND 6</ref>\n\n===Queen===After becoming Queen of England, Eleanor promoted the interests of her maternal relatives from Savoy. This subsequently led to friction with Henry III's Lusignan half-brothers after they came to England in 1247.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1242-3 Eleanor accompanied Henry III when he embarked on an unsuccessful attempt to recover some of the French lands lost by King John. In 1253 she acted as one of the Regents in England when Henry went to Gascony: she joined him in France the next year.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1258 Eleanor's wife's uncle [[Savoie-1251|Peter of Savoy]], [[Montfort-35|Simon de Montfort]] and others forced Henry to agree to the Provisions of Oxford, under which a Council of 15 magnates was chosen to govern England and his powers curtailed, and the Lusignans were driven out of England.<ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\"/> In 1261 she helped her husband regain much of his authority, but unrest continued.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> Simon de Montfort was one of the main leaders of the baronial opposition. Some of Eleanor's lands were plundered. When Eleanor attempted to go to her son Edward, who was at Windsor, she was stopped at London Bridge by Londoners, who hurled stones and insults at her.<ref>Matthew Paris (ed. Henry Richards Luard). ''Flores Historiarum'', Vol. 2, pp. 481-482, [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_dv8KAAAAYAAJ/page/480/mode/2up?q=jamque Internet Archive]</ref> Eleanor went to France, where she involved Louis IX in the disagreements between her husband and Simon. Henry and Simon sought the arbitration of Louis, but this did not resolve matters.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\"/>\nIn 1264 full-scale rebellion erupted, led by Simon de Montfort. Henry III was defeated in the Battle of Lewes on 14 May 1264 and surrendered to the rebels. Henry and Eleanor’s son Edward was held hostage. Eleanor went to Flanders, but her plans to invade England did not materialise, and she then made her base in Gascony, from where she fostered opposition to Simon. Simon was defeated and killed in the Battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265. Eleanor returned to England that November. The Pope agreed to her recovering some of the costs she had incurred out of a tax on the clergy.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Last Years===Henry III died on 16 November 1272. This left Eleanor a wealthy widow, with a dower giving her income of some £4000 a year, in addition to what she had from other sources. She became a generous benefactor of religious establishments. After her grandson [[Plantagenet-170|Henry]] died in 1274, she founded a Dominican priory at Guildford, Surrey in his memory.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1286 Eleanor became a nun at Amesbury Priory, Wiltshire, a Benedictine establishment.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Death===Eleanor died at Amesbury Priory on 24 June 1291 and was buried there on 9 September, the ceremony being delayed while Edward I was in Scotland.<ref>Henry Richards Luard (ed.). ''Flores Historiarum'', Vol. III (continuation of the chronicle of Matthew Paris), GHMSO, 1890, p. 72, [https://archive.org/details/floreshistoriaru03pari/page/72/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref> In December her heart was buried at the Franciscans' church in London.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Research notes ===\n===Date of Marriage===The ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' entry for Henry III says that Henry III and Eleanor of Provence were betrothed at Canterbury, Kent on 14 January 1236 and married at Westminster on 20 January 1236.<ref name=\"ODNB Henry III\"/> This accords with the 13th century chronicle of Matthew Paris.<ref>Matthew Paris (ed. He and his wife, Aleide, were buried in the church of the Dominicans in Valenciennes.  \n\n=== Charters ===*Datering: 1261 November 18 (in octavo obitus beati Martini);  Wilhelmus de Domo Lapidea, verklaart met toestemming van '''vrouw Aleydis, weduwe van heer Johannes de Avesnes, voogdes van Hollandia én Zeelandia''', verkocht te hebben aan heer Lubbertus, abt, en het convent van Hecmunda tienden in Poelgheest, door hem van het graafschap Hollandia in leen gehouden, terwijl hij belooft brieven van bevestiging te zullen leveren van de graaf (wanneer deze meerderjarig zal zijn) en van de bisschop van Traiectum, en stelt als borgen verder heer Simon van Hairlem, Johannes genaamd Persijn, Hugo van Naeldwyck, Theodericus de Poelghiest, ridders H(eidenricus), abt van St. Paulus in Traiectum, voegt hieraan toe het stuk op verzoek van de oorkonder bezegeld te hebben. <ref>Archieven.nl; Abdij van Egmond, regesten;  [https://www.archieven.nl/nl/zoeken?mivast=0&mizig=210&miadt=236&miaet=1&micode=356&minr=878758&miview=inv2 Charter 18 November 1261] Afschrift (Inv.no. 3, fol, 40).       "notes": "[[Category:Ostrów Tumski-Śródka-Zawady-Komandoria (Poznań miasto-powiat), Wielkopolskie, Polska]][[Category:Bazylika Archikatedralna Świętych Apostołów Piotra i Pawła, Poznań, Wielkopolskie]]\n[[Category:Poland, Monarchs (960-1571)]]\n[[Category:House of Piast]]\n{{Polish Roots}}\n{{Succession|position1=Duke of Greater Poland<br>1245-1279'''<br><br> 1245-1247: co-rule with<br>his brother [[Piast-40|Przemysł I]]<br>1247-1257: territories divided <br>with his brother<br>1257-1273: sole ruler<br>1273-1279: territories<br>divided with nephew [[Piast-164|Przemysł II]]'''<br>\n|before1=[[Piast-40|Przemysł I]]<br>his brother\n|after1=[[Piast-164|Przemysł II]]<br>his nephew\n}}\n== Biography =={{Notability|location=Poland|text=Bolesław Pobożny (Pious) was Duke of Greater Poland during the 13th century. He is particularly known for issuing the Statute of Kalisz in 1264, which established legal rights and protections for the Jewish population of his territories.}}\n\n([[#Biografia|Wersja polska]])\n===Origins===Bolesław, later known as Pobożny (\"the Pious\"), was a son of [[Piast-2|Władysław]], Duke of Poland, and [[Sobiesławic-6|Jadwiga]].  His birth is estimated at about 1226.<ref name=\"Jasinski\">Kazimierz Jasi��ski, “Uzupełnienia do genealogii Piastów,” ''Studia Źródłoznawcze'', vol. 3 (1958), [https://rcin.org.pl/ihpan/Content/41528/PDF/WA303_39412_B88-SZ-R-3-1958_Jasinski.pdf pp. 205–206, ].</ref>\nHis parentage is directly documented in a charter from 1235, in which Władysław names Jadwiga as ''uxor mea Hadewigis'' (“my wife Jadwiga”) and identifies Przemysł and Bolesław as ''nostris filiis'' (��our sons”).<ref name=\"KDW184\">''Kodeks dyplomatyczny Wielkopolski'', t. 1 (Poznań: Biblioteka Kórnicka, 1877), [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #184], dokument z 1235 r.; Władysław Odonic występuje wraz z żoną Jadwigą (''uxor mea Hadewigis'') i ich synami Przemysłem i Bolesławem (hereafter Kodeks).</ref> After Władysław's death, Bolesław continued to appear in documents with his mother and brother. On 4 May 1243, Przemysł identified Jadwiga as ''dilecta matre nostra domina Hadwiga'' (“our beloved mother, Lady Jadwiga”) and Bolesław as his younger brother.<ref name=\"Kodeks238\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #238].</ref> In 1244, Przemysł and Bolesław again appeared with Jadwiga in a grant to the Dominican friars at Poznań, where Przemysł identified her as ''matre mea Hadviga'' (“my mother Jadwiga”).<ref name=\"Kodeks243\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #243].</ref> In 1254, the ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' explicitly described Przemysł and Bolesław as “''fratres uterini''” (“brothers of the same mother”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1254\">Max Perlbach, ed., “Annales Capituli Posnaniensis,” ''Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores'', vol. 29 (Hannover: Hahn, 1892), [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/450/mode/2up p. 450].</ref>\nBolesław was known as Pobożny (“the Pious”). The ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' refers to him as “''Boleslaus Pius ... Polonie dux''” (“Bolesław the Pious ... Duke of Poland”).<ref name=\"BoleslawPius1261\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/460/mode/2up p. 461].</ref>\n===Early Life and Rule===Following his father's death in 1239, Bolesław remained under the guardianship of his older brother Przemysł I, who governed their inheritance during Bolesław's minority.<ref name=\"Wajs\">Anna Wajs, “Siemowit I — przy ojcu Konradzie Mazowieckim — rola młodego księcia na dworze piastowskim,” ''Miscellanea Historico-Archivistica'', t. 4 (Warszawa: Naczelna Dyrekcja Archiwów Państwowych and Wydawnictwo DiG, 1994), [https://agad.gov.pl/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/tom-4_0_merged.pdf p. 2].</ref>\nIn 1245, Bolesław was knighted by his brother Przemysł. The ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' records: “''dux Przemisl fratrem suum Boleslaum gladio cinxit''” (“Duke Przemysł girded his brother Bolesław with the sword”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1245\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/442/mode/2up p. 442].</ref>\nIn 1247, Bolesław and his brother Przemysł divided their territories. The ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' records them as “''domini duces Polonie Premisl et Boleslaus fratres''” (“the lords Przemysł and Bolesław, dukes of Poland, brothers”). In the division, Bolesław received Kalis (Kalisz) with its dependencies and lands extending from the Prosna (Prosna River) to Premanth (Przemęt). The boundaries of his portion were further described by reference to Wartham (Warta), Mosinam (Mosina), the marsh called Sepno, Lemcha (Łęka), and the Obra (Obra River). Gneznam (Gniezno) and Poznanam (Poznań), with their dependencies, remained with Przemysł.<ref name=\"Boleslaw1247\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/442/mode/2up p. 443].</ref>\nIn 1251, Bolesław was imprisoned by his brother Przemysł. The ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' describes Bolesław as “''fratre Boleslao suo carceri tradito''” (“his brother Bolesław having been handed over to prison”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1251\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/446/mode/2up p. 446].</ref>  In 1253, Przemysł released Bolesław from captivity. The annal records that he freed “''fratrem ducem Boleslaum''” (“his brother Duke Bolesław”) and gave him Kalis (Kalisz) temporarily, until a definite portion of the territory could be assigned to him.<ref name=\"Boleslaw1253\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/448/mode/2up p. 449].</ref>\nIn 1257, Przemysł II was born in Poznań. The ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' records: “''Item anno Domini 1257. natus est filius Premislonis ducis boni Polonie in Poznania''” (“Likewise, in the year of the Lord 1257, a son of Przemysł, the good Duke of Poland, was born in Poznań”), adding, “''pater autem eius ante nativitatem ipsius quatuor mensibus obiit''” (“his father, however, died four months before his birth”). The same entry identifies Bolesław as “''Boleslao duce avunculo pueri''” (“Duke Bolesław, the boy's uncle”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1257\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/456/mode/2up p. 457].</ref>\nIn 1264, Bolesław issued at Kalisz a general privilege for the Jews living throughout his territories, later known as the Statute of Kalisz. In the document he styled himself “''Boleslaus Dei gracia dux Maioris Polonie''” (“Bolesław, by the grace of God Duke of Greater Poland”). Its thirty-six provisions regulated the legal status of the Jewish population and provided protections concerning judicial proceedings, personal security, property, commerce and lending, synagogues, and cemeteries. The privilege also provided that disputes between Jews were not subject to the jurisdiction of the city judge, but were to be judged by Bolesław, his palatine, or the palatine's judge.<ref name=\"Kodeks605\">''Kodeks'' [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #605]</ref>\n===Marriage and Children===About 1256, Bolesław married [[Arpadhazi-43|Jolenta]], who is called Helena in the ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis''. She had been raised at the court of her older sister Kinga, wife of Bolesław V.<ref name=\"Archidiecezja\">“[https://archidiecezja.pl/ksiezna-matka-klaryska-blogoslawiona-2/ Księżna, matka, klaryska, błogosławiona],” Archidiecezja Gnieźnieńska, 11 Jun 2025.</ref> The annal records that Bolesław married “''filiam regis Ungarie, nomine Helenam''” (“a daughter of the king of Hungary, named Helena”) in the land of Kraków. It further records that “''quam anno Domini 1258. adduxit in terram suam de terra Cracoviensi''” (“in the year of the Lord 1258 he brought her into his land from the land of Kraków”).<ref name=\"BoleslawMarriage1258\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/458/mode/2up p. 458].</ref>  In 1265, the ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' again identifies Bolesław's wife as Helena, recording “''pro uxore dicti ducis domina Helena, filia regis Ungarie''” (“on behalf of the wife of the said duke, Lady Helena, daughter of the king of Hungary”).<ref name=\"BoleslawJolenta1260\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/460/mode/2up p. 463].</ref>  Their confirmed children were:\n\n*[[Piast-1|Elżbieta]]\n*[[Piast-27|Jadwiga]]\n*[[Piast-28|Anna]]\n===Death and Burial===In 1279, Bolesław died. The ''Annales Posnanienses'' records: “''Anno Domini 1279. Dux Boleslaus Cracovie et dux Boleslaus Maioris Polonie obierunt''” (“In the year of the Lord 1279, Duke Bolesław of Kraków and Duke Bolesław of Greater Poland died”).<ref name=\"BoleslawDeath1279\">Perlbach, [https://archive.org/details/sim_monumenta-germaniae-historica_1892_29/page/470/mode/2up p. 470].</ref>  He was buried at the cathedral in Poznań.<ref name=\"Poznańska\">“[https://archpoznan.pl/pl/modlitwa-za-krolow-i-wladcow-polski Modlitwa za Królów i Władców Polski],” Archidiecezja Poznańska, 12 Nov 2023.</ref>\n\n==Biografia==\n([[#Biography|English Version]])\n===Pochodzenie===Bolesław, później znany jako Pobożny, był synem [[Piast-2|Władysława]], księcia polskiego, i [[Sobiesławic-6|Jadwigi]]. Jego narodziny datuje się w przybliżeniu na około 1226 rok.<ref name=\"Jasinski\" />\nJego pochodzenie jest bezpośrednio udokumentowane w dokumencie z 1235 roku, w którym Władysław nazywa Jadwigę ''uxor mea Hadewigis'' (���moja żona Jadwiga”), a Przemysła i Bolesława określa jako ''nostris filiis'' („naszych synów”).<ref name=\"KDW184\" /> Po śmierci Władysława Bolesław nadal występował w dokumentach wraz z matk�� i bratem. 4 May 1243 Przemysł określił Jadwigę jako ''dilecta matre nostra domina Hadwiga'' („naszą umiłowaną matkę, panią Jadwigę”), a Bolesława jako swojego młodszego brata.<ref name=\"Kodeks238\" /> W 1244 roku Przemysł i Bolesław ponownie wystąpili wraz z Jadwigą w dokumencie nadania dla dominikanów w Poznaniu, w którym Przemysł określił ją jako ''matre mea Hadviga'' („moją matkę Jadwigę”).<ref name=\"Kodeks243\" /> W 1254 roku ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' wyraźnie określiły Przemysła i Bolesława jako „''fratres uterini''” („braci z tej samej matki”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1254\" />\nBolesław był znany jako Pobożny. ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' określają go jako „''Boleslaus Pius ... Polonie dux''” („Bolesław Pobożny ... książę Polski”).<ref name=\"BoleslawPius1261\" />\n===Wczesne życie i rządy===Po śmierci ojca w 1239 roku Bolesław pozostawał pod opieką starszego brata, Przemysła I, który sprawował rządy nad ich dziedzictwem w okresie małoletności Bolesława.<ref name=\"Wajs\" />\nW 1245 roku Bolesław został pasowany na rycerza przez swojego brata Przemysła. ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' odnotowują: „''dux Przemisl fratrem suum Boleslaum gladio cinxit''” („książę Przemysł przepasał mieczem swojego brata Bolesława”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1245\" />\nW 1247 roku Bolesław i jego brat Przemysł podzielili między siebie swoje ziemie. ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' określają ich jako ���''domini duces Polonie Premisl et Boleslaus fratres''” („panowie książęta Polski Przemysł i Bolesław, bracia”). W wyniku podziału Bolesław otrzymał Kalisz wraz z jego przynależnościami oraz ziemie rozciągające się od Prosny do Przemętu. Granice jego części opisano ponadto przez odniesienie do Warty, Mosiny, bagna zwanego Sepno, Łęki i Obry. Gniezno i Poznań wraz z ich przynależnościami pozostały przy Przemyśle.<ref name=\"Boleslaw1247\" />\nW 1251 roku Bolesław został uwięziony przez swojego brata Przemysła. ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' opisują to słowami ''fratre Boleslao suo carceri tradito'' („jego brat Bolesław został oddany do więzienia”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1251\" /> W 1253 roku Przemysł uwolnił Bolesława z niewoli. Rocznik podaje, że uwolnił ''fratrem ducem Boleslaum'' („brata, księcia Bolesława”) i tymczasowo oddał mu Kalisz, do czasu wyznaczenia mu określonej części terytorium.<ref name=\"Boleslaw1253\" />\nW 1257 roku w Poznaniu urodził się Przemysł II. ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' odnotowują: „''Item anno Domini 1257. natus est filius Premislonis ducis boni Polonie in Poznania''” („Podobnie, w roku Pańskim 1257, w Poznaniu urodził się syn Przemysła, dobrego ksi��cia Polski”), dodając: „''pater autem eius ante nativitatem ipsius quatuor mensibus obiit''” („jego ojciec zmarł jednak cztery miesiące przed jego narodzinami”). Ten sam zapis określa Bolesława jako ''Boleslao duce avunculo pueri'' („księcia Bolesława, stryja chłopca”).<ref name=\"Boleslaw1257\" />\nW 1264 roku Bolesław wydał w Kaliszu przywilej generalny dla Żydów zamieszkujących jego ziemie, znany później jako Statut kaliski. W dokumencie tytułował się ''Boleslaus Dei gracia dux Maioris Polonie'' („Bolesław, z Bożej łaski książę Wielkopolski”). Trzydzieści sześć postanowień przywileju regulowało status prawny ludności żydowskiej i zapewniało jej ochronę w zakresie postępowania sądowego, bezpieczeństwa osobistego, własności, handlu i pożyczek, a także synagog i cmentarzy. Przywilej stanowił również, że spory pomiędzy Żydami nie podlegały jurysdykcji sędziego miejskiego, lecz miały być rozstrzygane przez Bolesława, jego wojewodę lub sędziego wojewody.<ref name=\"Kodeks605\" />\n===Małżeństwo i dzieci===Około 1256 roku Bolesław poślubił [[Arpadhazi-43|Jolentę]], którą ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' nazywają Heleną. Wychowywała się ona na dworze swojej starszej siostry Kingi, żony Bolesława V.<ref name=\"Archidiecezja\" /> Rocznik odnotowuje, że Bolesław poślubi�� w ziemi krakowskiej ''filiam regis Ungarie, nomine Helenam'' („córkę króla Węgier, imieniem Helena”). Dalej podaje: ''quam anno Domini 1258. adduxit in terram suam de terra Cracoviensi'' („którą w roku Pańskim 1258 sprowadził do swojej ziemi z ziemi krakowskiej”).<ref name=\"BoleslawMarriage1258\" /> W 1265 roku ''Annales Capituli Posnaniensis'' ponownie określają żonę Bolesława jako Helenę, odnotowując ''pro uxore dicti ducis domina Helena, filia regis Ungarie'' („w imieniu żony wspomnianego księcia, pani Heleny, córki króla Węgier”).<ref name=\"BoleslawJolenta1260\" /> Ich potwierdzonymi dziećmi były:\n\n*[[Piast-1|Elżbieta]]\n*[[Piast-27|Jadwiga]]\n*[[Piast-28|Anna]]\n===Śmierć i pochówek===W 1279 roku Bolesław zmarł.       "notes": "{{unsourced|Germany}}\n== Biography == \n\nAlbert I, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg\n\nFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia\n\nhttp://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_I,_Duke_of_Brunswick-L%C3%BCneburg\n Albert the Tall (Latin: Albertus Longus, German: Albrecht der Große) (1236–1279), of the House of Welf, was Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg from 1252 to 1269 and the first ruler of the newly created Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel from 1269 until his death.\n\nLife[edit]\nAlbert I of Brunswick was the second son of Otto the Child, the first Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and his wife, Matilda of Brandenburg. When his father died in 1252, he was the oldest surviving son, and took over the rule of the duchy; later his younger brother John joined him. In 1267, the brothers agreed to divide the duchy, which happened in 1269. Albert partitioned the territory while John obtained the right to choose his part. He took the northern half including the region of Lüneburg and the city of Hanover, while Albert received the southern part, including Calenberg, Helmstedt, the Harz mountains and Göttingen. The City of Brunswick was to remain common property of the brothers.\nAlbert died on August 15, 1279 and is buried at Brunswick Cathedral. He was succeeded by his elder three sons, the younger three joined the Church.\n\nMarriage and children[edit]\nIn 1254, Albert married Elizabeth of Brabant (1243 – October 9, 1261), the daughter of Henry II, Duke of Brabant and Sophie of Thuringia. They had no children [1]\nAfter Elizabeth's death in 1261, Henry married Adelheid (Alessia) (1242 – February 6, 1284/85), daughter of Boniface II of Montferrat around 1263.       "notes": "== Biography==Blanche of Brittany (1271–1327) was a daughter of John II, Duke of Brittany, and his wife Beatrice of England. She is also known as Blanche de Dreux. Through her mother she was the granddaughter of King Henry III of England and Eleanor of Provence.\n\n=== Marriage and issue ===Blanche was married in Paris sometime after November 1281 to Philip of Artois, who was the son of Robert II of Artois and Amice de Courtenay. They were third cousins once removed through a common descent from Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine.\n\nThe couple had two sons and five daughters:\n\n#Margaret (1285–1311), married in 1301 Louis, Count of Évreux\n#Robert III of Artois (1287–1342), married in 1318 Joan of Valois\n#Isabella (1288–1344), a nun at Poissy#Joan (1289 – aft. 1350), married in 1301 in Senlis, Gaston I, Count of Foix\n#Othon (died 2 November 1291)#Marie (1291 – January 22, 1365, Wijnendaele), Lady of Merode, married in 1309 in Paris John I, Marquis of Namur. She was the mother of Blanche of Namur.#Catherine (1296–1368, Normandy), married John II of Ponthieu, Count of Aumale\nBlanche's husband participated with his father at the Battle of Furnes, where he was wounded to the extent that he succumbed about one year later. His premature death led to a succession battle upon his father's death, when Artois was ceded to his sister Mahaut rather than his son Robert. Robert was never the proper Count of Artois; on Mahaut's death Artois passed to her daughter, Joan II, Countess of Burgundy.\nBlanche's daughter Margaret was the mother of Philip III of Navarre who was married to Joan II of Navarre. Her sister, Marie was married to Guy IV, Count of Saint-Pol.\nBlanche died on 19 March 1327 at the Chateau de Bois-de-Vincennes (Vincennes Castle) and was buried at the Église des Jacobins (Church of the Jacobins) in Paris.\n\n==Sources==\n<references />*Van Kerrebrouck, Patrick. Died of plague in Tunis. Canonized 1297 as St. Louis.\n: Louis successfully stood up to a dangerous coalition led by Hugh de Lusignan and Raymond VII of Toulouse with the backing of Henry III of England. During the Seventh Crusade (1248-1254), St. Louis captured Damietta, but he was defeated at al-Mansurah in February 1250. Despite the Pope's advice, the reticence of his lords, and his own poor health, Louis set off from Aigues-Mortes for the Eighth Crusade. He died from plague during the Seige of Tunis.\n: A diplomat with an innate sense of justice and equity, he created the French Parliament and kept an eye on his bailiffs, seneschals, and provosts. He founded a number of hospitals, including the Quinze Vingts for three hundred knights whose eyes had been put out by the Saracen.\n: Louis commissioned the building of the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, and was canonized in 1297.\n\n=== Death ===\n: 25 AUG 1270 Near Tunis, Tunisia: buried: Basilica of St Denis (Basilique Saint-Denis) in Saint-Denis, now Paris suburb.\n: relics in the Basilica of Saint Denis, Paris, France but were destroyed in 1793 during the French Revolution\n\n=== Veneration ===\n: Canonized by Pope Boniface VIII in 1297\n\n: Feast Day: August 25 (formerly August 24)\n\n: Representation: king holding a cross or a crown of thorns\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n* Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. III page 28* [http://catholicsaints.info/saint-louis-ix/ \"Saint Louis IX\"] CatholicSaints.Info. 3 August 2017.       "notes": "[[Category: Christ Church Greyfriars, City of London]] \n== Biography == \n{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Plantagenet\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-16.png}}\n{{Notables Sticker}}'''Beatrice of England''' (25 June 1242[1] – 24 March 1275), also known as '''Beatrice de Dreux''', was a Princess of England as the daughter of King Henry III of England and Eleanor of Provence. Her siblings were Edward I of England, Margaret, Queen of Scotland, Edmund Crouchback, 1st Earl of Lancaster, Richard of England, John of England, Katherine of England, William of England, and Henry of England. She and her family were members of the Royal house of Plantagenet, which first ruled in the 12th century and was founded by Henry II of England.\nAt one point, Henry conducted negotiations for Beatrice to marry the king of France and also rejected a proposal that she should wed the son of the King of Norway. When she was eighteen she married John de Dreux, heir to the dukedom of Brittany. Beatrice later changed her name to Beatrice de Dreux, and she and John II had six children:\n*Arthur II, Duke of Brittany\n*John of Brittany, Earl of Richmond*Marie of Brittany, Countess of Saint-Pol, wife of Guy III of Châtillon (1268–1339)\n*Pierre, Viscount de Leon (1269–1312)\n*Blanche of Brittany, wife of Philip of Artois (1271–1327)\n*Eleonore, Abbess of Fontevrault (1274–1329)\nBeatrice died on 24 March 1275 in London, England. Her death was once said to have occurred in childbirth, but the dates do not bear out this theory, which has been disproved in several articles. John II honoured his wife with a chantry, an institutional chapel on private land or within a greater church, which was to be finished when he died, so that he and Beatrice would be together again. Beatrice was buried at Grey Friars Church in Greenwich, London.[2] Her husband succeeded as duke 11 years after her death, therefore Beatrice was never styled Duchess of Brittany.\nFrom ''[http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatrice_of_England Wikipedia: Beatrice of England], accessed Jan 22, 2014''\n\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n\n* '''ROYAL ANCESTRY by Douglas Richardson Vol. I, page 549'''",
