      "notes": "[[Category:House of Sobiesław]][[Category: Bazylika Prymasowska Wniebowzięcia Najświętszej Maryi Panny, Gniezno, Wielkopolskie]]\n{{Disputed Parents}}\n{{Polish Roots}}\n== Biography =={{Notability|location=Poland|text=Jadwiga was the wife of  Władysław Odonic, the mother of two Dukes of Greater Poland and the grandmother of Przemysł II, King of Poland.}}\n\n([[#Biografia|Wersja polska]])\n===Origins===Jadwiga was probably a daughter of [[Sobiesławic-1|Mściwój I]], Duke of Pomerania, and [[Unknown-284536|Zwinisława]]. Her parentage is not directly stated in surviving contemporary records, but this identification is supported by medieval narrative and kinship evidence, although alternative interpretations have been proposed.\n===Marriage and Children===Jadwiga was married to [[Piast-2|Władysław]]. Their marriage and two sons are directly documented in a charter from 1235. In his grant of Ninkowo to the Church of St. Peter in Poznań, Władysław names Jadwiga as ''uxor mea Hadewigis'' (“my wife Jadwiga”) and identifies Przemysł and Bolesław as ''nostris filiis'' (“our sons”).<ref name=\"KDW184\">''Kodeks dyplomatyczny Wielkopolski'', t. 1 (Poznań: Biblioteka Kórnicka, 1877), [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458  #184], dokument z 1235 r.; Władysław Odonic występuje wraz z żoną Jadwigą (''uxor mea Hadewigis'') i ich synami Przemysłem i Bolesławem (hereafter Kodeks).</ref>  The following were their children:\n\n* [[Piast-40|Przemysł]]\n* [[Piast-79|Eufemia]]\n* [[Piast-8|Bolesław]]\n* [[Piast-78|Salomea]]\n* [[Piast-80|Ziemomysł]]\nAfter Władysław's death, Jadwiga continued to appear in documents issued with or by her sons. On 4 May 1243, she joined Przemysł I and Bolesław in granting the hospital at Gniezno and its possessions to the Order of the Holy Sepulchre. Przemysł called her ''dilecta matre nostra domina Hadwiga'' (“our beloved mother, Lady Jadwiga”) and identified Bolesław as his younger brother.<ref name=\"Kodeks238\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #238].</ref>  In 1244, Przemysł and Bolesław again appeared with Jadwiga in a grant to the Dominican friars at Poznań, where Przemysł identified her as ''matre mea Hadviga'' (“my mother Jadwiga”).<ref name=\"Kodeks243\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #243].</ref>\nJadwiga continued to participate in her son's acts during the following years. On 1 Jul 1247, she joined Przemysł in granting the village of Pakolisse to the Cistercian monastery at Paradyż, where he described her as ''dilecta matre nostra nomine Adwigis'' (“our beloved mother named Jadwiga”).<ref name=\"Kodeks262\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #262].</ref>  On 30 Apr 1248, she interceded when Przemysł confirmed privileges previously granted by Władys��aw to the monastery at Trzebnica. In that document Przemysł described her as ''nostra dilectissima matre seniori ducissa Polonie'' (“our most beloved mother, the elder Duchess of Poland”).<ref name=\"Kodeks269\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #269].</ref>\n===Death===Jadwiga was dead by 24 April 1250, when her son Przemysł I made a grant to the Cistercian convent at Owińska “pro remedio animarum parentum nostrorum” (“for the salvation of the souls of our parents”).<ref name=\"Kodeks284\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #284].</ref>\nOn 3 Aug 1254 her son Przemysł I confirmed a privilege previously granted by his parents, naming them as Władysław, son of Odon, and Jadwiga, Duchess of Poland, and referring to them as “beate memorie” (“of blessed memory”).<ref name=\"Kodeks324\">''Kodeks'', [https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/publication/12458 #324].</ref>\nJadwiga died on 29 Dec 1249. The Rocznik Wielkopolski preserves her death under the year 1250 with the date IV Kalendas Januarii (29 Dec). Balzer, comparing this entry with the surviving documentary evidence, concluded that the date corresponds to 29 Dec 1249.  She was buried in Gniezno Cathedral. The ''Rocznik Wielkopolski'' records: ''“mater domini ducis Premislonis, Adviga, diem clausit extremum, et est sepulta in ecclesia Gneznensi”'' (“Jadwiga, mother of Lord Duke Przemysł, died and was buried in the church of Gniezno”).<ref name=\"RocznikWielkopolski\">''Monumenta Poloniae Historica'', t. 2 (Lwów: Akademia Umiejętności, 1872), \"Boguphali II episcopi Posnaniensis Chronicon Poloniae, cum continuatione Basconis custodis Posnaniensis\", [https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File%3AMonumenta_Poloniae_Historica_T3.djvu&page=37 pp. 16 & 17] (Hereafter ''Monumenta'')</ref><ref name=\"BalzerJadwiga\">Oswald Balzer, ''Genealogia Piastów'' (Kraków: Akademia Umiejętności, 1895), [https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File%3APL_Balzer_-_Genealogia_Piast%C3%B3w.djvu&page=244 p. 222].</ref>\n==Research Notes==No surviving contemporary document has been found that identifies Jadwiga's parents. Her proposed relationship to the Sobiesławice dynasty is based principally on two medieval sources.\nThe principal evidence comes from the ''Kronika wielkopolska''. In its account of Władysław Odonic's exile, the chronicler states that Władysław married a sister of Świętopełk II. The statement is qualified by the words ''ut quidam ajunt'' (“as some say”), showing that the chronicler was reporting a tradition rather than a relationship he could independently establish.<ref name=\"KronikaJadwiga\">''Monumenta'', [https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File%3AMonumenta_Poloniae_Historica_T2.djvu&page=601 p. 555].</ref> Władysław's wife is identified as Jadwiga in surviving charters, so if the chronicle's account is correct, Jadwiga was Świętopełk's sister and therefore a daughter of his parents, Mściwój I and Zwinisława.\nThere is additional evidence for this relationship. The ''Rocznik Wielkopolski'' describes Bolesław Pobożny, Jadwiga's son, as the ''frater amitivus'' of Mściwoj II, the son of Świętopełk II.<ref name=\"RocznikAmitivus\">''Monumenta'', [https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File%3AMonumenta_Poloniae_Historica_T3.djvu&page=58 p. 37].</ref> This term indicates a relationship through an ''amita'', or paternal aunt, and therefore supports the possibility that Jadwiga was Mściwoj II's paternal aunt, the sister of his father Świętopełk II.\nThe uncertainty comes from the ''Kronika wielkopolska'' itself. Later in the chronicle, the author discusses the relationship between these families. He refers to Przemysł's mother as the reported sister of Świętopełk, but considers other possible explanations for the kinship. Unable to determine which explanation was correct, he concludes, ''Quid autem certi sit, non invenio'' (“What, however, is certain, I do not find”).<ref name=\"KronikaJadwiga576\">''Monumenta'', [https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File%3AMonumenta_Poloniae_Historica_T2.djvu&page=622 p. 576].</ref>\nThe surviving evidence therefore favors identifying Jadwiga as Świętopełk II's sister and a daughter of Mściwoj I, but does not establish her parentage with certainty. Her parents are therefore shown as probable, with the relationships marked uncertain. [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nA son named Mieszko was attributed to Władysław Odonic and Jadwiga by Oswald Balzer on the basis of an entry in the Lubin necrology commemorating ''Mesconis ducis piae memoriae'' on 7 Jan. Kazimierz Jasiński rejected this identification. He noted that Mieszko does not appear in Władysław Odonic's documents, despite Odonic's practice of including his sons in legal acts, and that identifying the deceased as a young son of Odonic is difficult to reconcile with the necrology's description of him as ''dux.'' Jasiński instead considered convincing Władysław Semkowicz's identification of the entry with Mieszko, the known son of Bolesław II Szczodry, and concluded that the necrology probably records that Mieszko's death on 7 Jan 1089. A Mieszko son should therefore not be included among the children of Władysław Odonic and Jadwiga.<ref name=\"JasinskiMieszko\">Kazimierz Jasiński, “Uzupełnienia do genealogii Piastów,” ''Studia Źródłoznawcze'', t. 3 (1958),  [https://rcin.org.pl/ihpan/Content/41528/PDF/WA303_39412_B88-SZ-R-3-1958_Jasinski.pdf pp. 211-212].</ref>  [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nA daughter named Zofia, sometimes given the dates about 1230–1276, has been attributed to Władysław Odonic and Jadwiga in online genealogies. She is not included among their children in modern scholarly reconstructions. No contemporary evidence has been found identifying a daughter named Zofia. She is therefore not included among the children of Władysław and Jadwiga.  [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nAnother daughter named Jadwiga has been proposed as a child of Władysław Odonic and Jadwiga. She was probably the first wife of [[Piast-113|Kazimierz I]], Duke of Kujawy, whom she married about 1230/1231. Her identification as a daughter of Władysław Odonic is not certain. She is therefore not included among the children of Władysław and Jadwiga.  [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n==Biografia==\n([[#Biography|English Version]])\n===Pochodzenie===Jadwiga była prawdopodobnie córką [[Sobiesławic-1|Mściwoja I]], księcia pomorskiego, i [[Unknown-284536|Zwinisławy]]. Jej pochodzenie nie jest bezpośrednio określone w zachowanych współczesnych dokumentach, ale taką identyfikację wspierają średniowieczne przekazy narracyjne oraz świadectwa dotyczące pokrewieństwa, choć proponowano również inne interpretacje.\n===Małżeństwo i dzieci===Jadwiga była żoną [[Piast-2|Władysława]]. Ich małżeństwo oraz dwóch synów są bezpośrednio poświadczone w dokumencie z 1235 r. W nadaniu Ninkowa kościołowi św. Piotra w Poznaniu Władysław nazywa Jadwigę ''uxor mea Hadewigis'' („moja żona Jadwiga”), a Przemysła i Bolesława określa jako ''nostris filiis'' („naszych synów���).<ref name=\"KDW184\" /> Ich dziećmi byli:\n\n*[[Piast-40|Przemysł]]\n*[[Piast-79|Eufemia]]\n*[[Piast-8|Bolesław]]\n*[[Piast-78|Salomea]]\n*[[Piast-80|Ziemomysł]]\nPo śmierci Władysława Jadwiga nadal pojawiała się w dokumentach wystawianych wspólnie z synami lub przez nich. 4 maja 1243 r. wraz z Przemysłem I i Bolesławem nadała szpital w Gnieźnie wraz z jego posiadłościami Zakonowi Grobu Bożego. Przemysł określił ją jako ''dilecta matre nostra domina Hadwiga'' („nasza umiłowana matka, pani Jadwiga”), a Bolesława jako swojego młodszego brata.<ref name=\"Kodeks238\" /> W 1244 r. Przemysł i Bolesław ponownie wystąpili wraz z Jadwigą w nadaniu dla dominikanów w Poznaniu, w którym Przemysł określił ją jako ''matre mea Hadviga'' („moja matka Jadwiga”).<ref name=\"Kodeks243\" />\nJadwiga nadal uczestniczyła w czynnościach prawnych swojego syna w kolejnych latach. 1 lipca 1247 r. wraz z Przemysłem dokonała nadania wsi Pakolisse klasztorowi cystersów w Paradyżu, gdzie określił ją jako ''dilecta matre nostra nomine Adwigis'' („nasza umiłowana matka imieniem Jadwiga”).<ref name=\"Kodeks262\" /> 30 kwietnia 1248 r. wstawiła się za klasztorem w Trzebnicy, gdy Przemysł potwierdzał przywileje nadane mu wcześniej przez Władysława. W dokumencie tym Przemysł określił ją jako ''nostra dilectissima matre seniori ducissa Polonie'' („nasza najukochańsza matka, starsza księżna Polski”).<ref name=\"Kodeks269\" />\n===Śmierć===Jadwiga nie żyła już 24 kwietnia 1250 r., kiedy jej syn Przemysł I dokonał nadania na rzecz klasztoru cysterek w Owińskach ''pro remedio animarum parentum nostrorum'' („dla zbawienia dusz naszych rodziców”).<ref name=\"Kodeks284\" />\n3 sierpnia 1254 r. jej syn Przemysł I potwierdził przywilej nadany wcześniej przez swoich rodziców, wymieniając ich jako Władysława, syna Odona, i Jadwigę, księżną Polski, oraz określając ich jako ''beate memorie'' („błogosławionej pamięci”).<ref name=\"Kodeks324\" />\nJadwiga zmarła 29 grudnia 1249 r. ''Rocznik Wielkopolski'' odnotowuje jej śmierć pod rokiem 1250, podając datę ''IV Kalendas Januarii'' (29 grudnia). Balzer, porównując ten zapis z zachowanymi dokumentami, uznał, że data ta odpowiada 29 grudnia 1249 r. Została pochowana w katedrze gnieźnieńskiej. ''Rocznik Wielkopolski'' podaje: ''“mater domini ducis Premislonis, Adviga, diem clausit extremum, et est sepulta in ecclesia Gneznensi”'' („Jadwiga, matka pana księcia Przemysła, zmarła i została pochowana w kościele gnieźnieńskim”).<ref name=\"RocznikWielkopolski\" /><ref name=\"BalzerJadwiga\" />\n==Notatki badawcze==Nie odnaleziono żadnego zachowanego współczesnego dokumentu, który identyfikowałby rodziców Jadwigi. Jej proponowane pokrewieństwo z dynastią Sobiesławiców opiera się przede wszystkim na dwóch średniowiecznych źródłach.\nGłównego świadectwa dostarcza ''Kronika wielkopolska''. W relacji dotyczącej wygnania Władysława Odonica kronikarz podaje, że Władysław poślubił siostrę Świętopełka II. Stwierdzenie to zostało opatrzone słowami ''ut quidam ajunt'' („jak niektórzy powiadają”), co wskazuje, że kronikarz przekazywał tradycję, a nie pokrewieństwo, które mógł niezależnie potwierdzić.<ref name=\"KronikaJadwiga\" /> W zachowanych dokumentach żona Władysława jest identyfikowana jako Jadwiga, zatem jeśli przekaz kroniki jest poprawny, Jadwiga by��a siostrą Świętopełka, a tym samym córką jego rodziców, Mściwoja I i Zwinisławy.\nIstnieje dodatkowe świadectwo przemawiające za tym pokrewieństwem. ''Rocznik Wielkopolski'' określa Bolesława Pobożnego, syna Jadwigi, jako ''frater amitivus'' Mściwoja II, syna Świętopełka II.<ref name=\"RocznikAmitivus\" /> Termin ten wskazuje na pokrewieństwo przez ''amita'', czyli ciotkę ze strony ojca, i tym samym wspiera możliwoś��, że Jadwiga była ciotką Mściwoja II ze strony ojca, a więc siostrą jego ojca Świętopełka II.\nNiepewność wynika z samej ''Kroniki wielkopolskiej''. W dalszej części kroniki autor omawia pokrewieństwo między tymi rodzinami. Nazywa matkę Przemysła domniemaną siostrą Świętopełka, lecz rozważa także inne możliwe wyjaśnienia tego pokrewieństwa. Nie mogąc ustalić, które z nich jest poprawne, stwierdza: ''Quid autem certi sit, non invenio'' („Co jednak jest pewne, tego nie znajduję”).<ref name=\"KronikaJadwiga576\" />\nZachowane świadectwa przemawiają zatem za identyfikacją Jadwigi jako siostry Świętopełka II i córki Mściwoja I, lecz nie pozwalają ustalić jej pochodzenia z całkowitą pewnością. Jej rodzice są zatem wskazani jako prawdopodobni, a relacje z nimi oznaczone jako niepewne. [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nOswald Balzer przypisywał Władysławowi Odonicowi i Jadwidze syna imieniem Mieszko na podstawie zapisu w nekrologu lubińskim, upamiętniającego ''Mesconis ducis piae memoriae'' pod datą 7 stycznia. Kazimierz Jasiński odrzucił tę identyfikację. Zauważył, że Mieszko nie pojawia się w dokumentach Władysława Odonica, pomimo praktyki Odonica polegającej na uwzględnianiu synów w czynnościach prawnych, oraz że utożsamienie zmarłego z młodym synem Odonica trudno pogodzi�� z określeniem go w nekrologu jako ''dux''. Jasiński uznał natomiast za przekonującą identyfikację Władysława Semkowicza, według której zapis odnosi się do Mieszka, znanego syna Bolesława II Szczodrego, i doszedł do wniosku, że nekrolog prawdopodobnie odnotowuje śmierć tego Mieszka 7 stycznia 1089 r. Mieszka nie należy zatem zaliczać do dzieci Władysława Odonica i Jadwigi.<ref name=\"JasinskiMieszko\" /> [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nCórka imieniem Zofia, której czasami przypisuje się daty około 1230–1276, bywa uznawana w genealogiach internetowych za córkę Władysława Odonica i Jadwigi. Nie jest ona uwzględniana wśród ich dzieci we współczesnych opracowaniach naukowych. Nie odnaleziono żadnego współczesnego źródła identyfikującego córkę o imieniu Zofia. Dlatego nie została uwzględniona wśród dzieci Władysława i Jadwigi. [[Kobus-79|Kobus-79]] 19:28, 31 August 2026 (UTC)\n\n----\nJako dziecko Władysława Odonica i Jadwigi proponowano również inn�� córkę o imieniu Jadwiga. Była ona prawdopodobnie pierwszą żoną [[Piast-113|Kazimierza I]], księcia kujawskiego, którego poślubiła około 1230/1231 r. Jej identyfikacja jako córki Władysława Odonica nie jest pewna. Dlatego nie została uwzględniona wśród dzieci Władysława i Jadwigi. He succeeded his mother in 1279 as OTHON IV Comte Palatin de Bourgogne.\nOtto IV, Count of Burgundy (1248-1302) was the son of Hugh de Chalon and Adelaide, Countess Palatine of Burgundy. By his mother, he was a grandson of Countess Beatrice II of Burgundy. By his father, he was descended from another branch of the Counts of Burgundy.\n \nUpon his father's death in 1266/1267, he became Count of Chalons.\n \nHe married Philippa of Bar in 1271. The marriage was childless.\nHis coat of arms (''die greue van Bourgondien'') is included in the attendees of the Tournament of Compiègne of 1278, when King Philippe III celebrated the visit of his cousin, Charles II d'Anjou, Prince of Salerno.<ref>[https://www.kb.nl/en/discover-admire/masterpieces/armorial-beyeren Armorial-Beyeren]. However, he was unable to secure real power in the County until 1295.\n He married his second wife, Mahaut of Artois, in 1285. They had three children: Jeanne, Blanche, and Robert. Of these, his daughters would marry eventual Kings of France, and both his son and elder daughter were to succeed him in the County.\n \nUpon his death in 1302, his titles were inherited by his son.\n\n=== Birth ===\n:: Date:  ABT 1248 TO ABT 1248\n:: Place:  Châlons-Salins, Saône-et-Loire, Bourgogne, France\n\n=== Death ===\n:: Date:  17 MAR 1302\n:: Place:  Melun,Seine Et Oise,Ile De France,France\n\n=== Marriage ===\n:: Date:  ABT 1285 TO 1 MAY 1271\n:: Place:  Paris,Seine,,France\n: Wife:  [[Flanders-343|Mahaut Flanders]]\n: Husband:  [[Bourgogne-93|Otto IV de Bourgogne]]\n: Child:  [[Bourgogne-94|Blanche Bourgogne]]\n: Child:  [[Burgundy-162|Count Robert of Burgundy]]\n: Child:  [[Bourgogne-90|Jeanne II Bourgogne]]\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />* http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/BURGUNDY%20Kingdom.htm#OthonVComtedied1303B\n\n\n* WikiTree profile Bourgogne-93 created through the import of export-BloodTree.ged on Aug 19, 2011 by [[Heinzelmann-4 | Luiz Sergio Heinzelmann]].       "notes": "[[Category: House of Capet]]\n{{Succession\n|image=Bourgogne-349.png\n|position1=Comte de d'Artois \n|before1=[[Capet-533|Robert de Capet d'Artois]]<br>1250-1302\n|after1=[[Bourgogne-349|Jeanne de Capet]] <br>1329-1330\n|years1=1302-1329\n}}\n== Biographie ==\n([[#Biography |'''English version below''']])\nMahaut d'Artois, dite aussi Mathilde d'Artois, comtesse palatine de Bourgogne par mariage, puis comtesse d'Artois, était la seule fille<ref name=medlands>Medieval Lands, Northern France, [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/NORTHERN%20FRANCE.htm#MahautArtoisdied1329 Mathilde d'Artois]</ref> de Robert II, comte d'Artois, et d'Amicie de Courtenay<ref name=anselme>Histoire généalogique et chronologique de la maison royale de France, des pairs, grands officiers de la Couronne, de la Maison du Roy et des anciens barons du royaume.... Tome 1, par le Père Anselme de Sainte-Marie, continuée par Honoré du Fourny, ed. la compagnie des libraires (Paris). Chapitre XIII, pages 383-384 [http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k76026j/f398.image Link], consulté le 26 mai 2017 via Gallica</ref>.\nElle fut mariée le 9 juin 1291<ref name=anselme />à Othon IV, comte de Bourgogne. De ce mariage sont nés trois enfants:# Jeanne, femme de Philippe V, roi de France, comtesse d'Artois (1329) et de Bourgogne (1317)# Blanche, première femme de Charles de France, futur Charles IV, mariage annulé en 1322, morte en 1326.# Robert, comte palatin de Bourgogne à la mort de son père, né vers 1300, mort vers 1315-1317<ref name=anselme />.\nLe 22 décembre 1297 Mahaut et son mari Othon signèrent un acte par lequel Mahaut recevait pour la succession de sa mère Amicie de Courtenay la moitié des châtellenies de Château-Renard et de Charny, l'autre moitié revenant à son frère Philippe. Mais Philippe étant mort en 1298 et leur père Robert II en 1302, Mahaut devenue veuve en 1303, plaida contre son neveu Robert, le fils de Philippe, pour récupérer le comté d'Artois<ref name=anselme />. Le comté fut adjugé à Mahaut par le roi Philippe IV le 9 octobre 1309. Mahaut obtint encore en 1318 un arrêt lui confirmant la possession du comté-pairie d'Artois contre son neveu<ref name=anselme /><ref name=medlands />. En 1317 Mahaut avait été accusée de faits criminels par Isabeau de Fresne (que le Père Anselme décrit comme une personne de mauvaise réputation) et avait été acquittée<ref name=anselme /><ref name=medlands />.\nMahaut mourut le 27 octobre 1329 à Paris. On soupçonna un empoisonnement. Elle fut enterrée dans l'église de l'abbaye de Maubuisson<ref name=anselme />.\n\n== Biography ==\n([[#Biographie |'''Version française ci-dessus''']])\nMahaut of Artois, also known as Mathilda, countess of Burgundy by marriage and later countess of Artois, was the only daughter<ref name=medlands /> of Robert II, Count of Artois and Amicie de Courtenay<ref name=anselme />.\nHer paternal grandparents were Robert I, Count of Artois and Matilda of Brabant<ref name=anselme/>. Her maternal grandparents were Pierre de Courtenay, Seigneur de Conches, and Perronelle de Joigny. She had two brothers: * Philip of Artois (c. 1269-1298) who married Blanche de Dreux, daughter of John II, Duke of Brittany, by whom he had five children.\n* Robert of Artois. (Born 1271). Died young<ref name=medlands />.\nIn 1291<ref name=anselme />Mahaut married Otto IV, Count of Burgundy, to whom she bore three children:# Jeanne, married to Philippe V, king of France. She was countess of Burgundy from 1317 and countess of Artois from 1329.# Blanche, first wife of Charles of France, later king Charles IV. The marriage was annulled in 1322. She died in 1326.# Robert, count of Burgundy upon his father's death (1303), born around 1300, died around 1315-1317<ref name=anselme />.\nBecause of the premature death of her brother Philip in 1298 Mahaut inherited the County of Artois at her father's death in 1302, rather than her nephew Robert (her inheritance being based upon proximity of blood). Although Robert repeatedly challenged the decision, her rights to the County were consistently upheld (in 1309 by king Philip IV, and again in 1318)<ref name=anselme /><ref name=medlands />. Her vassals in Artois rebelled against her in 1315<ref name=medlands />. She was accused of criminal acts by an Isabeau de Fresne (a dubious person according to Père Anselme) but acquitted 9 Oct 1317<ref name=anselme/><ref name=medlands />.\nMahaut died in Paris in October 1329, and was buried in the church of the Abbey of Maubuisson near Pontoise<ref name=anselme />. Upon her death the county was inherited by her daughter Jeanne II, Countess Palatine of Burgundy (d 1329).\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n* WikiTree profile Flanders-343 created through the import of export-BloodTree.ged on Aug 19, 2011 by [[Heinzelmann-4 | Luiz Sergio Heinzelmann]].       "notes": "[[Category:Pre-1500 Notables]]\n[[Category:England Managed Profiles, Pre-1500 PPP]]\n[[Category:England, Monarchs]][[Category: Battle of Bouvines]] [[Category: First Barons' War]][[Category: Feudal Barony of Gloucester]][[Category:Ireland, Governors]][[Category: Early Barony of Launceston]][[Category:Earls of Cornwall]][[Category: Early Barony of Wallingford]][[Category: Honour of Tickhill (or Blyth)]]\n[[Category:Nominated Profiles]]\n[[Category: Early Barony of Berkhamsted]]\n[[Category: Day-1904 Temporary Euroaristo Project]] \n[[Category: Magna Carta Profiles]]\n[[Category: Time Team]]\n{{England}}\n{{Succession\n|position1=King of England\n|years1= 1199 -1216\n|before1= [[Plantagenet-248|Richard I]]\n|after1= [[Plantagenet-167|Henry III]]\n}}\n== Biography =={{Notability|location=England|text=John \"Lackland\" Plantagenet was the king of England who signed the Magna Carta}}\n{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Plantagenet\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-16.png}}\n===Birth and Parents===John was the youngest son of [[Plantagenet-1627|Henry II]] of England and [[Aquitaine-84|Eleanor of Aquitaine]].<ref name=\"RA 1.43\">Douglas Richardson. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham (Salt City: the author, 2013), Vol. I, pp. 43-58, ENGLAND 5</ref> His exact birth date is uncertain, but it was probably in the Christmas season of 1166/7 - from 24 December 1166 to 6 January 1167. He was probably born in either the Palace of Westminster or the Tower of London.<ref name=\"ODNB\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by John Gillingham for King John, print and online 2004, revised online 2021</ref><ref name=\"Church 2020\">Church, Stephen. ''The Date and Place of King John's Birth together with a Codicil on his Name'', in 'Notes and Queries', Vol. 67, 2020, PDF viewable on [https://ueaeprints.uea.ac.uk/id/eprint/75395/1/Accepted_Manuscript.pdf University of East Anglia website], accessed 15 January 2024</ref> (See [[#Research Notes|Research Notes]] for more discussion.)\n\n===Reign of Henry II===John was his parents' youngest son, and his father had already made significant provision of land for his older brothers, leaving relatively little available for John. Probably because of this, he was nicknamed \"Lackland\" from at least the early 1180s: it is believed that this nickname may have been given him by his father. Henry II sought to remedy this. In 1173 Henry bestowed Chinon, Loudun, and Mirebeau on him: this provoked a rebellion by John's brother [[Plantagenet-33|Henry]] which ended the next year, and Henry II then granted John substantial income from England, Normandy and Anjou. In 1175 [[Dunstanville-20|Reginald de Dunstanville]], Earl of Cornwall and an illegitimate son of Henry I, died: Henry II took the opportunity to appropriate the Earl's estates for John's use.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1173 John was betrothed to [[Savoie-665|Alix]], daughter of Humbert/Umberto III, Count of Maurienne: the contract stipulated that John would inherit the County if Humbert had no legitimate sons. Alix's death the next year meant the marriage never took place.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\">Charles Cawley. [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLAND,%20Kings%201066-1603.htm#JohnKingdied1216B King John], entry in “Medieval Lands” database (accessed 17 January 2024</ref>\nIn 1177 Henry II gave John the title King of Ireland.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> He attempted to increase John's resources by transferring Aquitaine to him. This was held by his brother, the future [[Plantagenet-248|Richard I]], and Richard declined to hand it over. John and his brother [[Plantagenet-29|Geoffrey]] launched an unsuccessful attack on Richard, and Henry II was compelled to agree to Richard retaining Aquitaine.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nHenry II knighted John in March 1185 and sent him with a sizeable army to Ireland, where [[Lacy-287|Hugh de Lacy]]'s activities were a cause of concern.  John alienated some Irish kings by his grants of lands to his own followers, and was defeated several times. John was back in England in September 1185. The next year Hugh de Lacy died, and a second Irish expedition was envisaged, but this never took place.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nJohn's brother Geoffrey died in August 1186, and Henry wished to use the opportunity to increase John's possessions. Rumours that Henry planned to disinherit the future Richard I, and Henry's reluctance to acknowledge Richard formally as his heir, led Richard into rebellion. Initially John supported his father, but he defected when it became clear in the summer of 1189 that Henry II was unlikely to prevail.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===First Marriage===On 28 September 1176 John was betrothed to [[FitzWilliam-517|Isabel]], daughter of William, Earl of Gloucester. Like him she was a great-grandchild of Henry I and the betrothal contract allowed for the possibility that the Pope might prevent the marriage on grounds of consanguinity. Isabel's father died in 1183 (the 1176 death date given in John's own entry in the ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' is a mistake<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>), and, rather than allow the marriage to take place soon after, Henry II made her a royal ward, allowing him to benefit from the income from her estates.<ref name=\"ODNB Isabel of Gloucester\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Robert B Patterson for 'Isabella, suo jure countess of Gloucester', print and online 2004, revised online 2005</ref>\nThe marriage finally went ahead after Henry II's death: they married on 29 August 1189 at Marlborough, Wiltshire. No papal dispensation from the consanguinity rules had been obtained, and the Archbishop of Canterbury summoned John to defend himself. John did not obey the summons, and his lands were placed under interdict. When John appealed to the Pope, the interdict was lifted by the papal legate,<ref name=\"ODNB Isabel of Gloucester\"/> who accepted the validity of the marriage subject to the outcome of the appeal: John, though, did not pursue the appeal, and this left the status of the marriage in a degree of ambiguity.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\nJohn and Isabel had no children.<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>\n\n===Reign of Richard I===In 1189 Richard I became King of England. He awarded John extensive estates in England, and made him Count of Mortain in Normandy (in charters of that year confirming rights of the people of Nottingham, John styles himself Count of Mortain<ref>''Records of the Borough of Nottingham'', Vol. I, '', Bernard Quaritch, 1882, pp. 6-10, [https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=eT8uAAAAMAAJ&vq=Pierrepont&pg=PA6&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q=Pierrepont&f=false Google Books]</ref>). But Richard may not altogether have trusted him: before he went on crusade in 1190, he secured an oath from John that he would stay out of England for three years. Richard subsequently gave [[DeLongchamp-4|William de Longchamp]], left in charge of England, permission to free John from the oath if he considered this right. In 1191 John returned to England, quite likely without William de Longchamp's permission. This may have been precipitated by the belief that William regarded John's nephew [[Plantagenet-154|Arthur of Brittany]] (son of John's older brother Geoffrey) as heir to the English throne. John took control of some important castles, and attempts to secure a lasting accord between him and William de Longchamp in the summer of 1191 failed.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn October 1191 William de Longchamp was compelled to resign and Walter de Coutances took his place. John continued to try to bolster his position in England, He was also in contact with [[Capet-12|Philippe Auguste]], king of France, who offered to help him gain control of his family's lands in France if he agreed to marry Philippe Auguste's sister [[Capet-653|Alice]], who had previously been spurned by Richard I. In January 1193 John entered into a formal agreement to marry Alice even though he was still married to Isabel of Gloucester, and to cede the territory of the Vexin to Philippe Auguste. The marriage never took place.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nJohn now engaged in open rebellion in England. In the spring of 1193, fearing he would be charged with treason, he sought refuge in France. In July 1193 it was agreed that he could retain his lands if he contributed to the huge ransom for Richard I's release from captivity. Back in Normandy, keepers of castles he had previously held refused to return them to him. John then entered into alliance with Philippe Auguste. They invaded Normandy, and sought to bribe the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI to detain Richard I for longer. John was excommunicated and his lands and his lordship of Ireland were declared forfeit.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nJohn switched sides again after Richard I, now freed, came to Normandy, begging Richard's pardon. For the rest of Richard's reign, he kept a lower profile. The lordship of Ireland and the Counties of Mortain and Gloucester were restored to him.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===King===Richard I died on 6 April 1199. There followed a dispute over whether the new king should be John or his nephew Arthur of Brittany. In northern France a number of leading barons, supported by Philippe Auguste, backed Arthur, and they almost captured John at Le Mans on 20 April. On 25 April John was formally acknowledged as Duke of Normandy; he was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on 27 May.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref>E B Fryde, D E Greenway, S Porter and I Roy. ''Handbook of British Chronology'', 3rd edition, Royal Historical Society, 1986, p. 29</ref> Soon afterwards, he ended his ambiguous marriage to Isabel of Gloucester, securing an official annulment on grounds of consanguinity. He made her a royal ward again, which gave him access to her estates and the associated revenues.<ref name=\"ODNB Isabel of Gloucester\"/>\nConflict with Philippe Auguste continued. A treaty was signed in May 1200 under which John ceded some of his French possessions to the French king and paid homage to him for the remainder, while Arthur of Brittany paid homage to John.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Second Marriage===After his accession to the throne John initiated negotiations for marriage into the royal house of Portugal. In the end his second marriage was to [[Angoulême-40|Isabella d'Angoulême]], only child of Audemar, Count of Angoulême. They married on 24 August 1200:<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"ODNB Isabella d'Angoulême\">''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Nicholas Vincent for 'Isabella [Isabella of Angoulême], suo jure countess of Angoulême', print and online 2004, revised online 2023</ref> Douglas Richardson and Charles Cawley give the marriage place as Bordeaux Cathedral;<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/> Isabella's entry in the ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' says it was at Angoulême.<ref name=\"ODNB Isabella d'Angoul��me\"/>  She had been betrothed earlier that year to [[Lusignan-30|Hugues de Lusignan]], and one motivation for the marriage was probably to prevent Hugues from acquiring the strategically important territory of Angoulême. But the marriage alienated the Lusignans, who had earlier given John valuable support.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"ODNB Isabella d'Angoulême\"/> \n\nJohn and Isabella had five children:* [[Plantagenet-167|Henry]], , who succeeded his father as King Henry III and who was born at Winchester Castle, Hampshire on 1 October 1207<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/>* [[Plantagenet-39|Richard]], who became the first Earl of Cornwall and who was born at Winchester Castle, Hampshire on 5 January 1209<ref name=\"Medlands\"/><ref>Douglas Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry'', Vol. II, pp. 298-306, CORNWALL 6</ref><ref>G E Cokayne. ''Complete Peerage'', revised edition, Vol. III, st Catherine Press, 1913, pp. 430-432, [https://archive.org/details/completepeerageo03coka/page/430/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref>* [[Plantagenet-296|Joan]], who married [[Dunkeld-4|Alexander II of Scotland]], and who was born on 22 July 1210,<ref name=\"Medlands\"/><ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Keith Stringer for 'Joan (1210–1238)', point and online 2004</ref> at Gloucester according to Douglas Richardson<ref>Douglas Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry'', Vol. IV, pp. 590-593, SCOTLAND 5</ref>* [[Plantagenet-18|Isabella]], who became the third wife of [[Staufer-52|Frederick II]], Holy Roman Emperor, and who was born in 1214,<ref name=\"Medlands\"/><ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by D S H Abulafia for 'Isabella [Elizabeth, Isabella of England] (1214–1241)', print and online 2004</ref> at Gloucester according to Douglas Richardson<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* [[Plantagenet-19|Eleanor]], who married [[Marshal-43|William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke]] and [[Montfort-35|Simon de Montfort]],<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> and who was probably born in 1215,<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Elizabeth Hallam for 'Eleanor, countess of Pembroke and Leicester', print and online 2004</ref> at Gloucester according to Douglas Richardson<ref>Douglas Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry'', Vol. III, pp. 563-566, LEICESTER 10</ref>\n\n===Loss of French Possessions===In 1201 John granted the County of La Marche to Isabella d'Angoulême's father. He had previously granted it to Hugues de Lusignan, who had been betrothed to Isabella, and Hugues appealed to Philippe Auguste. John was summoned to appear before Philippe Auguste but did not do so. In April 1202 the French king formally deprived him of his French fiefs, and took the homage of John's nephew Arthur of Brittany for all of them except Normandy. Philippe Auguste then invaded Normandy. John's mother Eleanor of Aquitaine was almost trapped by Arthur of Brittany and the Lusignan family at Le Mans, but John rescued her, capturing Arthur. Later that year, though, John lost Anjou.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nArthur of Brittany's captivity provoked rebellion in John's territories in northern France. Arthur himself was killed, possibly in early April 1203 and probably either by John himself or on John's orders.<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by Michael Jones for 'Arthur, duke of Brittany', print and online 2004</ref> Soon after, Philippe Auguste again invaded Normandy. John retreated to England in  December 1203. By late summer of 1204 Normandy and Poitiers were in the French king's hands. By the close of the year John had lost most of his French possessions.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1205 John was forced to cancel a major expedition to France because of lack of English support, but he did succeed in regaining the Channel Islands. The next year a truce was agreed with Philippe Auguste, under which John retained Gascony and part of Poitou.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Middle Years of John's Reign===John found himself in dispute with Pope Innocent III over appointments to senior positions in the church, including the Archbishopric of Canterbury, a post John wanted [[Grey-525|John Grey]] to fill. When Innocent consecrated Stephen Langton as Archbishop in 1207, John took control of the estates of the see, and sent the monks of Canterbury, who had approved Stephen's election, into exile. In March 1208 England was placed under a papal interdict, and in November 1209 John was excommunicated. Most bishops left England. As king, John had a right to the income from the estates of unfilled bishoprics and abbacies, and these substantially swelled his revenues.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nMeanwhile John's authority in Ireland was threatened by the English lords there. In 1210 he launched a major campaign, which subdued them in the space of some two months, and increased the territory under direct royal control.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn 1209 John planned an invasion of Scotland, leading to the Treaty of Norham (August 1209) under which [[Dunkeld-2|William the Lion]] agreed to pay a substantial sum to John, and gave John among other hostages two of his daughters.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn Wales John had an uneasy relationship with [[Ap_Iorwerth-26|Llywelyn ap Iorwerth]]. In 1201 a treaty was concluded between them and in 1204 Llywelyn married John's illegitimate daughter [[FitzJohn-120|Joan]]. Llywelyn sought to take advantage of John's absence in Ireland in 1210 to increase the extent of his power, but was defeated in 1211 and forced to come to humiliating terms. Fighting broke out again in 1212, with the Pope and Philippe Auguste encouraging Llywelyn. The Pope secured a truce the next year.<ref>''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'', entry by A D Carr for 'Llywelyn ab Iorwerth', print and online 2004</ref>\n\n===Renewed Conflict with France===John still had ambitions to regain possessions lost in France and he encouraged a coalition against Philippe Auguste, who responded in April 1213 by threatening an invasion of England. In May John came to terms with the Pope, formally surrendering the Kingdom of England, and Innocent III now gave John his backing. At the end of May the threat of invasion was lifted when [[Plantagenet-1612|William de Longespée]] destroyed much of the French fleet. In February 1214 John invaded at La Rochelle, persuading the Lusignan family to support him in return for a promise of his legitimate daughter Joan in marriage to Hugues de Lusignan and a grant of lands. William de Longespée took other forces to join allies in Flanders. The invasion ended badly: John was forced to retreat, and on 27 July the French won a decisive victory against his allies in the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bouvines Battle of Bouvines]. William de Longespée was captured. John's dreams of recovering French possessions were ended. The cost of his efforts drained his coffers.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n===Baronial Rebellion and Magna Carta===Back in England, baronial unrest, strengthened by the return of prominent exiles at the Pope's insistence, came to a head in 1215. In January that year John met leading barons in London, and agreed to a further meeting on 26 April after he had considered their demands. Civil war loomed. In March John took a crusading vow, which increased the support he had from the Pope. The April meeting never happened, and on 5 May baronial opponents renounced their allegiance. On 17 May London went over to the rebels. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth sided with them and captured Shrewsbury. Forced to make concessions, John agreed to the Magna Carta at Runnymede, Surrey on 15 June. This safeguarded the rights of the church and generally set limits to royal powers and was a major landmark in British constitutional history. The Magna Carta included a provision that 25 barons - often known as the \"Surety Barons\" - would be chosen to ensure it was observed.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> They included the then Mayor of London, a sign of the importance of the city.<ref>Douglas Richardson. ''Magna Carta Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'' 4 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham, 2nd edition (Salt Lake City: the author, 2011), Vol. I, p. ix, [https://books.google.co.uk/books?redir_esc=y&id=8JcbV309c5UC&q=hardel#v=snippet&q=hardell&f=false Google Books]</ref>\nJohn did not intend to keep to the terms of the Magna Carta. Within two months he approached the Pope to secure his backing for annulling it. The Pope excommunicated the rebels, who sought French support, offering Philippe Auguste's son [[Capet-11|Louis]] the English throne. The Surety Barons granted Northumberland, Cumberland, and Westmorland to Alexander II of Scotland. Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, having gained the support of other Welsh kings, captured English castles there and became in effect ruler of most of Wales.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nOver the following months John invaded Scotland, and had some success in England. But on 22 May 1216 Louis of France ignored the Pope and landed in Kent, going on to wrest control of much of the eastern half of England, with the support of most of the more important barons, and Alexander II of Scotland paid Louis homage for his English lands. John retreated west, before moving towards Lincoln and East Anglia. \n\n===Death and Burial===John began to suffer dysentery at King's Lynn, Norfolk during the night of 9-10 October 1216 and over the next few days his health worsened. Despite this he reached Newark-on-Trent, Nottinghamshire. En route some of his baggage was lost, and some of his men drowned, in the Wash. He died at Newark Castle during the night of 18/19 October.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nJohn's short will requested burial at \"the church of Saint Mary and Wulstan of Worcester\" - Worcester Cathedral. It is undated, but must have been made not long before his death as it refers to \"Lord Sylvester, Bishop of Worcester\"<ref name=\"Newark\">Cornelius Brown. ''The annals of Newark-upon-Trent'', H Sotheran and Co, 1879, pp. 13-15, [https://archive.org/details/annalsnewarkupo00browgoog/page/n28/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref><ref>Nicholas Harris Nicolas. ''Testamenta Vetusta'', Vol. I, Nicholas and Son, 1826, p. 5, [https://archive.org/details/testamentavetus00nicogoog/page/n68/mode/2up Internet Archive]</ref> and Sylvester of Evesham was not elected Bishop until 1216, and was consecrated on 3 July 1216.<ref>E H Fryde, D E Greenway, S Porter and I Roy (eds.). ''Handbook of British Chronology'', 3rd edition, Royal Historical Society, 1966, p. 279</ref> He was buried at the Cathedral, with the same cap on his head as he had worn at his coronation.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> The tomb was before the high altar; he was re-interred there in a new tomb in 1232 in the presence of Henry III. In 1529 a new tomb-chest was added.<ref>Mark Duffy. ''Royal Tombs of Medieval England'', The History Press, 2003, pp. 60-65</ref> The Abbot of Croxton, Leicestershire had heard his final confession, and his heart was buried at the Abbey.<ref>'House of Premonstratensian canons: The abbey of Croxton Kerrial', in ''A History of the County of Leicestershire: Volume 2'', ed. W G Hoskins and R A McKinley (London, 1954), pp. 28-31, [http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/leics/vol2/pp28-31 British History Online], accessed 15 January 2024</ref>\n\n===Illegitimate Children===The exact number of John's illegitimate children is uncertain. They included:* [[FitzJohn-120|Joan]], born by 1189, who married [[Ap_Iorwerth-26|Llywelyn ap Iorwerth]],<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/> and who was legitimised by the Pope in 1226:<ref name=\"Medlands\"/><ref>Douglas Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry'', Vol. V, pp. 298-302, WALES 6</ref> see her profile for discussion of who her mother was* [[FitzRoy-86|Richard]],<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> whose mother was a daughter of [[Plantagenet-32|Hamelin de Warenne, Earl of Surrey]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* [[FitzRoy-290|Oliver]], who died in Egypt while on crusade in 1219:<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> Douglas Richardson names his mother as [[FitzWarin-22|Hawise FitzWarin]], daughter of Fulk FitzWarin of Alveston, Gloucestershire<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* [[FitzRoy-289|John]], who became a priest<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/>\n* [[Giffard-706|Osbert]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/>* [[FitzRoy-291|Eudo/Yvo]],<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> who died on crusade in January 1241/2<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* [[Plantagenet-1577|Geoffrey]], who embarked with a group of mercenaries to Poitou that year<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/>* [[FitzRoy-100|Henry]], who was alive in September 1242<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> and whom Richardson says dies shortly before 8 April 1245<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* [[FitzRoy-288|Bartholomew]], who became a friar preacher and chaplain to the Pope<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/>* [[FitzJohn-305|Maud/Matilda]], who became abbess of Barking Abbey, Essex in 1247 and died a little before 6 February 1252<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>\n\n==Research Notes==\n\n===Birth Date and Place===The contemporary Chronicle of Robert de Torigni could be read as meaning that John was born on the \"vigil\" of Christmas - that is, Christmas Eve - but this is uncertain: the entry is sandwiched between one for Christmas Eve and one for Christmas Day and does not give a specific date.<ref name=\"Torigni\">Howlett, Robert (ed.). ''Chronicles of the Reigns of Stephen, Henry II., and Richard I, Vol. IV, Chronicle of Robert of Torigni'', HMSO, 1889, p. 233, [https://archive.org/details/chroniclesofreig04howl/page/232/mode/2up?q=1266 Internet Archive]</ref> Douglas Richardson gives the birth date as about 27 December.<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/> \nHis birthplace is also uncertain. Many sources suggest it was Oxford, including Douglas Richardson<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/> and John's entry in the original ''Dictionary of National Biography''.<ref name=DNB>''Dictionary of National Biography'', 1885-1900, Vol. 29, pp. 402-417, [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Dictionary_of_National_Biography,_1885-1900/John_(1167%3F-1216) Wikisource]</ref> This suggestion appears to stem from an insertion made in the 15th century to the Chronicle of Robert of Gloucester: it is proved improbable by a Pipe Roll entry for 1166-7 for expenditure on a chamber in the Tower of London or the Palace of Westminster for Eleanor of Aquitaine to use during her confinement. This strongly points to John being born in one of those places, and his entry in the ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography'' was revised in 2021 to reflect this.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> For more detailed discussion, see a 2020 article by Stephen Church in ''Notes and Queries''.<ref name=\"Church 2020\"/>\nCharles Cawley's 'Medieval Lands' database says John was born either on 24 December 1166 or 1167 at Oxford, and gives Robert de Torigni's Chronicle as source for it possibly being the latter:<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> this is a misreading of the dating in this Chronicle.<ref name=\"Torigni\"/> The Pipe Rolls entry on expenditure for his mother's confinement for his birth shows December 1167 is definitely wrong.<ref name=\"Church 2020\"/>\nJohn's entry in the original ''Dictionary of National Biography'' gives the birth year as \"?1167\", citing among other sources the Chronicle of Robert de Torigni,<ref name=DNB/> and again misreading the dating in that Chronicle.<ref name=\"Torigni\"/>\n\n===Doubtful Illegitimate Children===* Isabel, wife of Richard FitzIves of St Keverne, Cornwall<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/>* Philip, who married someone called Lavina: they are recorded in 1263 as transferring lands to a Henry FitzRoy: Douglas Richardson speculates that Henry was their son, producing no evidence to confirm this, and that Henry's name FitzRoy suggests Philip '''may''' have been an illegitimate son of John* the parent, gender not known, of a Roger de Meulan, a papal chaplain said to be a \"nepos\" of Henry III (Douglas Richardson assumes this was a daughter of John, with no clear evidence,<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/> while Charles Cawley suggests this may possibly have been a son<ref name=\"Medlands\"/>): the term \"nepos\" can mean nephew but covered a range of relationships and it is far from certain this person was a child of John\n\n==Sources==\n<references />\n\nSee also:* Faris, David. Most of her dower lands from her marriage to John were released to her, but castles she claimed at Exeter and Rockingham were withheld as also were 3500 marks which she said John had willed to her. She appears to have been given no significant role in the government of England.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\nIn JUL 1217 Isabella abandoned England, leaving her children behind. Over the next few years she secured control over Angoulême, despite resistance from officials acting for Henry III.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n=== Marriage to Hugues de Lusignan ===In 1220 Isabella married [[Lusignan-2|Hugues de Lusignan]], son of the Hugues to whom she had been betrothed in 1200. The exact date of their marriage is uncertain, but it was no later than MAY 1220.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"Medlands\"/> The marriage was not a smooth one: Hugues was unfaithful, and several times threatened to divorce her.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\nIsabella and Hugues had the following children:* [[Lusignan-3|Hugues]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\">Charles Cawley. [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ANGOULEME.htm#HuguesIXLusignandied1219 Hugues XII de Lusignan], entry in “Medieval Lands” database, accessed 29 January 2024</ref> * [[Lusignan-22|Guy]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-23|Geoffroi]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-78|William de Valence]]<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-26|Aymer]],<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"ODNB\"/> who became Bishop of Winchester<ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/><ref>E B Fryde, D E Greenway, S Porter and I Roy (eds.). ''Handbook of British Chronology'', 3rd edition, Royal Historical Society/University College (London), 1986, p. 276</ref>* [[Lusignan-48|Agnės]], who married Guillaume de Chauvigny<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-1|Alice]], who married John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-25|Isabella]],<ref name=\"ODNB\"/> who married Maurice de Craon<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>* [[Lusignan-24|Marguerite]], who married Raymond VII, Count of Toulouse, Amaury IX, Viscount of Thouars, and Geoffroi de Châteaubriant<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"Medlands Hugues\"/>\n\n=== Relations with England ===Isabella's relations with the English government were uneasy. In 1221 her English estates were briefly confiscated. They were finally declared forfeit in 1224, when her second husband entered into alliance with Louis VIII of France. Two years later, in 1226, she met her son Henry III, when he engaged in an unsuccessful military expedition to Poitou and Brittany. In 1241 she and Hugues de Lusignan are said to have sought to negotiate with Henry III over Poitou, but when Henry launched an expedition to Poitou the next year Hugues supported the French king.<ref name=\"ODNB\"/>\n\n=== Final Years, Death and Burial ===Isabella spent her final years at [[Wikipedia:Fontevraud_Abbey|Fontevrault Abbey]], where she died on 4 JUN 1246<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"ODNB\"/> (Charles Cawley gives the death date as 31 May.)<ref name=\"Medlands\"/> Initially she was buried in the main cemetery of the Abbey: in 1254 Henry III visited Fontevrault and oversaw the removal of her remains to the choir of the Abbey's church, near where several Plantagenets were buried.<ref name=\"RA 1.43\"/><ref name=\"ODNB\"/><ref>Mark Duffy.       "notes": "==Biography==Ramon Berenguer IV (1195 – 19 August 1245), Count of Provence and Forcalquier, was the son of Alfonso II of Provence and Garsenda of Sabran, heiress of Forcalquier. After his father's death (1209), Ramon was imprisoned in the castle of Monzón, in Aragon until he was able to escape in 1219 and claim his inheritance. He was a powerful and energetic ruler who added Forcalquier to his domain. Giovanni Villani in his Nuova Cronica had this to say about Raymond: \nCount Raymond was a lord of gentle lineage, and kin to them of the house of Aragon, and to the family of the count of Toulouse, By inheritance Provence, this side of the Rhone, was his; a wise and courteous lord was he, and of noble state and virtuous, and in his time did honourable deeds, and to his court came all gentle persons of Provence and of France and of Catalonia, by reason of his courtesy and noble estate, and he made many Provençal coblas and canzoni of great worth.\nOn 5 June 1219, Ramon married [http://www.wikitree.com/wiki/De_Savoie-101 Beatrice of Savoy], daughter of Thomas I of Savoy. She was a shrewd and politically astute woman, whose beauty was likened by Matthew Paris to that of a second Niobe. Along with two stillborn sons (1220 & 1225), Ramon and Beatrice had four daughters, all of whom married kings. \n1. [http://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Barcelona-62 Margaret of Provence] (1221–1295), wife of Louis IX of France 2. [http://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Barcelona-29 Eleanor of Provence] (1223–1291), wife of Henry III of England 3. [http://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Barcelona-63 Sanchia of Provence] (1228–1261), wife of Richard of Cornwall, king of Germany 4. [http://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Barcelona-64 Beatrice of Provence] (1234–1267), wife of Charles I of Sicily \nRamon Berenguer IV died in Aix-en-Provence. At least two planhs (Occitan funeral laments) of uncertain authorship (one possibly by Aimeric de Peguilhan and one falsely attributed to Rigaut de Berbezilh) were written in his honour. \nBeginning in 1220, Provence east of the Rhone had a new ruler, Ramon Berenguer IV, of the Catalan dynasty. He was the first Count of Provence to actually reside in Provence permanently, usually living with his court in Aix. He launched a military campaign to impose his authority over the cities of Provence, ending the independence of Grasse and Tarascon, occupying Nice, which had tried to ally with Genoa; and founding a new town, Barcelonette, in the far east of Provence, near the Italian border. \nThe ambitions of Ramon Berenguer were energetically resisted by the new Count of Toulouse, Raimond VII, who had lost most of his own territory to France. Raimond VIl became an ally of Marseille and Avignon in their fight against Ramon Berenguer. In 1232 his army devastated the terrorities of Ramon Berenguer around Tarascon and Arles. \nRamon Berenguer responded to this attack by strengthening his alliance with France; he married his daughter, Marguerite, to King Louis IX of France, and appealed to Frederic II, the Holy Roman Emperor, for support. In exchange for his support, Frederic demanded that the cities of Arles and Avignon be governed by the Holy Roman Empire. A prolonged struggle took place between Raimond VII and his allies, the cities of Marseille and Avignon, against Ramon Berenguer for authority in Provence. Arles was blockaded and all traffic on the Rhone River stopped. \nThe French army finally intervened to help Ramon Berenguer, the French king's father-in-law. Raimond VII was forced to abandon his quest, and Ramon Berenguer was able to appoint his own candidate as bishop of Avignon and to subdue the rest of eastern Provence. When Ramon Berenguer died in 1245, not quite forty years old, he controlled all of Provence between the Rhone and Italian border except the rebellious city of Marseille.[51] \nRamon Berenguer had four daughters, but no sons. \nAfter his death his youngest daughter and heiress, Beatrice, married Charles, Count of Anjou, the youngest son of Louis VIII. Provence's fortunes became even more closely tied to the Angevin Dynasty.\nHe was the Count of Provence from 1209–1245, Predecessor: Alfonso II, Successor: Beatrice. \n\n==Sources ==\n<references />\n* '''Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. IV. page 635'''\n•\tRoyalty for Commoners Author: Ancestry.com Publication: Online publication - Provo, UT, USA: The Generations Network, Inc., 2006.Original data - Stuart, Roderick W. W. Watson, \"The Seize Quartiers of Eleanor (of Castile) Queen Consort to Edward I.\" The Genealogist New Series XI (1895) Internet Archive [https://archive.org/details/genealogist11lond/page/n43/mode/2up Table XIII p. 31], [https://archive.org/details/genealogist11lond/page/n47/mode/2up Additions to table XIII pp. 34-36]</ref> Born about 1197, as her father's only surviving child Marie succeeded him, ruling as Countess of Ponthieu and Montreuil from 1221 to 1250.\nMarie's marriage was arranged before September 1208 [[Dammartin-6|Simon de Dammartin]] a younger son of Alberic II de Dammartin and Mathilde de Clermont.<ref name=\"Watson\" />\n\nAmong their children were: #[[Dammartin-5|Jeanne]] (died 16 March 1279), second wife of Ferdinand III of Castile.<ref name=\"Watson\" /> Through her daughter Eleanor of Castile she is an ancestor of the British royal family. #[[Dammartin-7|Philippa]] (died 1277/81) who married firstly Raoul II d' Issoudun, secondly Raoul II de Coucy, and thirdly Otto II, Count Geldern.\n#[[Dammartin-56|Marie]] (died after 1279), married Jean II de Roucy.#[[Dammartin-54|a daughter]] married to Jean viscount of Châtellerault. ''(Medieval Lands shows her name as Mathilde citing a charter of 1256. Parsons writes that the daughter of that name died before 1237 when her parents made a donation on her behalf. It could be possible there were two daughters named Mathilde, one born after the death of the first. Parsons gives the wife of Châtellerault the name Agnès. Confusion in some secondary sources give her the name Agatha and as having married Aimery of Châtellerault, but in reality Aimery and Agatha were the names of her husband Jean's parents.)\n''\nMarie's husband Simon allied himself with his brother Renaud and England's John Lackland combatting her uncle King Philippe II at Bouvines in July 1214. For this betrayal Simon and his wife were punished by the king, with a loss of lands and revenue. A reconciliation of the couple to the French crown occurred following the death of Marie's father Guillaume the Count of Ponthieu in 1221, when Marie and her children were recognized to be the rightful heirs to the county; Simon making his own submission circa 1230.\nFollowing the death of her first husband Simon, Marie married secondly sometime between September 1240 and December 1241 Mathieu de Montmorency, Seigneur d'Attichy, who was killed during the Battle of Mansourah fought in February 1250 during the Seventh Crusade led by King Louis IX of France.\n\n==Biographie==Marie de Ponthieu (vers 1197 † 1250), fut comtesse de Ponthieu de 1221 à 1250. Elle était fille de Guillaume II, comte de Ponthieu, et d'Alix de France.\nProbablement sous l'influence de Philippe II Auguste, elle épousa en septembre 1208 Simon de Dammartin (1180 † 1239), déjà comte d'Aumale. Vers 1211, Simon de Dammartin et son frère Renaud trahirent Philippe Auguste et s'allièrent à Jean sans Terre, roi d'Angleterre. Ils combattirent tous les deux à Bouvines, Renaud fut fait prisonnier et Simon s'enfuit et s'exila. Le roi de France s'empara des biens de Simon, ainsi que du Ponthieu lorsque Marie en hérita. Ce n'est qu'en 1230 que Simon fit sa soumission et que les époux purent récupérer leurs domaines. Les deux époux sont cités le 2 mai 1230 lorsqu'il confirment la donation d'une propriété à l'abbaye Notre Dame d'Ourscamp. De ce premier mariage naquirent :\n\n# Jeanne († 1279), comtesse de Ponthieu et d'Aumale ;# Philippe († 1278/81), mariée à Raoul de Lusignan († 1246), comte d'Eu, puis à Raoul († 1250), sire de Coucy, et à Otton II († 1271), comte de Gueldre ;# Marie († après 1279), mariée à Jean II de Pierrepont († 1251), comte de Roucy ;# Une fille mariée à Jean vicomte de Châtellerault, nommée Agnès ou Mathilde.\nVeuve, Marie se remarie vers 1240 avec Mathieu de Montmorency († 1250 Mansourah), seigneur d'Atichy, fils de Mathieu II, baron de Montmorency, et de Gertrude de Soissons.\n\nElle meurt en septembre 1250.\n\n==Research notes==A post by the genealogist John Carmi Parsons to the Soc Gen-Medieval newsgroup dated 18 February 1999 (subject line Re: Alais de France) includes detailed information about the children of Marie de Ponthieu and Simon de Dammartin.       "notes": "[[Category: Poland, Monarchs (960-1571)]][[Category:Bazylika Katedralna Wniebowzięcia Najświętszej Maryi Panny, Płock, Mazowieckie]]\n[[Category: House of Piast]]\n{{Polish Roots}}\n== Biography ==\n\n\n===Origins===\n===Marriage & Children===\n===Reign===Władysław divided the realm between Bolesław and his half-brother Zbigniew while retaining the principal seats of the realm under his own control. Bolesław received a portion of the realm, and Władysław provided that after his death Bolesław was to receive the principal seats at Wrocław, Kraków, and Sandomierz. Gallus Anonymous records that each son subsequently went to his allotted territory.<ref name=\"GallusDivision\">Gallus Anonymus, ''Chronicon Polonorum'', Book II, chs. 7-8, in Georg Heinrich Pertz, ed., ''Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores'', vol. 9 (Hannover: Hahn, 1851), [https://www.dmgh.de/mgh_ss_9/index.htm#page/447/mode/1up pp. 447-448], (herafter Gallus Anonymus).</ref>\n\n\n\n----\n\nFamily and issue With his first wife, Zbyslava, daughter of Grand Duke Sviatopolk II of Kiev, Bolesław had one son:\n\nVladislav II Wygnaniec, born 1105, Prince of Poland. \nBolesław subsequently married Salome von Berg-Schelklingen, by whom he had 14 children (six sons and eight daughters), of whom six sons and five daughters are known:\nLeszek (born 1115); Casimir the Older (d. 1131); Bolesław IV the Curly (born 1125); Mieszko III the Old (born 1126); Henryk of Sandomierz (born 1127); Casimir II the Just (born 1138); Rikissa of Poland (born 1116), who married firstly Magnus the Strong, pretender of Sweden and Denmark; secondly Volodar of Polatsk, Prince of Minsk; and thirdly king Sverker I of Sweden Dobronega of Poland (born 1128), who married Marquis Dietrich of Niederlausitz; Gertruda of Poland; Judith of Poland (born 1130-1135), who married Otto I of Brandenburg; and Agnes of Poland (born 1137), who married Mstislav II Kyjevský.\n\n=== Marriage ===\n:: Note:  By 16 November 1102 Boleslaw married Zbyslava (b. ca. 1085/90 - d. ca. 1112), daughter of Grand Duke Sviatopolk II of Kiev. They had three children:\n::: Wladyslaw II the Exile (b. 1105 - d. Altenburg, 30 May 1159).\n::: A son (b. ca. 1108 - d. aft. 1109).::: A daughter [Judith?] (b. ca. 1111 - d. aft. 1124), married in 1124 to Vsevolod Davidovich, Prince of Murom.::: Between March and July of 1115, Boleslaw married his second wife, Salomea (b. bef. 1101 - d. 27 July 1144), daughter of Henry, Count of Berg-Schelklingen. Boleslaw successfully defended Silesia from invasion by Holy Roman Emperor Henry V, wh o he defeated at Glasgow and Wroclaw (Breslau) in 1109. The ''Chronicon Polono-Silesiacum'' names (in order) the five sons of Bolesław III ''\"'''Vladislaum''', Boleslaum, Mesiconem, Kazimirum, Henricum\"'', specifying that Władysław succeeded in Silesia.  The ''Annales Capituli Cracoviensis'' record the birth in 1105 of ''\"'''Vladizlaus''' secundus\"''.  The ''Chronica principum Polonie'' records that the mother of ''\"Boleslaus suo primogenito '''Wladislao''' filio\"'' was ''\"ex  quadam Ruthena nobili\"''.  He succeeded in 1138 as '''WŁADYSŁAW II \"Wygnaniec/the Exile\" Prince of Kraków and Silesia'''.  He was expelled from Poland by his brother Bolesław IV.  The ''Annales Capituli Cracoviensis'' record that in 1146 ''\"'''Wladizlaus''' fugit et Cracovia devastatur\"''.  In 1146, Konrad III King of Germany (whose half-sister was Władysław's wife) unsuccessfully tried to reinstate him.  After Bolesław IV refused tribute to Friedrich I \"Barbarossa\" King of Germany, the latter invaded Poland in Aug 1157, forced Bolesław and his other brothers to submit, and compelled them to accept arbitration with their brother Władysław.  The ''Annales Cracovienses Compilati'' record the death in 1148 ''\"Wladyzlaus\"''.  This person has not been identified.  The entry could indicate the exiled Duke Władysław II, the date being mistaken, but his own death is recorded in the same source in 1159.  The ''Annales Capituli Cracoviensis'' record the death in 1159 of ''\"'''Wladizlaus''' dux Polonie\"'' and the ''Annales Cracovienses Compilati'' the death in 1159 of ''\"'''Wladyslaus''' in exilio\"''.  The ''Epytaphia ducum Slezie'' record the death ''\"4 Non Iun\"'' of ''\"dux '''Wladizlaus''' Cracovie, Gnezdne, Syrazye, Kalisie et Slezie, pater fundatoris Bolezlai\"''. * '''m''' ([1120/25]) '''AGNES of Austria''', daughter of LEOPOLD III \"der Heilige\" Markgraf of Austria [Babenberg] & his second wife Agnes of Germany [Staufen] ([1108/1113]-Altenburg/Thür 24/25 Jan [1160/63], bur Kloster Pforte an der Saale).  The information concerning the wife of Duke Władysław II is contradictory.  The ''Continuatio Claustroneoburgensis'' names ''\"'''Agnes'''\"'' as second daughter of ''\"Liupoldus marchio Austrie\"'' and ''\"Agnetem imperatoris Heinrici IV filiam\"'', specifying that she married ''\"Poleslaus dux de Polan\"'', although there appears to be no \"Bolesław\" at the time to whom this could refer.  The Chronicle of Alberic de Trois-Fontaines names ''\"'''Agnetam'''\"'' as ''\"Leopoldis marchio et Henricus…sororem germanam\"'' and wife of ''\"dux Vergescelaus de Polonia\"''.  Her origin is further confirmed by a charter dated Jan 1150 in which Cardinal-deacon Guido informs Konrad III King of Germany of the steps he took against ''\"ducis Poloniæ et coniugis eius sororis vestræ…ducis W\"''.  On the other hand, according to the ''Chronicon Polono-Silesiacum'', the wife of Duke Władysław was Christina, daughter of Emperor Heinrich IV (stating in one passage that ''\"Heinricum quintum\"'' was ''\"fratrem uxoris [=Wladislai]\"'' and in a later passage that she was ''\"filia imperatoris Henrici quarti…Cristine domine\"'').  The ''Chronica principum Polonie'' also states that ''\"Boleslaus suo primogenito Wladislao filio\"'' married ''\"filiam imperatoris Cristinam\"''.  The ''Epytaphia ducum Slezie'' provides a third possibility, naming her ''\"Adilheidis uxor eius filia imperatoris Heinrici IV\"'' (the entry follows that recording the death of Duke Władysław, to whom ''\"eius\"'' presumably refers) when recording her death ''\"VIII Kal Sep\"''.  The ''Chronicon Polono-Silesiacum'' specifies that ''\"filia imperatoris Henrici quarti…Cristine domine\"'', mother of ''\"Boleslam, Mesicone, Conrado Loripade\"'', was ''\"in Porta sepulta\"''.  It is chronologically implausible for the wife of Duke Władysław to have been the daughter of Emperor Heinrich IV, the births of whose known children are recorded between 1070 and 1086, assuming that the estimated birth dates of the couple's children are in the range [1127] to [1146] as shown below.  The explanation is presumably confusion with the mother-in-law of Duke Władysław who was one of the emperor's daughters.  Concerning her first name, the records of Kloster Neuburg make no known errors in recording the names of the numerous children of Leopold III Markgraf of Austria, although it is true that (as noted above) the name ''\"Boleslas\"'' is in error for ''\"Wladislas\"''.  Onomastics help little in finding a solution, as both \"Agnes\" and \"Adelheid\" were names given to her descendants.  The further complicating factor is the curious story concerning her grandson Jaroslav and his reported hatred of his stepmother ''\"Adelheid\"'', while elsewhere the second wife of Jaroslaw's father Bolesław is named Christina.  The issue appears to be resolved by two necrology entries:  the necrology of Kloster Neuburg records the death ''\"VIII Kal Feb\"'' of ''\"'''Agnes''' ducissa Polonie filia marchionis\"'', and the necrology of Lilienfeld records the death ''\"VI Kal Oct\"'' of ''\"'''Agnes''' ux Wlaslai ducis Zlezorum filia fundatoris S Crucis\"''. He was born 26 Dec 1194 in Jesi, Apulia.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_rer._Germ._53_S._15 Ryccardi de Sancto Germano notarii Chronica], MGH SS rer. Conradi dominicani ad B. Episcopum Cathanensem, sive brevis Chronica ab anno 1027 ad 1283], Mediolanum 1725, p. 278</ref> In 1211 he was elected again ''rex Romanorum'',<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_rer._Germ._16_S._99 Burchardi Praepositi Urspergensis Chronicon], MGH SS rer. The first document in which he uses the title.</ref><br/>Friedrich died in 1250 in Castel Fiorentino.<ref>Rosario Gregorio, Bibliotheca scriptorum qui res in Sicilia gestas sub Aragonum imperio retulere: Eam uti accessionem ad Historicam bibliothecam Carusii instruxit, Tomus I, [https://books.google.com/books?id=7tUwAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA15#v=onepage&q&f=false Bartholomei de Neocastro Historia Sicula], Panormi 1791, p. 15 </ref>\n\n\n=== Wives and Concubines ===\nFriedrich was married at least three times, a fourth marriage may have happened on the deathbed of his long-time mistress [[Lancia-1|Bianca Lancia]]. In addition he may have had at least 11 (12 if counting [[Lancia-1|Bianca Lancia]]) concubines.\n: His first marriage was to [[Aragón-130|Constance of Aragon]] (b. 1179 - d. 23 June 1222) in August of 1209,<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_19_S._334 Ryccardus de S. Germano A. 1209], MGH SS 19, p. 334</ref><ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_9_S._634 Continuatio Claustroneoburgensis Tertia], MGH SS 9, p. 634, to the year 1208.</ref><ref>Ximénez de Embún y Val, Tomás, Historia de la Corona de Aragón : (la más antigua de que se tiene noticia) conocida generalmente con el nombre de Crónica de San Juan de la Peña : Part aragonesa, [https://www.cervantesvirtual.com/obra-visor/historia-de-la-corona-de-aragon-la-mas-antigua-de-que-se-tiene-noticia-conocida-generalmente-con-el-nombre-de-cronica-de-san-juan-de-la-pena-part-aragonesa--0/html/000201c8-82b2-11df-acc7-002185ce6064_22.html#I_42_ Capítulo XXXIV Del rey Pedro II, y de sus hechos], p. 136, Alacant : Biblioteca Virtual Joan Lluís Vives, 2004</ref> either in Messina or Palermo, Sicily.  One child: [[Staufer-64|Heinrich]] (b. 1211- d. 1242).\n: His second wife was [[Brienne-35|Isabella II de Brienne]], Queen of Jerusalem (b. about 1211 - d. 25 Apr 1228).  The marriage took place 9 November 1225 in Brindisi, Apulia.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_17_S._338 Annales Scheftlarienses Maiores], MGH SS 17, p. 338</ref><ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_19_S._345 Ryccardus de S. XXX], MGH SS 24, p. 166</ref><ref>Jean Louis Alphonse Huillard-Bréholles, Frederici secundi historia diplomatica, Tomus I pars II, [https://books.google.com/books?id=4io-AAAAcAAJ&pg=PA897#v=onepage&q&f=false Breve chronicon de rebus siculis ...], Paris 1852, p. 897</ref> Of note is that all sources listing her name call her Isabelle as well as documents issued by Friedrich shortly after the marriage: Isabela, Jan 1226;<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_DD_F_II._5,1_S._524 Nr. 1152], MGH DD F II. 5,1, p. 524</ref> and by herself: Ysabella, Jan 1226.<ref>Jean Louis Alphonse Huillard-Bréholles, Frederici secundi historia diplomatica, Tomus II pars I, [https://books.google.com/books?id=yiduC5jAAtgC&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&pg=PA536#v=onepage&q&f=false Ann. 1226 .. Januario], Paris 1855, p. 536</ref>  Two children: An unnamed daughter in 1226 for whom only one source exists: ''... videns eum ex sua filia quandam filia genuisse ...'';<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_26_S._476 Ex Chronico Sancti Martini Turonensi], MGH SS 26, p. 476</ref> and [[Staufer-65|Konrad IV von Schwaben]] (b. 25 Apr 1228 - d. 21 May 1254).\n: His third wife was [[Plantagenet-18|Isabella of England]] (b. 1214 - d. 1 December 1241).  The marriage took place on 15 Jul 1235 in Worms.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_16_S._30 Annales Erphordenses], MGH SS 16, p. 30</ref><ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_28_S._130 Ex Mathei Parisiensis Cronicis Maioribus], MGH SS 28, p. 130</ref><ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_23_S._937 Chronica Albrici Monachi Trium Fontium A Monacho Novi Monasterii Hoiensis Interpolata], MGH SS 23, p. 937</ref><ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_27_S._309 E Gervasii Cantuariensis Gestorum Regum Continuatione], MGH SS 27, p. 309</ref>  Three children:  [[Staufer-70|Margarethe]] (b. 1237 - d. 1270 Frankfurt), [[Staufer-71|Heinrich]] aka Karlotto (b. 1236 or 1238 - d. 1253), unknown child, possibly a stillbirth in 1241.\n:[[Lancia-1|Bianca Lancia]] (b. abt 1200/10, d. abt 1246) was a longtime concubine, a relationship lasting 20 years according to Matthew Paris.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_28_S._360 Ex Mathei Parisiensis Cronicis Maioribus], MGH SS 28, pp. 360-361</ref> The same source and the ''Cronica Fratris Salimbene de Adam'' report a marriage on her deathbed.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_32_S._349 Cronica Fratris Salimbene de Adam Ordinis Minorum], MGH SS 32, p. 349</ref> She bore him 2 children: Konstanze (b. 1230 - d. 1307), Manfredi (b. 1232 - d. 1266). A third, widely called Violanta ( b. abt 1233 - d. bef 1264) in the literature and based on a single reference without a name (''... per comitissam de Caserta, cuius filius duxerat filiam imperatoris naturalem ...'')<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._540 Annales Sancti Pantaleonis Coloniensis], MGH SS 22, p. 540</ref> is not supported by any other source.\n: The names of other concubines are unknown or poorly documented: 1) The mother of Federico di Pettorano is only identified as ''nobili comitissa quo in regno Sicilie erat heres'';<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._517 Thomae Tusci Gesta Imperatorum et Pontificum], MGH SS 22, p. 517</ref> 2) Enzo di Svevia (b. abt 1220 - d. 1272) is identified either as born of ''une haute dame d'Alemaigne''<ref>Recueil des historiens des croisades. Historiens occidentaux, Tome II, [https://archive.org/details/RecueilDesHistoriensDesCroisadesOccidentaux2/page/n449/mode/2up L'Estoire de Eracles Empereur, Li Trentetroisiesmes Livres, Chapitre XLII], Paris 1859, p. 409</ref> or ''ex matre infami et ignobili''<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._515 Thomae Tusci Gesta Imperatorum et Pontificum], MGH SS 22, p. 515</ref> and ''ex Theotonica''.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._517 Thomae Tusci Gesta Imperatorum et Pontificum], MGH SS 22, p. 517</ref> No document has been found naming her Adelhaid von Urslingen and no such name appears in the Stammliste of house Urslingen.<ref>de.wikipedia [https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urslingen#Stammliste Urslingen]</ref> Enzo appears to have had a full sister Caterina da Marano.<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._517 Thomae Tusci Gesta Imperatorum et Pontificum], MGH SS 22, p. 517</ref> 3) The mother of Federico di Antiochia (b. btw 1222 and 1224 - d. 1256) is commonly called Maria or Matilda in secondary literature without any primary source. Thomas Tusci only mentions she was called de Antiochia,<ref>[http://www.mgh.de/dmgh/resolving/MGH_SS_22_S._517 Thomae Tusci Gesta Imperatorum et Pontificum], MGH SS 22, p. 517</ref> and Bartolomeo de Neocastro calls her ''Beatrix filia principis Antiochiae''.<ref>Bartholomaei de Neocastro Historia Sicula, a cura di Giuseppe Paladino, [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101064935552&view=1up&seq=40&skin=2021 Prooemium], Bologna 1922, p. 2</ref> It is unlikely that she was a daughter of [[Poitiers-53|Bohémond IV de Antiochia]], but could have been a member of the Sicilian family d'Antiochia, descendants of the 12th century Giorgio d'Antiochia.<ref>Fulvio Delle Donne - Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani - Volume 55 (2001), [https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giorgio-d-antiochia_(Dizionario-Biografico)/ GIORGIO d'Antiochia], Istituto della Enciclopedia Italiana fondata da Giovanni Treccani S.p.A.</ref><ref>en.wikipedia, [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_of_Antioch George of Antioch]</ref> 4) Manna, the mother of Riccardo conte de Chieti, appears to exist only in an unsourced footnote.<ref>Benoist-Méchin, J. (1980) Frédéric de Hohenstaufen ou le rêve excommunié, Librairie Académique Perrin, 1980, p. 667, footnote 375, quoted in: Charles Cawley, Medieval Lands, [https://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/GERMANY,%20Kings.htm#FriedrichIIGermanydied1250B KONSTANTIN ROGER FRIEDRICH von Staufen]</ref> 5) No primary sources exist for the mother of [[Hohenstaufen-59|Margherita di Suevia]], she appears only in the 17th century. 6) Nothing is known about the mothers of Salvaggia, Blanchefleur, and Gerardo.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />*Eduard August Winkelmann, Geschichte Kaiser Friedrichs des Zweiten und seiner Reiche, [https://books.google.com/books?id=c4XTAAAAMAAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false 1212-1235], Berlin 1863, and [https://books.google.com/books?id=_8zJ562CCMMC&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0#v=onepage&q&f=false 1235–1250], Reval 1865.*Jean Louis Alphonse Huillard-Bréholles, [https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/000412339 Historia diplomatica Friderici Secundi], Paris 1852-1861\n*Royal Ancestry by Douglas Richardson Vol. IV. p. 553  *[[Wikipedia: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor]]; [[Wikipedia:it: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor]]\n*http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/SICILY.htm#_ftnref676",
