      "notes": "[[Category:House of Plantagenet]]\n[[Category: Day-1904 Temporary Euroaristo Project]]\n== Biography ==\n{{European Aristocrat \n| house = House of Plantagenet\n| image = European Aristocrats Project-16.png}}\n{{Notables Sticker}}\n\n===Birth==='''Matilda (Maud) of England''' was born in June of 1156 in London, England. She was the daughter of [[Plantagenet-1627|Henry II 'Curtmantle' d'Anjou, King of England]] and [[Aquitaine-84|Eleanor, Duchesse d'Aquitaine]].<ref name=\"RA 1.29\">Douglas Richardson. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'', 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham (Salt Lake City: the author, 2013), Vol. I, pp. 29-31, ENGLAND 4.</ref> Through her marriage with [[Welf-11|Heinrich (Henry) V Herzog von Braunschweig-Lüneburg]], son of Heinrich X Herzog von Bayern and Gertrude von Sachsen, on 1 February 1168 at Minden Cathedral, Minden, Nordrhein-Westfahlen, Germany, she became the  Duchess of Saxony and later of Bavaria.<ref name=\"RA 1.29\"/>\n\n===Marriage and Children===In 1165 Rainald of Dassel, Archbishop of Cologne, arrived at the court of King Henry II at Rouen, to negotiate a German match for Matilda. There was conflict during the negotiations, however, when Robert de Beaumont, 2nd Earl of Leicester refused to greet the archbishop, alleging him to be a schismatic and a supporter of the anti-pope, Victor IV. The original plan to match a daughter of Henry II with a son of Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor was abandoned, and instead Matilda left England in September 1167 to marry Henry the Lion.\nChildren of Matilda of England and Heinrich V Herzog von Braunschweig-Lüneburg:\n\nEleanor von Sachsen4\nIngibiorg von Sachsen+4\nMatilda von Sachsen4 b. c 1172, d. c 1209\nRichenza von Sachsen+1 b. c 1172, d. 1210Heinrich I von Zelle, Duke of Saxony and Bavaria+4 b. c 1175, d. 28 Apr 1227\nOtto IV von Braunschweig, Holy Roman Emperor4 b. 1175, d. 19 May 1218\nLothaire von Sachsen4 b. 1181, d. 15 Oct 1190\nson von Sachsen4 b. c 1182, d. c 1182William of Winchester Herzog von Braunschweig-Lüneburg+4 b. 11 Apr 1184, d. 13 Dec 1213\nCitations[S11] Alison Weir, Britain's Royal Families: The Complete Genealogy (London, U.K.: The Bodley Head, 1999), page 60. Hereinafter cited as Britain's Royal Families.[S130] Wikipedia, online http;//www.wikipedia.org. Hereinafter cited as Wikipedia.\n[S11] Alison Weir, Britain's Royal Families, page 59.[S106] Royal Genealogies Website (ROYAL92.GED), online ftp://ftp.cac.psu.edu/genealogy/public_html/royal/index.html. Hereinafter cited as \nhttp://www.thepeerage.com/p10202.htm#i102017\n\n===Siblings===Matilda was a younger maternal half-sister of [[Capet-526|Marie de Champagne]] and [[Capet-107|Alix of France]]. She was a younger sister of [[Plantagenet-37|William, Count of Poitiers]] and [[Plantagenet-33|Henry the Young King]]. She was also an older sister of [[Plantagenet-248|Richard I of England]], [[Plantagenet-29|Geoffrey II, Duke of Brittany]], [[Plantagenet-517|Leonora of Aquitaine]], [[Plantagenet-14|Joan of England]] and [[Plantagenet-143| John of England]]. Matilda seems to have spent much of her early life in the company of her mother, Queen Eleanor.\nRichenza (English chroniclers call her Matilda) (1172–1209/10), at the time of her marriage, her husband Henry the Lion was one of the most powerful allies of Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor. Matilda governed her husband's vast estates during his absence in the Holy Land from 1172 to 1173. In 1174, Henry the Lion became involved in a conflict with the Emperor Frederick, and Henry and Matilda were forced to flee Germany and take refuge in Normandy at her father's court in 1182. During this time at the royal court at Argentan, Matilda became acquainted with the Troubadour Bertran de Born, who, calling her \"Elena\" or \"Lana\", made her the object of his desire in two of his poems of ''Courtly Love''.\n\n===Death===Matilda, her husband, and their family remained in Normandy under the protection and support of  her father King Henry until 1185, when they were allowed to return to Saxony. Early in 1189, the Emperor again ordered Henry the Lion into exile. This time, Matilda remained at Brunswick to defend the interests of her husband, but died just three months later on 28 June1189 at Braunschweig. She was buried at Brunswick Cathedral, Braunschweig, Germany.<ref name=\"RA 1.29\"/>\n\n==Research Notes==Not to be confued with that of her half-sister, [[Plantagenet-1066|Matilda of Barking]], who never married.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n:See also:* Cawley, Charles.       "notes": "{{EuroAristo Sticker}}\n[[Category: Early Barony of Rothersthorpe]]\n== Biography ==He was heir to his brother Daniel, advocate of Arras, lord of Dendermonde and Béthune, but for a time he had taken over the family barony in England, before Daniel died, because Daniel fought on the side of France against King John and the young King Henry III.\n\nFarrer (p.26) wrote::Robert was the younger son of William, but was no doubt preferred by the king because Daniel the heir was a loyal adherent of the French king. Robert, on the other hand, took service with the count of Flanders, who courted King John's alliance against France and sent Robert as his ambassador, and later himself visited England with Robert and others in his company. In July 1214 Robert obtained full seisin of all the lands and rents which his father William had held at his death, belonging to his heritage in the counties of Nottingham, Northampton, Kent, Gloucester, and Hertford.\nHowever, continues Farrer, Daniel received the English lands back again in October 1217, when France and England reconciled after the Battle of Bouvines. Robert, instead, received their mother's lordship of Dendermonde. And when Daniel died in October 1226 his lands in England were held by the king, and Robert had to come to England to appeal. Farrer (p.27) writes::His negotiations were successful, and on 29 December 1233 a mandate was issued to the sheriff of Northampton to give Robert the advocate such seisin of the manor of Gayton as his father and brother Daniel, whose heir he was, had had until the latter took his journey towards the Holy Land and died, as it was said, on the way. Similar mandates were issued to the sheriff of Lincoln in respect of of 1/2 fee in Boothby ; to the sheriff of Gloucester to enjoin the abbot of Winchcombe to answer thereafter to Robert for the £9 fee-farm rent he used to render to Robert's father and brother ; to the sheriff of Kent to enjoin the abbot of Faversham to answer similarly for £10 fee-farm rent; to the sheriff of Hertford to enjoin William Basset to answer similarly for £6 fee-farm rent ; and to the sheriff of Northampton and to him of Bedford and Buckingham to certify the knights and free tenants holding the lands and fees of the Advocate of Bethune to be thenceforth answerable and intendant to Robert touching the rents and services which they used to render to William his father. Thus the fee of Sigar de Chokes was recovered, and that of Gunfrid [Rothersthorpe] appears to have been restored with it, as will be seen by the inquisition of 1252\nAccording to Nieus (p.163), Robert was one of the most important lieutenants of King John for a time::Robert [...] fut pour un temps l’un des plus proches lieutenants de Jean sans Terre (1199-1216), ainsi que le remémore une chronique vernaculaire commanditée après son retour sur le Continent – une des premières du genre en France.\nRobert sold his English lands to his kinsman [[Guines-22|Robert de Gu��nes or Guisnes]] in 1242.<ref>Sanders, p.142; Farrer, pp.27-28.</ref>\nRobert de Guisnes' maternal grandmother was a sister of Robert's father.\n\n===Research===Connections with Breda.       "notes": "[[Category:Battle of Golden Spurs 1302]][[Category:Tournament of Compiègne (1278)]]\n{{Succession\n|image=Bourgogne-349.png\n|position1=Comte de d'Artois \n|before1=[[Capet-662|Robert de Capet d'Artois]]<br>1216-1250\n|after1=[[Bourgogne-349|Jeanne de Capet]] <br>1302-1329\n|years1=1250-1302\n}}\n== Biographie ==\n([[#Biography | English version below]])\n'''Robert II d'Artois'''<ref>[[Wikipedia:FR:Robert_II_d%27Artois]].</ref> (septembre 1250 - 11 juillet 1302), fils posthume de Robert I<sup>er</sup> et de Mathilde de Brabant, il devient dès sa naissance comte d'Artois.\nFait chevalier par son oncle et parrain, le roi Louis IX (1267), il prit part à la croisade de Tunis (1270) et se montra un farouche combattant, voulant venger son père qui avait été tué lors de la précédente croisade.\nSa sœur Blanche d'Artois épousa d'Henri I<sup>er</sup> de Navarre, mort en 1274 en laissant une fille de trois ans. Elle se réfugia en France afin d'échapper aux luttes pour le pouvoir et la régence. Le roi de France, Philippe III le Hardi, son cousin, lui confia le soin de rétablir la paix. Il assiégea Pampelune, prit la ville et rétablit l'autorité de la reine.\nÀ la suite des Vêpres siciliennes (1282), il se rendit en Italie pour secourir son oncle paternel Charles I<sup>er</sup> d'Anjou. À la mort de ce dernier, il fut nommé régent du royaume de Naples dont le souverain, Charles II, était prisonnier du roi Pierre III d'Aragon. Mais Charles II, redevenu libre, conclut un arrangement avec le roi d'Aragon, et Robert courroucé quitta l'Italie en septembre 1289<sup>1</sup>.\nPhilippe IV le Bel l'envoya combattre les Anglais en Guyenne (1296), puis en Flandre. Robert battit les Flamands à Furnes en 1297, mais son fils Philippe qui combattait à ses côtés y fut gravement blessé et mourut un an après.\nRobert fut tué à la bataille de Courtrai le 11 juillet 1302 (les chroniqueurs français mentionnent qu'il s'est battu avec courage jusqu'�� la mort, des chroniqueurs flamands ou anglais racontent qu'il s'est rendu pour une demande à rançon mais qu'un boucher de Bruges<sup>2</sup> lui a tranché la langue<sup>3</sup>) et inhumé en l'abbaye de Maubuisson. Son fils unique étant mort avant lui, sa fille Mahaut et son petit-fils Robert III revendiquèrent tous les deux la succession du comté d'Artois. Trois jugements, de 1309, de 1317 et de 1329 tranchèrent en faveur de Mahaut, et Robert III, mécontent, se réfugia en Angleterre et incita le roi Édouard III d'Angleterre à engager la guerre de Cent Ans.\n\n== Biography ==\n([[#Biographie | Version française ci-dessus]])\nRobert was born about September 1250 to [[Capet-662|Robert I Count of Artois]] and [[Brabant-13|Mathilde de Brabant]].<ref name=Van>Van Kerrebrouck, Patrick. Les Capétiens 937-1328. Villeneuve d’Ascq, 2000. Page 227.</ref> Born posthumously he was from his birth recognized as Count of Artois.\nIn 1279 Henrik, landgrave of Hesse renounced all his rights on the duchy of Brabant in favour of Jan I, witnessed by his sisters Mathilde, countess of Artois and Saint-Pol, and Beatrix, lady of Kortrijk, and his nephews Robert count of Artois, Jan of Hainaut and Henrik lord of Herstal.<ref>A. Verkooren, Inventaire des chartes et cartulaires des duchés de Brabant et de Limbourg et des pays d'Outre-Meuse, Première partie: chartes originales et vidimées, Tome I, nr. 104.</ref>\n\n===Marriages & Children===His first marriage was arranged by a treaty of 13 June 1659 at Paris -celebrated in  1262, with [[Courtenay-175|Amicie de Courtenay (1250-1275)]],<ref name=Van/> the only daughter of [[Courtenay-504|Pierre de Courtenay (1218-1250)]], Lord of Conches and Mehun, and [[Joigny-15|Petronille de Joigny]], daughter of Gaucher de Joigny. They had the following children: \n\n#[[Artois-67|Mahaut (1268-1329)]]\n#[[Capet-670|Philippe (1269-1298)]]\n#[[Artois-88|Robert (1271-1272)]]\nFollowing the death of Amicie in 1275 Robert was married before 13 June 1277 to [[Dampierre-4|Agnès de Dampierre (1237-1288)]], daughter of [[Bourbon-45|Archambaud IX de Bourbon]], Lord of Bourbon, and [[Châtillon-16|Yolande de Châtillon]], Countess of Nevers.\nFollowing the death of Agnès, Robert married in October 1298 [[Avesnes-5|Marguerite of Hainault]] (died in 1319), daughter of [[Avesnes-83|Jean [I] d'Avesnes]], count of Hainaut, and [[Luxembourg-99|Philippa]] (daughter of Henri V, Count of Luxembourg). There were no children from the two later marriages.\n\n===Death===He was considered the best French knight and captain of his time. That is why he was put in charge of the army that moved to Flanders in 1302. He had lived in Kortrijk for a number of years during his youth and therefore probably knew the battlefield well.\nRobert was killed at the Battle of Courtrai 11 July 1302 and was buried in the abbey of Maubuisson. His widow Marguerite died 29 July 1319 and was buried in the church of the Cordeliers at Valenciennes.<ref name=Van/><ref>Richardson, Douglas. ''Royal Ancestry'', Vol. I pp. 144-5.</ref>\n\n(The veracity of the following account of Robert's death is unknown.)\nSeeing that the French knights were in danger of being thrown back, he attacked with his beautiful warhorse Morel. His attack was so powerful that he penetrated deep into the Flemish ranks and, according to legend, also managed to tear a piece out of the Flemish banner. However, he was knocked down by lay brother Willem van Saeftinghe of Ter Doest abbey. Also according to legend, he begged to spare his horse's life. In vain, because that legend goes on to say that the Flemish who attacked him sneered at him that they did not understand his Walloon (French). He died together with his horse and hundreds of French knights at the Battle of Courtrai on 11 July 1302. <ref>De Liebaart: De Franse Hoofdrolspelers. ''Robert, Graaf van Artois'' </ref>\nHis coat of arms (''li comte d'artoys'') is included in the attendees of the Tournament of Compiègne of 1278, when King Philippe III celebrated the visit of his cousin, Charles II d'Anjou, Prince of Salerno.<ref>[https://www.kb.nl/en/discover-admire/masterpieces/armorial-beyeren Armorial-Beyeren]. At the age of 12, Louis was married to Blanche of Castile on 23 May 1200, following prolonged negotiations between Philip Augustus and Blanche's uncle John of England.\n\n===Birth and Parentage===\nLouis Capet VIII, King of France \"The Lion-heart\" was born 5 Sep 1187 in Paris, France and married 23 May 1200 in Pont-Audemer (Beaumont), Normandy. He died 8 Nov 1226 in Montpensier, Auvergne région, France and was buried in Saint Denis Abbey, Seine-Saint-Denis département, Paris région, France. Louis married Blanca de Castilla, Regent of France. <a href=\"/aqwg20.htm#1636\">[Parents]</a>\n: Louis VIII, King of France, eldest son of Philip Augustus and of Isabella of Hainaut, was born in Paris on the 5th of September 1187. Louis was short, thin, pale-faced, with studious tastes, cold and placid temper, sober and chaste in his life. He left the reputation of a saint, but was also a warrior prince.\n\n===1200 Marriage to Blanche of Castile===\nAt the age of 12, Louis was married to Blanche of Castile on 23 May 1200, following prolonged negotiations between Philip Augustus and Blanche's uncle John of England. <ref name=\"eb\"/>  (as represented in William Shakespeare's historical play King John).\nOn May 23, 1200, Louis married Blanche of Castile , daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile, who effectively acted as regent after Louis's death. \n\nBlance was born March 4, 1188 and died November 26, 1252.\nIn 1212 Louis seized Saint-Omer and Aire to prevent a powerful Flanders from being on the flank of his county of Artois. \nIn 1213 he led the campaign against Ferrand, count of Flanders; in 1214, while Philip Augustus was winning the victory of Bouvines, he held John of England in check, and was victorious at La Roche-aux-Moines.\n\n===1216 First Barons War===\nIn 1216 the English barons rebelled in the First Barons' War against the unpopular King John of England (1199-1216) and offered the throne to Prince Louis. Louis invaded and was proclaimed King in London in May 1216, although he was not crowned. There was little resistance when the prince entered London. At St Paul's Cathedral, Louis was accepted as ruler with great pomp and celebration in the presence of all of London. Many nobles, including Alexander II of Scotland (1214-49), gathered to give homage to him.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\nOn June 14 he captured Winchester and soon conquered over half of the English kingdom. After a year and a half of war, most of the rebellious barons had defected and so Louis had to give up his claim to be the King of England by signing the Treaty of Lambeth in 1217. The effect of the treaty was that Louis agreed he had never been the legitimate king of England.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\nAfter a year and a half of war, King John's death, and his replacement by a regency on behalf of the boy king Henry III (John's son), many of the rebellious barons deserted Louis. When his army was beaten at Lincoln, and his naval forces (led by Eustace the Monk) were defeated off the coast of Sandwich, he was forced to make peace under English terms.\nThe principal provisions of the Treaty of Lambeth were an amnesty for English rebels, land possession to return to the status quo ante, the Channel Islands to be returned to the English crown, Louis to undertake not to attack England again, and to attempt to give Normandy back to the English crown, and 10,000 marks to be given to Louis. The effect of the treaty was that Louis agreed he had never been the legitimate king of England.\nIn 1216, after the barons rebelling against King John of England had offered the English throne to Louis in return for his aid, Louis went to England to aid the rebels. Initially he was successful, but eventually he was defeated at sea and suffered defections. \nIn 1217, when peace was concluded at Kingston, Louis was secretly paid 10,000 marks. \nIn the autumn of 1215 Louis received from a group of English barons, headed by Geoffrey de Mandeville, a request to \"pluck them out of the hand of this tyrant\" (John). Some 7000 French knights were sent over to England during the winter and two more contingents followed, but it was only after twenty-four English hostages had arrived in Paris that Louis himself prepared to invade England. The expedition was forbidden by the papal legate, but Louis set out from Calais on the 20th and landed at Stonor on the 22nd of May 1216. In three months he had obtained a strong foothold in eastern England, and in the end of July he laid siege to Dover, while part of his army besieged Windsor with a view to securing the safety of London.\nThe pretexts on which he claimed the English crown were set down in a memorandum drawn up by French lawyers in 1215. These claims -- that John had forfeited the crown by the murder of his nephew, Arthur of Brittany, and that the English barons had the right to dispose of the vacant throne -- lost their plausibility on the death of King John and the accession of his infant son as King Henry III in October 1216.\nThe papal legate, Gualo, who had forbidden the enterprise, had arrived in England at the same time as Louis. He excommunicated the French troops and the English rebels, and Henry III found a valiant defender in William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke. After the \"Fair of Lincoln\", in which his army was defeated, Louis was compelled to resign his pretensions, though by a secret article of the treaty of Lambeth (September 1217) he secured a small war indemnity.\nLouis had assisted Simon de Montfort in his war against the Albigenses in 1215, and after his return to France he again joined the crusade. With Simon's son and successor, Amauri de Montfort, he directed the brutal massacre which followed the capture of Marmande.\nPhilippe II, suspicious of his son until the close of his life, took precautions to assure his obedience, narrowly watched his administration in Artois, which Louis held from his mother Isabella, and, contrary to the custom of the kings of France, did not associate his son with him by having him crowned. When Philip Augustus was dying on the 14th of July 1223, Louis VIII was anointed at Reims on the 6th of August 1224.  Louis surrounded himself with councillors whom his father had chosen and formed, and continued his father's policy.\n\n===1223 King of France=== \nLouis VIII succeeded his father on July 14, 1223; his coronation took place on August 6 of the same year in the cathedral at Reims. As King, he continued to seek revenge on the Angevins and seized Poitou and Saintonge from them in 1224. There followed the seizure of Avignon and Languedoc.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\nLouis The Lion, or The Lion-heart was known (in French) as Louis Le Lion, or Louis Coeur-de-lion. He was the Capetian king of France from 1223 who spent most of his short reign establishing royal power in Poitou and Languedoc. \nIn 1224, now king, he seized Poitou and, in 1226, he launched a successful crusade against the Albigensian heretics, capturing the major fortress of Avignon, He took a personal role in this, and was responsible for the massacre of a vast number of people, including women and children. He then returned to Paris because of dysentery. His doctor's medical opinion was that he would be cured \"by using a woman\". A suitable virgin was found, unknown to Louis, and was sent to his room. Louis said, \"I will not commit mortal sin for whatever reason\" and gave instructions that the girl should be honorably married. He then died at age thirty-nine. \nLouis was the first Capetian to grant appanages on a large scale and to have a reversion clause that made alienation of royal property more difficult. Louis also developed other particular rights for the kingship, such as the concept that fealty was sworn not only to the individual king but also to the kingship. His eldest son, Louis IX (afterward St. Louis), peacefully succeeded him while his other sons received appanages. \n Louis VIII the Lion (French: Louis VIII le Lion) (September 5, 1187 - November 8, 1226) reigned as King of France from 1223 to 1226. He was a member of the House of Capet. Louis VIII was born in Paris, France, the son of Philip II of France and Isabelle of Hainaut.<ref name=\"eb\">Encyclopædia Britannica. Retrieved June 26, 2003, from Encyclopædia Britannica Premium Service.</ref>\n\n===1223  Persecution of Jews===\nOn 1 November 1223, he issued an ordinance that prohibited his officials from recording debts owed to Jews, thus reversing the policies set by his father Philip II of France (1180-1223). Usury (lending money with interest) was illegal for Christians to practice, according to Church law it was seen as a vice in which people profited from others' misfortune (like gambling), and was punishable by excommunication, a severe punishment. However since Jews were not Christian, they could not be excommunicated, and thus fell in to a legal gray area which secular rulers would sometimes exploit by allowing (or requesting) Jews to provide usury services, often for personal gain to the secular ruler, and to the discontent of the Church. Louis VIII's prohibition was one attempt at resolving this legal problem which was a constant source of friction in Church and State courts.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\nTwenty six barons accepted, but Theobald IV (1201-53), the powerful Count of Champagne, did not, since he had an agreement with the Jews that guaranteed him extra income through taxation. Theobald IV would become a major opposition force to Capetian dominance, and his hostility was manifest during the reign of Louis VIII. For example, during the siege of Avignon, he performed only the minimum service of 40 days, and left home amid charges of treachery.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\nTheobald IV, the powerful Count of Champagne, would become a major opposition force to Capetian dominance, and his hostility was manifest during the reign of Louis VIII. For example, during the siege of Avignon, he performed only the minimum service of 40 days, and left home amid charges of treachery. \n\n===1225 Campaign Against Southern Barons===\nIn 1225, the council of Bourges excommunicated the count of Toulouse, Raymond VII, and declared a crusade against the southern barons. Louis happily renewed the conflict in order to enforce his royal rights. Roger Bernard the Great, count of Foix, tried to keep the peace, but the king rejected his embassy and the counts of Foix and Toulouse took up arms against him. The king was largely successful, but he did not complete the work before his death.<ref name=\"eb\"/>\n\n===1226  Death===\nWhile returning to Paris, King Louis VIII became ill with dysentery, and died on November 8, 1226 in the chateau at Montpensier, Auvergne.\nWhile returning to Paris, King Louis VIII became ill with dysentery, and died on November 8, 1226 in the chateau at Montpensier, Auvergne. The Saint Denis Basilica houses the tomb of Louis VIII. His son, Louis IX (1226-70), succeeded him on the throne.\nLouis' reign was taken up with two great designs: to destroy the power of the Plantagenets, and to conquer the heretical south of France. An expedition conquered Poitou and Saintonge (1224); in 1226 he led the crusade against the Albigenses in the south, forced Avignon to capitulate and received the submission of Languedoc.\nHis reign, short as it was, brought gains both to the royal domains and to the power of the crown over the feudal lords\n\n===Issue===\nBlanche of Castile, daughter of Alphono IX of Castile and granddaughter of Henry II Plantagenet of England, bore him twelve children; his eldest surviving son, Louis IX, was his successor.\n #[[Capet-213|Philippe]] (September 9, 1209 - July 1218). Hugh was son of Gaucher III of Châtillon and Elisabeth, daughter of Hugo IV, Count of Saint-Pol.\nHe married Agnes of Bar-le-Duc, daughter of Thibaut I of Bar-le-Duc. Richardson describes it::Sometime before the end of 1220, he was probably placed in possession of the lordship of Gower. He subsequently repaired the castle of Swansea, by leave and counsel of his father-in-law, [[ap Iorwerth-26|Prince Llywelyn]]. About 1220 he recovered the estates of his grandfather, [[Braose-170|William de Brewes]], Sr., from his uncles, [[Braose-12|Reynold]] and [[Braose-63|Giles]], including the barony of Bramber, Sussex, half the barony of Totnes, Devon, and the manor of Tetbury, Gloucestershire, but the Welsh lands remained with his uncle [[Braose-12|Reynold]]. He fought in France in 1230. About the year 1230, he confirmed the gifts of his predecessors to Sele Priory, and made additional grants, including the bridges of Bramber, five salt pits and five houses in New Shoreham. He also made a small grant of land at Gelli-wann and Gelli-drum to the canons of Talley Abbey, Carmarthenshire.<ref name=\"RA\"/>\nJohn died shortly before 16 July 1232, having been thrown from his horse on his land in Bramber, Sussex, England.<ref name=\"RA\"/> His widow [[Ferch_Llywelyn-5|Margaret]] married (2) [[Clifford-248|Walter de Clifford]], Knt., before 2 November 1234 and had a daughter, [[Clifford-47|Maud]].<ref name=mcaI316 />\n\n== Research Notes ==The profiles for both of John's parents ([[Braose-11|William de Braose]] and [[Clare-672|Maud de Clare]]) include lengthy discussions of uncertainty, including Cawley's noting that while primary sources show [[Braose-11|William]]'s wife was Matilda (Maud<ref>In [https://groups.google.com/d/msg/soc.genealogy.medieval/tsPzfg4Bn7o/Lcn6O5KJEq8J this SGM discussion], Richardson states \"Matilda is Latin for Maud and should be avoided.\"</ref>), only secondary sources suggest she was [[Clare-651|Richard de Clare]]'s daughter.<ref>See [http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLISH%20NOBILITY%20MEDIEVAL1.htm#MatildaClareM1WilliamBraoseM21219RhysGry Matilda de Clare's entry] in Cawley's database.</ref> However, a discussion in soc.gen.medieval shares that \"Dugdale's Baronage cites Pat Roll 17 John m 23 as giving this William de Braose as married to a younger daughter of [[Clare-651|Richard, Earl of Clare]]. This is [[Clare-651|Richard]], earl of Hertford, b c1153. Her mother was [[FitzWilliam-253|Amicia]], Countess of Gloucester.\"<ref>Doug Thompson. [https://groups.google.com/d/msg/soc.genealogy.medieval/7LorM224M04/xK3Ea4ZSJJwJ SGM post], \"Clare & Braose,\" 8 February 1999 (accessed 18 December 2019).</ref>\nRichardson's entry in his 2013 ''Royal Ancestry'' for [[Clare-672|Maud de Clare]] includes the following information, which would appear to be conclusive circumstantial evidence in support of [[Clare-672|Maud de Clare]] as [[Braose-11|William]]'s wife/John's mother::\"[[Braose-11|His]] [William's] wife, [[Clare-672|Maud]], escaped when her husband was captured. She was imprisoned in Corfu Castle, and was restored to her father 28 July 1213. In June 1215 custody of the town of Buckingham, Buckinghamshire was granted to Maud's father, Earl [[Clare-651|Richard de Clare]]. In 1217 she had letters of conduct to come to England. In 1219 [[Clare-672|Maud]] sued her brother-in-law,  [[Braose-12|Reynold de Brewes]], for dower in the manors of Shoreham, Bramber, Beeding, Styning, Findon, Knepp (in Shipley), Horsham, Warnham, and Washington, Sussex.\"<ref>Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry,'' I:527-528 BREWES 6.</ref> \n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\nSee also:* Rees, William. This is consistent with other estimates of her birth year. If we accept the possibility that Margaret might be Joan's daughter, it makes things EXTREMELY crowded in the nursery at the beginning of Llywelyn's marriage to Joan. Besides Gladys and Ellen, Llywelyn and Joan also had their son and heir, David, at the first part of their marriage. I frankly can't possibly see how Margaret would fit chronologically to be Joan's daughter. Margaret either has to be the child of one of Llywelyn's earlier two marriages or else illegitimate. III, pages 324-327, PEMBROKE 4.</ref><ref name=CP6>Cokayne, George Edward and H.A. Doubleday et. al eds. Henry had been summoned for military service from 1 August 1260 to 25 May 1263 by writs directed to ''Henrico de Hasting''.<ref name=CP6/> He was summoned to Wales in 1260,<ref name=MCA3/> but by 1261 he had joined the rebellion against Henry III. In May 1263, he supported [[Montfort-35|Simon de Montfort]]'s complaint at Parliament and, that same month, when he was summoned to fight against the Welsh,<ref name=MCA3/> he refused, joining the baronial opposition for which was excommunicated by the Archbishop of Canterbury.<ref name=MCA3/><ref name=ODNB>Kingsford, C. L., and H. W. Ridgeway. \"Hastings, Sir Henry (1235?–1269), nobleman and baronial leader\" in ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography''. 23 Sep 2004, Oxford University Press. Accessed 29 Feb 2020 at [https://www.oxforddnb.com/view/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-12573 ODNB] with subscription.</ref> Henry went on to become one of the most violent Barons in Arms against King Henry III.<ref name=MCA3/> \nIn 1264, Henry was at the Siege of Rochester<ref name=MCA3/> in Kent with Gilbert de Clare. He was knighted by Simon de Montfort before the 14 May 1264 Battle of Lewes,<ref name=CP6/> during which Henry and a few others commanded the Londoners, and \"took part in their flight from Prince Edward\".<ref name=MCA3/><ref name=ODNB/> After Lewes, Montfort made Henry Constable of Scarborough, Kirtling and Winchester castles. Henry was summoned to Montfort's Model Parliament on 14 December 1264,<ref name=MCA3/><ref name=ODNB/> \"from which the extant barony of Hastings dates\" (Report on Dignity of a Peer, iii. 34).<ref name=DNB>Kingsford, Charles Lethbridge. \"Hastings, Henry (d.1268)\" in the ''Dictionary of National Biography, 1885-1900'', Volume 25, online at [https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Hastings,_Henry_(d.1268)_(DNB00) WikiSource].</ref> \nSimon de Montfort was killed at the battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265. Henry was wounded during the Battle and was taken prisoner<ref name=CP6/> by Thomas de Clare.<ref name=ODNB/> In January and February 1265/6, while Henry was in prison, the king granted to his wife £100 per annum from Henry's estates for the maintenance of herself and their children,<ref name=CP6/> with the residue being granted to at least eight royalists.<ref name=MCA3/><ref name=ODNB/>\nHenry was released from prison after February 1266 and joined [[Ferrers-225|Robert de Ferrers]] at Chesterfield, Derbyshire, where he narrowly escaped capture.<ref name=MCA3/> He then moved on to Kenilworth, joining John de la Ware, and held Kenilworth Castle, Warwickshire against the king<ref name=MCA3/> from 27 June to 13 December 1266.<ref name=CP6/><ref name=ODNB/><ref>\"'Chron. Majorum et Vicecomitum London’, [https://archive.org/stream/deantiquislegib00fitzgoog#page/n360/mode/1up p. 89]; Annales de Dunstaplia, pp. [https://archive.org/stream/chronicondomini01hemigoog#page/n345/mode/1up/ p. 327]\", all regarding the siege of Kenilworth.</ref> Henry fled and  joined the disinherited on the Isle of Ely as their leader,<ref name=MCA3/> but eventually, on 27 Jul 1267, he submitted to the revised terms of the [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictum_of_Kenilworth Dictum of Kenilworth], in which he received a severe fine: seven years value of his estates.<ref name=MCA3/> \n\n===Marriage and Children===He married in or before 1261 to [[Cantilupe-70|Joan de Cantelowe]] (aka Cantilupe or Cantelou), daughter and coheiress of Sir William de Cantelowe<ref name=CP6/> and Joan de Brewes (or Breuse).<ref name=MCA3/> They had two sons and three daughters:*[[Hastings-1246|John]], Knt., 1st Lord Hastings, son and heir, born 6 May 1262, died 10 February 1312/3, married first to Isabel de Valence, and second to Isabel le Despenser<ref name=MCA3/>*[[Hastings-334|Edmund]], Knt., killed at the Battle of Bannockburn 24 June 1314, married Isabel Russel and had no children<ref name=MCA3/>*[[Hastings-328|Ada]], married first to Sir Rhys ap Maredudd and second to Robert de Champaine<ref name=MCA3/>*[[Hastings-337|Lora]], married Sir Thomas le Latimer, 1st Lord Latimer<ref name=MCA3/>*Joan, nun, Prioress of Grace Dieu, died before 7 December 1330<ref name=MCA3/>\n\n===Death and Burial===Henry died before 5 March 1268/9 and his widow, Joan, died before June 1271.<ref name=MCA3/><ref name=CP6/> They are both buried in the church of the Grey Friars, Coventry, Warwickshire.<ref name=Richardson-441 />\nBoth [[Despenser-19|Sir Hugh le Despenser]] and his son, also [[Despenser-6|Sir Hugh le Despenser]], were executed as traitors in 1326. His son was executed on November 24, 1326 at Hereford, Herefordshire (see [[Despenser-6|his profile]]). Sir Hugh was '''executed''' October 27, 1326: \"Sir Hugh le Despenser, Earl of Winchester, was tried — without being allowed to speak in his own defence — condemned to death as a traitor, and hanged on the common gallows, all his honours forfeited. His head was sent to Winchester.\"<ref name=Richardson-441 />\n\n=== Career ===\n:Following apparently from [[#Wikipedia]] and [[#The_Peerage]]\nAbout Hugh \"the Elder\" le Despenser (Bigod), Earl of Winchester, Chief Advisor to King Edward II\n\nHugh le Despenser, 1st Earl of Winchester\nHugh le Despenser (1 March 1261 – 27 October 1326), sometimes referred to as \"the Elder Despenser\", was for a time the chief adviser to King Edward II of England.[1]\nHe was the son of Hugh le Despencer, 1st Baron le Despencer (or Despenser), and Aliva Basset, sole daughter and heiress of Philip Basset. His father was killed at the Battle of Evesham when Hugh was just a boy, but Hugh's patrimony was saved through the influence of his maternal grandfather (who had been loyal to the king).[2]\nHe married Isabella de Beauchamp, daughter of William de Beauchamp, 9th Earl of Warwick and Maud FitzJohn. He served Edward I on numerous occasions in battle and in diplomacy and was created a baron by writ of summons to Parliament in 1295. However, when he became close to Edward II his place was always with the king, which worried the barons. To that time, his highest office was justice of the forests.[3]\nHe was one of the few barons to remain loyal to Edward during the controversy regarding Piers Gaveston. Despenser became Edward's loyal servant and chief administrator after Gaveston was executed in 1312, but the jealousy of other barons - and, more importantly, his own corruption and unjust behaviour - led to his being exiled along with his son Hugh Despenser the younger in 1321, when Edmund of Woodstock, Earl of Kent replaced him as Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports.\nEdward found it difficult to manage without them, and recalled them to England a year later, an action which enraged the queen, Isabella, the more so when Despenser was created Earl of Winchester.\n\nDeathWhen Isabella and her lover, Roger Mortimer, led a rebellion against her husband Edward, they captured both Despensers—first the elder, later the younger. Queen Isabella interceded for Hugh the elder, but his enemies, notably Roger Mortimer and Henry, Earl of Lancaster, insisted both father and son should face trial and execution.\nThe elder Despenser was hanged immediately in his armor at Bristol on 27 October 1326. He was then beheaded and his body cut into pieces for the dogs. His head was sent for display to Winchester, which had supported the king.[4]\n\n==Sources==\n <references />* <span id=Richardson></span>Richardson, Douglas. ''Magna Carta Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families'', 4 vols., ed. Kimball G. Everingham. 2nd edition. He was summoned to Parliament by writs dated 29 December 1299 to 18 September 1322 directed to ''Willelmo de Brewosa''. He also took part in the Baron's letter to the Pope dated 12 February 1300/1.<ref name=CP2/>\nWilliam married first to [[Unknown-288163|Agnes]] ______.<ref name=MCA1/><ref name=RA1/> The date and place of marriage are unknown and are estimated. It is thought that this property transfer and subsequent confiscation precipitated the civil war between King Edward II and the Barons in 1321/2.<ref name=MCA1/>\nWilliam died before 1 May 1326; his widow, Elizabeth, died before 24 August 1328.<ref name=MCA1/><ref name=CP2/> \n\n==Sources==\n<references/>\nSee also:\n* [[Space:Stirling_Roll|The Stirling Roll of Arms, c. 1304]]* For additional information about early baronies, see the top-level category page [[:Category: Early English Feudal Baronies|Early English Feudal Baronies]]. Chief Justice and Keeper of the King's forest North of Trent, Sheriff of Yorkshire, Constable of York and Scarborough Castles, son and heir, adult by 1260 (minor at his father's death). \nHe is thought to have been one of the inspirations for the legend of Robin Hood. <ref>Pilling, David, (2020), ''Rebellion Against Henry III: The Disinherited Montfortians, 1265–1274''. Pen and Sword History. [https://books.google.de/books?id=ZPjtDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT186&dq=Earl+Ranulf+III+D%27Eyville&hl=en&newbks=1&newbks_redir=0&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwi58ZyTtLuLAxWJ7LsIHVG2AUcQ6AF6BAgGEAM#v=onepage&q=Earl%20Ranulf%20III%20D'Eyville&f=false Google Books. ] Accessed 11 Feb 2025.</ref>\n\n===Life===\nIn 1267-8 his cousin, William de Percy, sued him for the advowson of Catton, Yorkshire. \nHe married (1st) before 5 Feb 1275/6 (date of pardon for marrying without license) MAUD ____, widow of James de Audley (died 1273), of Audley, Staffordshire. They had two sons, John, Knt., and Thomas. <ref>Douglas Richardson, Plantagenet Ancestry: 2nd Edition, Vol. II, p. 1.</ref>\nIn 1257 he was the overlord of 60 acres in Scheg-Hawe or Scheghawe, Nottingham, for which John de Lessington had done homage to him, until the latter's death in that year.<ref>Great Britain. Public Record Office, Kirby, J. L.; White, Andrew Dickson, (1904), ''Calendar of inquisitions post mortem and other analogous documents preserved in the Public Record Office'', London: Printed for H.M. Stafford, which James d. shortly before 7 Nov. 1273 (j).  He m., 2ndly, Alice.<ref>https://groups.google.com/d/msg/soc.genealogy.medieval/VGcP6mIxMLA/QJN5oLDZPxcJ</ref>\nFollowing the death of Simon de Montfort, he became one of the most active leaders of the disinherited barons. He occupied the Isle of Axholme in 1265 with Simon de Montfort the young. He was the leader of those who took Lincoln and seized the Isle of Ely in 1266, after which they plundered Norwich and Cambridge.  :'''313.''''' Writ to the sheriff of Lincoln to enquire by the oath of upright and law-abiding men who were not against the king during the disturbances, and in the presence of Walter de Escures, Geoffrey son of Ralph de Bradele, and Robert of Kyrketon in Lyndese, if they wish to be present, whether the said Walter, Geoffrey, and Robert were with Baldwin Wake and '''John Deyvill''' at the sack (''depredacionem'') of Lincoln and the assault on the castle, or with the said John at other plunderings or burnings, or with the king’s enemies at Ely or elsewhere during the disturbances; and if so, to extend their lands.''<ref name=\"Cal. of Inquisitions Misc.\">Great Britain. Public Record Office, (1916), ''Calendar of inquisitions miscellaneous, Chancery, preserved in the Public Record Office, Vol.1'' (pp.107, 260, 284, 300), prepared under the superintendence of the Deputy Keeper of the Records. London H.M. Stationery Office [https://archive.org/details/calendarofinquis01lond/page/106/mode/2up?q=Deyvill Internet Archive.] Accessed 17 Feb 2025.  </ref>\n\nHis lands:''were seized in Landeford by Sir William de Grey after the battle of Evesham and before the Exaltation of the Cross because he was keeper in the county of York by the appointment of the barons. The lands, &c. are worth 4 marks. Sir William de Grey received 2 6d. in Michaelmas rent.''<ref name=\"Cal. of Inquisitions Misc.\"/>\n\nHe was pardoned in 1267. \nIn 1274/5, he arraigned a jury against the Prior of Newburgh touching common of pasture in Cokewald, Yorkshire.  In the same period he arraigned a jury against the Prior of Newburgh touching common of pasture in Selclif, Yorkshire.  In the same period de Lungilers arraigned an assize of novel disseisin against him and others touching a tenement in Egmanton, Nottinghamshire, and the same against him and others touching a tenement in Barlborough, Nottinghamshire. \nIn the same period Richard Bolax arraigned an assize of novel disseisin against him and others touching a tenement in Egmanton, Nottinghamshire.  In the same career he arraigned an assize of mort d'ancestor against John de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, touching the manor of Greetwell, Lincolnshire.  \nIn 1275-6 he arraigned a jury against the Prior of Newburgh touching common in pasture in Kilburn, Yorkshire.  In the same period, William le Noble and Clemence his wife arraigned an assize of novel disseisin against him and others touching a tenement in Egmanton, Nottinghamshire.  \nIn 1276-7 Clemence de Lungvilers arraigned an assize of novel disseisin against him and others touching a tenement in Barnbrough, Yorkshire.  \nHe was with the King in Wales in 1282.  He served as a banneret in King Edward I' s household. \nIn 1288, he presided over an inquisition. <ref>Great Britain.       "notes": "[[Category: Battle of Evesham]]\n==Biography==\"He was a rich knight from a well-connected midlands family. His date of birth is unknown, but it was probably no later than 1230, since his son was active politically in 1265. He succeeded his father, Ralph, on the latter's death between 1255 and 1257, inheriting five manors in Staffordshire (including Drayton, by which name he is usually distinguished), Leicestershire, Nottinghamshire, and Dorset, worth something over £100 p.a. The impressive aisled hall at Drayton Basset may well date from his era. He married, presumably before c.1245, Margaret, daughter of Roger de Somery of Dudley, Worcestershire, an heiress in her own right through her mother, Nichola d'Aubigny. Although Basset is normally described as a baronial leader, there is no evidence linking him as such with Simon de Montfort until after the battle of Lewes. Between 1257 and 1262 he answered several military summons of the king, but in the early summer of 1263 he joined the anarchic rebellion of Roger Leyburn, Roger Clifford, Hamo L'Estrange, and other knights expelled from the Lord Edward's household. \" <ref> Oxford Dictionary of National Biography </ref>\n\nChildren:\n* Ralph Basset* [possible] Roger Basset<ref name=\"Wrottesley1903\">Wrottesley, G. History of the family of Wrottesley of Wrottesley, co. Stafford. 1903, pp 62-63 [https://archive.org/details/historyoffamilyo00wrot/page/62/mode/2up Internet Archive]. </ref>\nHe was killed at the battle of Evesham on 4 August 1265; his death (as a knight-banneret) was noted by several chroniclers, but Rishanger's story that Basset, Hugh Despenser, and others refused Montfort's offer to escape before the battle seems apocryphal. Although, after Evesham, Basset's manors were granted to royalists-Roger Clifford, Robert de Tibetot, Robert of Tattershall, and William Bagot-they were quickly restored to his widow, Margaret, and his heir, Ralph, as a reward for Roger de Somery's services to the king. Margaret remarried about 1270; her new husband was another midlands knight, Ralph of Cromwell (d. 1289); she became a nun in 1293. <ref> Oxford Dictionary of National Biography </ref>\n\n== Research Notes ==\"Lord of Drayton, co. He fell, however, before the close of the same year, at the battle of Evesham. Maud, m. to John, Lord Grey deWilton.\" - Burke's \"Dormant and Extinct Peerages,\" 1883. Ralph descends from Thurston the Norman who founded the family soon after the Conquest.       "notes": "== Biography ==\nJoan de Peyver, daughter and coheir of Thomas LE Esquire, a Justice, who was the widow of Sir Paulin Peyvere. She had writ for dower dated 15 June. In August she obtained custody of the lands and marriage of the heirs for 500 marks. This marriage she sold for that sum to Sir John DE GREY (of Shirland), father of the first Lord Grey of Wilton, he undertaking to discharger her of any fine to the king; whereupon John married the son to his own daughter.\nIt is suggested that the king had given her in marriage (as a widow) to one Stephen de Salines, and that she, by the advice of her friends in London, matched herself to John de Grey and she married him, presumably as his 3rd wife, before 17 October 1251.\n\ni) m: Sir Paul 'Paulin Peyvere' Peyver 1215-1251 See Below\tSon of Roger Peyvere; Bishop of Salisbury and his concubine Maud de Ramsbury\n\nChildren: John Peyvre 1237-1267\n          William Peyver 1240-\n\nii) JOHN SIR de GREY 1202-1266\n\nchild: Hawise (Helewise)1255-1343 m: Ralph Basset\n SIR PAULIN PEYVERE, was put in possession, in January 1226/7, of land in Chesham, Bucks, as heir of his brother Lawrence, whose wife was Emma de Pinkeny. He obtained a footing at Court, and served the King in numerous responsible positions till his death.\n\nIn 1237 he was a collector in Beds of the Aid granted to the King. From 1238 to 1244 he was keeper of the Bishopric of Winchester during the vacancy; sheriff of Beds and Bucks, 1239-41. In 1242 he was attorney for the King in a case before the Council; and in 1250, as Paulin Peyvre the elder, a justice before whom a fine was levied. In 1242 he was also charged with the provision of ships for the expedition to Poitou, where he followed the King. He was the King's steward in 1245, and in 1249 \"Master Paulin, the King's buyer.\" In that year he was fellow justice with the Bishop of Salisbury to partition the lands of William Marshal, late Earl of Pembroke.\nHe married Joan, daughter and coheir of Thomas LE ESQUIER, a Justice. He died early in June 1251, in London, and was buried there (a). His widow had writ for dower 15 June. In August she obtained custody of the lands and marriage of the heirs for 500 marks. This marriage she sold for that sum to Sir John DE GREY (of Shirland), father of the first Lord Grey of Wilton, and she married Sir John, presumably as his 3rd wife, before 17 October following.\nShe died at Layham, Suffolk, in 1256, and was buried at Woburn. \n(b) His heart was taken to Toddington, resting one night on the way at St. Albans Abbey, of which, as well as of Oseney Abbey and Dunstable Priory, he was a benefactor. His arms are given by Paris, who records his epitaph, as silver, on a chevron gules 3 fleurs de lys gold. He left a younger son William, to whom he gave the manor of Thorpe (Market), Norfolk.\nPaulin is placed as son of Roger, the 1st known Peyvre but this is not proven\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />* Verified from the Genealogy worksheets compiled by [[Pryor-355 | Ralph Pryor]] during his 40 years of research, traveling extensively in the military and in retirement. [[Clare-696|Isabel de Clare]], married in 1257 \"[[Montferrat-18|Guglielmo]] (or William) VII, Marquis [Marchese] of Monferrato\"<ref name=mcaI460 /># [[Clare-114|Margaret de Clare]], married in 1272 \"[[Plantagenet-40|Edmund of Cornwall]] (usually styled Edmund of Almain), Knt.\"<ref name=mcaI460 /># [[Clare-341|Rose de Clare]], married [[Mowbray-39|Roger de Mowbray]], Knt.<ref name=mcaI460 />\n# Eglantine de Clare, married<ref name=mcaI460 />\n\n: by an unnamed mistress:\n# Guy (or Gaudin)\n\n'''Knighthood & Pilgrimage''' \nIn 1244-1245, Richard de Clare \"engaged in an expedition against the Welsh... and was knighted by the king in London in 1245.\"<ref name=mcaI460 />\nIn April 1248, Richard de Clare, earl of Gloucester, [[Beauchamp-265|Thomas de Bello Campo]], Walter de Scoteny, Roger de Clifford, William de Clare and Nicholas de Leuekenor, received a letter of protection with clause ''rolumus'', until a fortnight after Midsummer, to go on a pilgrimage beyond seas.<ref name=\"PatentsHenIIIp12\">Assistant Keeper of HM Public Records, ed., ''Calendar of the Patent Rolls Preserved in the Public Record Office,'' Henry III 1247-1258, (London: His Majesty's Stationery Office, 1908), [https://archive.org/stream/patentrollsreig00unkngoog#page/n24/mode/2up page 12] (accessed 10 October 2014).</ref><ref>Possibly the Nicholas de Leuekenor listed is represented by [[Lewknor-90|this profile]]. It is likely that the William de Clare listed is Richard's [[Clare-309|brother William]], who is probably also the William who died of poisoning in 1258 (which Richard survived).</ref>\n\n'''Poisoning'''\n\"In July 1258 he fell ill, being poisoned with his brother, as it was supposed, by his steward, Walter de Scotenay. He recovered, with the loss of his hair and nails, but his brother died.\" When Richard died four years later, it was \"rumored that he had been poisoned at the table of Peter of Savoy, the Queen's uncle\".<ref name=mcaI460 />\n\n'''Death and Burial''' \nRichard de Clare '''died''' at Ashenfield in Walham, Kent in July 1262 (on the 15th, 16th, or 22nd). On the following Monday, \"his body was taken to the Cathedral Church of Christ at Canterbury, where his entrails were buried before the altar of St. Edward the Confessor; the body was forthwith taken to the Collegiate Church of Tonbridge, Kent, where his heart was buried; and thence the body was finally borne to Tewkesbury, Gloucestershire, and buried there in the choir at Tewkesbury Abbey at his father's right hand 28 July 1262.\n \n== Sources ==\n<references />\nSee also:* ''[[Space:Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem|Calendar of Inquisitions Post Mortem and Other Analogous Documents preserved in the Public Record Office]]'' (H.M. Kimball G. Everingham, (Salt Lake City, Utah: the author, 2013), Vol V, p 238, VERDUN #8</ref><ref name=\"CP5\">The Complete Peerage. Vol V. Eardley to Goojerat. 1926, FitzJohn p.437. [https://archive.org/stream/CokayneG.E.TheCompletePeerageSecondEditionVolume5EAGO/Cokayne%2C%20G.%20E.%20-%20The%20Complete%20Peerage%2C%20Second%20Edition%2C%20Volume%205%20%28EA-GO%29#page/n231/mode/1up] </ref>\n\nLord of Kirtling,\nSheriff Co. York (1233-1234, 1234 - 1236) \nJusticiar of Ireland  1245 - 1256\nSeneschal of Gascony  1243\nChief Justice of the Southern Forests 1241 - 1242\nSheriff of Gloucestershire 1238 - 1246\n\nArms:  Quarterly or and gules a border vair.\nSeal of John Fitz Geoffrey dated 13th century  A shield of arms: quarterly, a label of (five?) points.\n1 Sep 1242 - ''The king has granted to John fitz Geoffrey the marriage of the sons and heirs of John de Vieuxpont by the fine of 200 m. that he made with him for this, and he has also granted that he may render 50 m. per annum of the aforesaid fine at the Exchequer, namely 25 m. at the Exchequer of Michaelmas in the twenty-seventh year, 25 m. at the Exchequer of Easter in the twenty-eighth year and 50 m. thus from year to year at the same terms until he has paid the aforesaid 200 m. to the king.'' (Ref: Henry III Fine Rolls Project: Fine Roll 26/573 & 27/52)\nHe did homage to the king on 3 June 1227, whereby for a fine of 300 marks,  he had livery of a portion of his father's lands, of which his half-brother, William, Earl of Essex, had died seized. Geoffrey fitz Peter had intended these to be extensive, for King John had granted to him and his heirs from his marriage with Aveline the castle and honour of Berkhamsted. This grant, however, never came to fruition, and Berkhamsted, after Geoffrey's death, remained in the hands of the king. Thus, with the earldom of Essex passing to the descendants of Geoffrey's first marriage, John had to make do with such manors as Aylesbury and Steeple Claydon in Buckinghamshire, Exning in Suffolk, and Cherhill and Winterslow in Wiltshire, the last the only part of the honour of Berkhamsted that he obtained. John was a substantial magnate but, in terms of land held in hereditary right, not one of the first rank. Probably this situation, and the example of his father, who had risen in the king's service from humble origins to the earldom of Essex, was the spur to his long career in the royal administration.\nMarried, as her second husband, Isabel le Bigod, widow of Gilbert de Lacy of Ewyas Lacy, daughter of Hugh le Bigod, 5th Earl of Norfolk, & his wife, Maud Marshal of Pembroke.\nThe sources which report the parentage of the wife of Gilbert de Lacy are conflicting. A manuscript which narrates the descents of the founders of Lanthony Abbey records that “Gilbertus de Lacy” married “Isabellæ Mareschal”[519], presumably confusing her with Isabel daughter of William Marshal Earl of Pembroke who married firstly Gilbert de Clare Earl of Gloucester and Hereford and secondly Richard Earl of Cornwall. The Chronicle of Tintern Abbey, Monmouthshire names \"Isabella soror Johannis\" as daughter of ”Rogerus sive Radulphus Bigod, secundus filius Hugonis le Bigod com. Norfolke et Suffolke…” and his wife “Bertam de Fornivale”, adding that she married firstly \"Gilberto de Lacy\" and secondly \"Johanni Fitz-Geffrey\"[520]. This must also be incorrect, as any children of Ralph Bigod could not have been born before the late 1220s at the earliest, which is inconsistent with the timing of Isabel´s first marriage. If Isabel was a member of the Bigod family, she must have been the daughter of Hugh and Maud Marshal of Pembroke. This is the solution adopted by the Complete Peerage[521], although the primary source on which this is based has not yet been identified.\n\nJohn FitzGeoffrey and his wife had six children:\ni) Lord FitzJohn, Sir Richard FitzJohn of Shere (-1297).m as her first husband, EMMA, daughter of --- (-1332). She married secondly Robert de Mohaut of Mold.\n\nii) Lord FitzJohn, Sir John FitzJohn of Shere (-1275). \n\niii) William FitzJohn (c 1234-1270)\niv) MAUD (-16/18 Apr 1301, bur 7 May 1301 Worcester, Friars Minor).  m firstly Gerard de Furnivalle Lord of Hallamshire (-1261). m secondly William de Beauchamp Earl of Warwick, son of William de Beauchamp of Elmley, Worcestershire and his wife Isabel Mauduit ([1237/41]-Elmley 5 or 9 Jun 1298, bur 22 Jun 1298 Worcester, Friars Minor).\nv) AVELINE (c 1242-20 May 1274], bur Dunmow Priory). m Earl of Ulster, Walter de Burgh, son of Richard de Burgh Lord of Connaught (c 1198-1243) and his wife Egidia (Gille) de Lacy of Meath (c 1198-Galway Castle 28 Jul 1271). He was created Earl of Ulster in [1264].\nvi) ISABEL (c 1236).  m Sir Robert de Vespont, Lord of Westmoreland (-1264).\nvii) JOAN (c 1248-1303), fourth & youngest daughter, married Thebaud BUTLER IV. \nJohn fitz Geoffrey was evidently a man of considerable parts, respected both by his fellow magnates and by the king. Indeed, despite his role in the revolution of 1258, when Henry III heard of John's death he ordered a solemn mass to be celebrated for his soul and donated a cloth of gold to cover his coffin. John was succeeded by his son, John fitz John, who became a leading supporter of Simon de Montfort.\n\nPlace of Burial: Stanlaw Abbey, Cheshire\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n* ''Royal Ancestry'' (2013), Douglas Richardson, Vol. II. p. 179* ''Magna Carta Ancestry'' (2011) 2nd ed., Douglas Richardson, Vol. IV p. 245-249 (also the 2005 edition)\n* ''Oxford Dictionary of National Biography''* ''Foundation for Medieval Genealogy'' (http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/ENGLISH%20NOBILITY%20MEDIEVAL1.htm#JohnFitzGeoffreydied1258)\n* http://www.oxforddnb.com/\n* [http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fitzgeoffrey Wikipedia page].* [http://knight-france.com/geneal/names/2724.htm Knight family] (website by Patrick R.       "notes": "[[Category:Early Barony of Flamstead]]\n== Biography == \n\"Roger de Tony, of Flamstead, Hertfordshire, Brinkley, Kirtling, Long Stanton, and Whittlesford, Cambridgeshire, Bliston, Carnonton (in Mawgan), and Helston, Cornwall, Walthamstow, Essex, Monnington and Winforton, Hereforedshire, Garsington, Oxfordshire, Painstscastle, Radnorshire, Stratford Tony, Wiltshire, Elmkey Lovett, Worcestershire, etc., 2nd but 1st surviving son and heir.\" <ref name=\"ra2013\">Douglas Richardson. ''Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families,'' 5 vols, ed. Kimball G. Everingham (Salt Lake City: the author, 2013), volume V, pages 174-175 TONY 8.</ref>\n\n===Names===\n\n: Roger de Tony\n: Roger de Toeni\n: Roger de Tosney\n\n: Name:  Roger (Ralph) De Tonee (Toeni)\n:: Surname:  Tonee (Toeni)\n:: Given Name:  Roger (Ralph) De\n\n===Birth and Parentage===\nRoger was born about 29 Sept 1235 (minor in 1251, came of age in 1256). <ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n~1230, Alice born in England, daughter of Humphrey de Bohun and Maud de Eu.\n9/29/1235, Roger de Toeni born in England, heir & 2nd son of Baron Ralph de Tosny and  Pernel de Lacy.\n1239, Roger’s father Ralph de Tony, Knt., died at sea on his way to the Holy Land.<ref name=\"raV173\">Richardson, ''Royal Ancestry,'' V:173 TONY 7.</ref>\n\nRoger became a ward to Humphrey de Bohun.\n\n===1239 Marriage to Alice de Bohun===\nHe married by agreement dated  30 June 1239 Alice de Bohun, daughter of Humphrey de Bohun, Knt, Earl of Hereford and Essex, by his first wife, Maud, daughter of Raoul (or Ralph) d'Exoudun (or d'Issoudun), Count of Eu.  Her maritagium included the manors of Newton Tony and East Coulston, Wiltshire.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n6/30/1239, agreement for Alice to marry Roger de Tony, Baron of Flamstead, Hertfordshire.\n\n===1242 Queen Eleanor Assumes Custody of Roger's Lands===:4/26/1242, Grant to Queen Eleanor of the custody, during the minority of the heir, of the lands of Ralph de Tony, to receive in her wardrobe all the issues thereof, with the wards and escheats belonging thereto.<ref>Epistolae: Women’s Biography, Eleanor of Provence. </ref>\n:10/15/1242, the Earl of Hereford & Wessex was ordered to deliver Paincastle to Roger, who held it by knight’s service.{{Citation Needed}}\n:6/20/1251, Memorandum … the Earl [H. de Boun, Earl of Essex and Hereford] … keep during the minority of Roger son and heir of Ralph de Thoeny. When he comes of age the Earl will restore it [Painscastle] to the king to surrender to the heir.<ref name=\"cpr\">(S) CPRs. </ref>\n\n===Issue ===\nThey had one son, Ralph, Knt, and one daughter, Alice.  His wife, Alice, was living in 1255.  At her death, she was buried in Llanthony Abbey outside Gloucester.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n4/26/1242, Grant to Queen Eleanor of the custody, during the minority of the heir, of the lands of Ralph de Tony, to receive in her wardrobe all the issues thereof, with the wards and escheats belonging thereto. (S) Epistolae: Women’s Biography, Eleanor of Provence.\n10/15/1242, the earl of Hereford & Wessex was ordered to deliver Paincastle to Roger, who held it by knight’s service.\n6/20/1251, Memorandum … the Earl [H. de Boun, Earl of Essex and Hereford] … keep during the minority of Roger son and heir of Ralph de Thoeny, when he comes of age the Earl will restore it [Painscastle] to the king to surrender to the heir. <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\n\n1254, Roger married Alice.\n\n1255, Alice living.\n\n===1255 Marriage to Isabel===\nHe married (2nd) after 1255 Isabel.  By an uncertain wife, he also had a son, Geoffrey.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\nRoger married 2nd Isabel ?. [1 son, Geoffrey.]\n1261, Roger, son of Ralph de Tony, grants the manor of Itton, alias South Tawton, to Moyhon in marriage. <ref> Devon Notes and Queries, Amery, 1905, P123</ref>\n\n===1256  Hunting===\n10/21/1255, Grant … the king’s gift by reason of his wardship of the lands of Roger de Thoney. <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\n12/8/1256, Roger had license to hunt in multiple counties with his own dogs, the hare, the fox, the cat and the badger. <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\nIn 1256 Roger had license to hunt with his own dogs the hare, fox, cat, and badger in Cos. Southampton, Somerset, Dorset, and Wilts.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\n===Public Activity===\n10/15/1256, Mandate to William de Sancto Omero and Pernell de Thoeny his wife to restore to Roger de Thony, son and heir of Ralph de Thony, who is of full age and has done homage … his lands, charters, … in the keeping of the said Pernell. <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\n10/1257, Roger went to Wales with Edward the king’s son and was among those asked to meet the king in London with all the service they owed.\n6/28/1258, Commission of oyer … touching trespasses and excesses committed against Roger de Mortuo Mari … in the parts of Wales by Roger de Thony, <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\n~1259, Grant of Roger, son of Ralph of Tony to William of Mohun, son of the Lord of Mohun. Marriage of William and Juliana, Roger's relation Premises: £10.13s. annual rent in the manor of South Tawton. <ref name=\"ukna\">(S) UKNA. </ref>\n10/28/1259, Of those who are crossing with the king to France and have protection … Roger de Thony, the elder … (S) CPRs. [French King Louis and Queen Margaret hosted a family Christmas gathering in Paris that included King Henry III and Queen Eleanor. Margaret and Eleanor were sisters.]\n1260, Roger patron of Brinkley church. <ref> Brinkley, A History of the County of Cambridge and the Isle of Ely, V6, 1978.  </ref>\n\n===1261  Law Suit===\nIn 1260-1 Robert Stocumbe and Joan his wife sued Roger de Tony and others for two-thirds of the manor of Elmley, Worcestershire which they claimed as Joan's dower and the rest in compensation for the stewardship for a third part of Roger's lands.  Roger pleased that Joan merely held the manor as custodian of Henry son of Henry Lovet.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\n===1262  Presentation to Church===\nIn 1262 he presented to the church in South Tawton, Devon.  He was crossing with the Queen beyond seas in 1262.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\n===1262  Action against Llywelyn===\nHe was summoned to be at Hereford Feb 1262/3 for action against llywelyn.  He adhered to King Henry III against the Barons.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\n===1262  Transactions with Sir Ralph de Arundel===\n1/27/1264, “Receipt of homage, and remission of rent. Roger de Tony, lord of Karneton = (1). Sir Ralph de Arundel = (2). Receipt by (1) of the homage of (2) for 1/2 acre of land in Retthelec.” <ref name=\"ukna\"/>\n\n===1264 Death===\nRoger de Tony died shortly before 12 May 1264.  In 1264 his castle of Kirtling, Cambridgeshire was committed by the barons during pleasure to Henry de Hastings.  \n\n===1264 Public Record of widow Isabel===\nIn 1264 the inhabitants of Flamstead, Hertfordshire complained to the king of the oppression of his widow, isabel, who had exacted from them services to which they had been unaccustomed.  About 1270, on the king's instructions, she remitted and quitclaimed to Randulf de Arundel 8d. rent in Reshelec (in Roche), Cornwall which she claimed during her widowhood.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n5/12/1264, Grant to Edmund the king’s son of the wardship of the castles and lands of Roger de Tony, tenant in chief, … dowers when they fall in … Humphrey de Bohun, earl of Hereford, the marriage of the heirs … to Isabel, late the wife of the said Roger her dower, … the said Edmund of the marriage of the said Isabel, or the fine which she will make for the same. <ref name=\"cpr\"/>\n1264, “Roger de Tony alias de Thony: Wales: Painscastle with the appurtenant honour; Devon: South Tawton manor with advowson; Norfolk: Necton manor; Necton, Little Fransham, Little Cressingham, Westacre, Godwick, Sparham, Bodney, Shingham, Downham, Gutland, Hales, Little Fransham, Great Cressingham, Little Cressingham, Wrotham, North Wrotham; [Essex]: Walthamstow manor; Hertfordshire: Flamstead manor” died. <ref name=\"ukna\"/> <ref>Inquisition Post Mortem</ref> \n\n2/1265, Isabel living.\n~1270, Quitclaim of rent Isabel who was wife of Roger de Thony. Randulf de Arundel. Remission and quitclaim by Isabel of 8d rent in Reshelec which she had claimed during her widowhood on the king's instruction (per preceptum domini regis), to Randulf and his heirs for ever; rent [henceforth] 1d or a pair of white gloves yearly. <ref name=\"ukna\"/>\n\n===Issue of Roger and Alice===\n#[[Toeni-7|Ralph de Tony, Knt]] born 1255 in England.<ref name=\"ra2013\"/>#[[Toeni-51|Alice de Tony]] born ~1260 in England.  Married Walter Beauchamp, Knt., of Alcester, Warwickshire.  <ref name=\"ra2013\"/>\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\n\n* Complete Peerage, 12i. p.769-771.\n*Sanders, English Baronies, pp.117-8.* Richardson, Douglas.       "notes": "[[Category: Battle of Evesham]][[Category:Early Barony of Wigmore]]\n== Biography ==Sir Roger de Mortimer was a famous and honoured knight from Wigmore Castle in Herefordshire, and a loyal ally of King Henry III of England. He was at times an enemy, at times an ally, of the Welsh prince, Llywelyn the Last. \nRoger was the son and heir of [[Mortimer-662|Ralph de Mortimer]] and [[ferch Llywelyn-6|Gladys]] (Gladusa) Duy (or Dark-eyed), daughter of Llewelyn ap Jorworth, by his second wife, Joan (the illegitimate daughter of King John), and widow of Reynold de Braose (d. June 1228). Roger was likely born at his father's castle of Cwmaron. He was a minor when his father died on 6 Aug 1246 and had \"livery of his inheritance\" on 26 Feb 1246/7. In 1253, he was made a knight by the King at Winchester. Roger served in Gascony in 1253 and 1254.<ref name=\"CP\"/>\nIn 1255/56 Roger went to war with his cousin, Llywelyn ap Gruffydd, when the latter invaded his lordship of Gwrtheyrnion or Rhayader. This war would continue intermittently until the death of both Roger and Llywelyn in 1282. They were both grandsons of Llywelyn ab Iorwerth. \nFrom 1255 to 1264, Roger was \"chiefly occupied with his duties on the March\" in opposition to Llywelyn. He was involved in the disputes between the King and the Barons in 1258, at first siding with the Barons, but by Apr 1259, he had been \"sworn of the Kings Council\".  On 19 May 1260 the Council of Magnates appointed Sir Roger Mortimer constable of Hereford Castle. Roger arrived in London to attend Council on 17 July 1260, the same day Llewelyn’s army took Builth Castle, which Roger had held as custodian for Prince Edward.<ref name=\"CP\"/>\nMortimer fought for the King against the rebel Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester, and almost lost his life in 1264 at the Battle of Lewes fighting Simon de Montfort's men. In 1265 Mortimer helped rescue Prince Edward and they made an alliance against de Montfort. \nIn August 1265, de Montfort's army was surrounded by the River Avon on three sides, and Prince Edward's army on the fourth. Mortimer had sent his men to block the only possible escape route, at the Bengeworth bridge. The Battle of Evesham began in earnest. Montfort's Welsh soldiers broke and ran for the bridge, where they were slaughtered by Mortimer's men. Mortimer himself killed Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester.\nRoger was rewarded for his efforts at Evesham, receiving grants of land including the \"county and honour\" of Oxford, or more specifically, the lands forfeited by Robert de Vere. In Sep 1265 Roger was at the Parliament at Winchester and was sheriff of Herefordshire from 1266-1267. In Aug 1270, Roger was named one of the trustees for Prince Edward’s estates while the Prince traveled to the Holy Lands on Crusade.<ref name=\"CP\"/>\nRoger Mortimer died shortly before 30 Oct 1282, at Kingsland, Herefordshire, aged about 50, and was buried at Wigmore Abbey, Wigmore, Herefordshire, England<ref name=\"CP\"/> where his tombstone read:<blockquote>Here lies buried, glittering with praise, Roger the pure, Roger Mortimer the second, called Lord of Wigmore by those who held him dear. While he lived all Wales feared his power, and given as a gift to him all Wales remained his. It knew his campaigns, he subjected it to torment.</blockquote><br>\n\n=== Immediate Family ===*Son of Ralph de Mortimer, Baron of Wigmore and Gwladus verch Llewelyn, daughter of Llewelyn ab Iorwerth, Princess of North Wales (Gwladys Ddu).*Brother of Peter de Mortimer; Hugh de Mortimer; John de Mortimer and Joan de Mortimer.\n*Half brother of Maud la Zouche.\n\n===Marriage===:Roger married circa 1247 to [[Braose-8|Maud de Braose]], Lady Mortimer, Baroness Wigmore. She was the eldest daughter and coheir of William de Braose, by Eve, sister and coheir of Richard Marshal, Earl of Pembroke, Marshal of England.<ref name=\"CP\">Doubleday, H.A. and Lord Howard de Walden, ed., ''The  Complete  Peerage or A History of the House of Lords and All Its Members From The Earliest Times'', London: The St Catherine Press, 1936. Accessed online at [https://dcms.lds.org/delivery/DeliveryManagerServlet?dps_pid=IE4496737 LDS], Vol. IX, pp. 276-281.</ref>  Maud was born c 1230 in Bramber Castle (or Arundel), England and she died before 20 Mar 1301.\n\n=== Children ===#Ralph Mortimer, (abt 1250 – bef 10 Aug 1274). A famed knight, but died in his youth, unmarried, s.p.#Edmund Mortimer, 2nd Lord Mortimer (1251- 17 Jul 1304). Edmund was recalled from Oxford University when his older brother Ralph died, and was made heir. Edmund married Margaret de Fiennes, the daughter of William II de Fiennes and Blanche de Brienne. Had issue, including Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March.#Isabella Mortimer, (c. 1248 - 1292). She married first 1260 John FitzAlan, 7th Earl of Arundel, (14 Sep 1246 - 18 Mar 1272). She married second Robert de Hastings.#Margaret Mortimer, (d. 1297). She married Robert de Vere, 6th Earl of Oxford.#Roger de Mortimer, (c. 1256 - 3 Aug 1326). He lived in Wigmore, Herefordshire, England.#Geoffrey de Mortimer, (b. c 1254). He lived in Wigmore, Herefordshire, England.#William Mortimer, (b. c 1258 - 1297). He lived in Wigmore, Herefordshire, England.\n\n== Sources ==\n<references />\nSee also:\n* Royal Ancestry 2013 Douglas Richardson Vol. IV. p. 166-168.\n* Royal Ancestry 2013 Douglas Richardson Vol. I page 557.*Brendan Smith, \"Transnational Lordship and the Plantagenet Empire: The Mortimer Lords of Wigmore, 1247-1425\".       "notes": "[[Category:Hiberno-Normans, Irish Nobility]] [[Category:Ireland, Governors]]\n\n== Biography ==\nGeoffrey de Geneville, Seigneur de Vaucouleurs (Meuse, arr. [https://maps.app.goo.gl/cjEbXaVwbWzHZkTJ9 Commercy]) in Champagne, France was born about or after 1226 <ref name=RICHARDSON>[Richardson, Douglas. Royal Ancestry: A Study in Colonial and Medieval Families, Vol. V (2013) pp. 239-241]</ref>.\nHe was the son of [[Joinville-3|Simon de Joinville]] and his 2nd. wife, [[Bourgogne-163|Beatrice Bourgogne]] daughter of [[Bourgogne-202|Etienne Bourgogne]], count of Burgundy and Auxonne. <ref name=DIB>[Mackay, Ronan in Dictionary of Irish Biography (rev 2009) Geneville (Joinville), Geoffrey de]</ref>\nHe was in France, as lord of [https://maps.app.goo.gl/CjS3g6r3d5mkhbUx7 Vaucouleurs] until 1252, when he went to England in the company of Peter of Savoy, his brother-in-law, and uncle of the queen of England, Eleanor of Provence <ref name=DIB/>\nIn that same year, 1252, before August, he married [[Lacy-216|Matilda (Maud) de Lacy]], the younger daughter of [[Lacy-217|Gilbert de Lacy]] and co-heir, with her sister [[Lacy-178|Margaret / Margery de Lacy]], of [[Lacy-279|Walter de Lacy]], Lord of Meath; Maud was the widow of [[Geneva-54|Peter de Genevre]] (d. 1249)\n(In right of his wife) he held Ludlow, Shropshire, and Drogheda and Blathagh' Castles in Ireland. <ref name=RICHARDSON/>\nOn 18 Sep 1254 King Henry III granted to Geoffrey, and Maud his wife, and her heirs, all the liberties and free customs in Meath, which Walter de Lacy, grandfather of Maud, had held, and that they might issue their own writs in Meath, according to the law and custom of Ireland. On 21 Sep following, they had livery of the castle of Trim and a moiety of 40 marcates of land, as the inheritance of Maud. <ref name=DIB/>\nIn 1255, Geoffrey was in Gascony with Edward, the King's son, and by charter dated 10 Jun 1260, he partitioned the barony of [https://maps.app.goo.gl/aPqh68V4zUYrhGig7 Weobley], Herefordhire with [[Butler-2695|John Butler de Verdun]] husband of Maud's elder sister Margery. <ref name=DIB/>\nIt seems he first visited Ireland in 1262 and  led a raid against the Irish  Ó Fearghail clan of Annaly ( now approximated [https://maps.app.goo.gl/v4Ym8FFk3jPZV3wf6 co. Longford] <ref name=DIB/>\nIn 1272 he was summoned by the King of France against the Count of Foix. He was in the Holy Land with Edward I, but returned before him.\nMade Justiciar of Ireland Sep 1273, which office he held until Jun 1276. and in 1207 he became King's Marshall <ref name=DIB/>\nIn 1283, he and his wife gave all their lands in England and Wales to their son, Piers, and in 1290 he was sent on a mission to the Pope to arrange matters for the aid of the Holy Land. \nFrom 1295 - 1297 Geoffrey de Geneville was constable of [Athlone Castle Athlone Castle] <ref>[https://www.academia.edu/37734184/Constables_of_Athlone_Castle O’Brien, Niall, C.J; Constables of Athlone Castle  in Co. Roscommon Historical and Archaeological Society Journal, Vol. 13 (2016) Journal page 122 - 128]</ref>\nHe was one of the commissioners sent to Rome in 1300 to negotiate concerning peace between England and France. \nHe was summoned to Parliament from 6 Feb 1298/99 to 3 Nov 1306, whereby he became Lord Geneville. In Dec 1307, he obtained license to surrender to Roger de Mortimer and Joan, his wife (granddaughter of Geoffrey) the lands and tenements in Ireland which he held by the courtesy after the death of his wife Maud, and which at his death would revert to the same Roger and Joan, Joan being heir of Maud. \n\nHis wife Maud, died 11 April 1304.<ref name=RICHARDSON>\nIn 1307 he obtained license to surrender to Roger de Mortimer and Joan his wife (granddaughter of Geoffrey) the lands and tenements in Ireland which he held by the courtesy after the death of Maud (de Lacy) his wife. He subsequently retired to the House of the Friars Preachers in Trim. \nIn late 1308, Roger and Joan took seizin of Meath, and Geoffrey entered the House of the Friars Preachers at [https://maps.app.goo.gl/HNMtvHzkV4wziDj36 Trim], co. Meath.\nSir Geoffrey de Geneville, Lord Geneville,  died 21 October 1314, and was buried at Friars Preachers<ref>[http://www.geneajourney.com/genvll.html The Geneville page at geneajourney.com]</ref>\nNote. Friars Preachers in Trim, co. Meath, Ireland, was also known as Black Friars Priory, Trim. It was dissolved in the 1530s by Henry VIII in the Dissolution of the Monasteries. \n\nIssue <ref name=DIB/> + {Citatio Needed}\n# [[Geneville-23|Geoffrey de Geneville]]# Sir [[Geneville-1|Piers / Peter de Geneville]] Knt.,  m.       "notes": "[[Category: Royal Mistresses]]\n== Biography ==\n\n===Mistress of Friederich II, Holy Roman Emperor===Bianca Lancia belonged to an illustrious family that had moved from Piedmont when the aristocracy had to give space to the development of the \"Comuni\" (free municipalities) to search fortune and opportunities in the South of Italy . Later their name in the South become \"Lanza\".  Bianca, likely born in 1210 when the family had already moved, at the age of only 16 in 1226 become mistress of the Emperor and remained such for 20 years. Frederich had just married Jolande of Brienne that at 13 was immature and quite unattractive.  She gave Birth to  Costanza and Manfredi (the favourite of Frederich 18 children) and, may be, Violante. Around 1256/7 she fell ill . As the third wife of Frederich, Isabel Plantagenet, had also died, he married her  \"in capitulo mortis\"  and legitimised the children.  This his confirmed by the fact  that Manfredi in a document dated 1246 is still mentioned as \"Manfredus Lancea\", while in his father will dated1250, he is entitled to the castle of monte S.Angelo from her mother dowry. From a rule established since the time of the Altavilla, this castle had to be in the dowry of all the queens of Sicily.For political reasons the Pope refused to aknowledge the marriage because in the frame of the fight between the Popes and Empire, he wanted Manfredi to remain an \"usurper\" to better support his own candidate Charles of Anjou.Federico II and Bianca gave origin to a lot of legends and popular novels/poetry in the South of Italy.\n\n==Sources==\n<references/>\n* '''Royal Ancestry by D. Richardson Vol. IV p. 553''' \n* http://fmg.ac/Projects/MedLands/SICILY.htm#_ftnref676 \n* https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/bianca-lancia/_(Federiciana)/\n* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bianca_Lancia, \nAt both addresses many primary sources are quoted \n \n=== Note ===: Wikipedia: no source definitively states who her parents were, although her grandfather is Manfred I of Lancia; historians have offered three theories:\n* granddau of Manfred I of Lancia, as daur of his dau (maybe named Bianca), by a son (unknown) of Guglielmo di Moncucco and Belda di Agliano.\n* granddau of Manfred I of Lancia, as dau of his son Bonifacio di Agliano by an unknown wife.[1]\n* granddau of Manfred I of Lancia, as daughter of his son Manfred II, possible from a marriage to a lady called Bianca, of the Maletta family.\nIn any case Bonifacio Lancia was an important supporter of Manfredi and in some circumstances acted as his vicar. The Whole family, coming from a different zone with a different political system) gave an important contribution to his reforms aimed to limit the power and independence of the Barons and to introduce  a modern state with a central administration\n\n: Luis Manzano Grant R.
